inline.s: The compiler of this book, Master Kuanlü, styled Foxing, is a native of Zhejiang and now in his eighties. In 1952 he came to Shanghai and took refuge with the Elder Master Xuyun, by whom he was shaved and ordained; afterwards the Elder directed him to take up residence at Nanhua Monastery. At that time Nanhua Monastery had suffered grievous ruin in the Cultural Revolution, and most of its scriptures and books were damaged beyond repair. The Master and six lay devotees of Shanghai made the vow to restore them together, and the work took more than ten months. Afterwards he went to stay at Guanghua Monastery in Putian for two years, and then returned to Shanghai, living for eight years in all at the Jade Buddha Monastery and the Jing’an Monastery. During those eight years the Master gathered the records of the passing of various Buddhists and compiled them into a book; and at the beginning of this year he returned once more to Nanhua Monastery to cultivate in seclusion.

In the middle of June this year I went to the mainland to pay homage at the Four Great Sacred Mountains; afterwards I came to Nanhua Monastery in Guangdong to bow before the golden body of the Sixth Patriarch and repent my former karma. There I had the good fortune to meet the Master, who entrusted this book to me to put in order, that it might serve as a model for later generations. In these days of the latter age, when the stream of Dharma runs thin, when men’s natures are given to doubt and arrogance and their afflictions blaze, the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land is truly the best door of salvation for the world: it gives those who are lost a refuge within the three realms of samsaric suffering, and gives men a direction in this life, so that they do not stray onto wrong roads. This book hopes only that those who cultivate the mind may give rise to faith in the Pure Land and be encouraged by it. May all living beings revere the Pure Land, die well and be reborn there, be received by Amitābha, and realize the Pure Land in their own minds.
Namo Amitayus Buddha
Respectfully recorded by Yuanfan, rustic of a desert isle, at the Haiyin Chan Cloister.
The winter solstice of the dingmao year

Shi Kuanlü, styled Foxing, and known also as the Beggar of Caoxi. His ancestral home was She County in Anhui; the Cheng clan was a great family of Xin’an. In the Jin dynasty Duke Yuantan served as governor of Xin’an and was enfeoffed as Duke Zhongzhang; his descendants multiplied and spread into several thousand households. At the end of the Ming, when the age fell into disorder, his forebears moved to Deqing in western Zhejiang. His grandfather Youqiu was a Grand Master of the Middle Constitution under the Qing; his father Zilian was an assistant prefect of Jiangsu. From childhood Lü received his family’s instruction and read the books of the sages and worthies. At the beginning of Liberation he left home under the Venerable Master Xuyun. Finding no accord in the study of Chan, he devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land; for more than thirty years now he has recited the Buddha’s name in all honesty. In vain has he reached eighty, yet his resolve has not wavered. He has no writings of his own; the ‘Record of Pure Land Rebirths, As Heard on Occasion’ that he gathered was first put into draft by the layman Fan Yuqin of Suzhou, and compiled into a book by the layman Yu Wenqin of Zhenhai. The accounts it collects are all true and not false, and from them one sees that in the practice of the latter age it is by relying on the Buddha’s power that one may easily attain realization. ‘If a man but recites Amitābha, this is called the supreme and wondrous Chan.’ Thus Buddha-recitation-samadhi is the king of all samadhis. And how then should Chan and Pure Land be divided? Caoxi is Lü’s ancestral monastery, and the true body of the Sixth Patriarch is there. At the beginning of Liberation, when Lü saw that part of the scriptures and books were damaged, he could not bear to sit by; he called together six monks and nuns, and day and night they copied for some ten months, until the repair was complete. To this day, more than thirty years later, though the Cultural Revolution has passed over it, these scriptures of the Dragon Treasury have survived unharmed together with the flesh-body of the Sixth Patriarch, unworn through the kalpas. This strengthens my faith that the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions who protect the true Dharma lend a hidden aid that is truly inconceivable. The abbot of this monastery, Weiyin, presides over the Chan seat; he merely recites the name of Amitābha Buddha and does not investigate who it is that recites, teaching people only to recite the Buddha’s name as a hen broods on her eggs. His instructions are plain and solid, and he has no fondness for the strange and wonderful; one may say that he has a unique eye. In the middle of the dingmao year it happened that the Venerable Yuanfan came from Singapore to the mountain, and Lü handed over to him the draft of the rebirth record, unprinted for eight years, to carry away and have printed and spread abroad. Rejoicing that the karmic conditions of a former life are thus fulfilled, we shall transform the great chiliocosm into the Land of Lotuses, and the world shall have lasting peace, and we shall be gathered in one place with all the good and virtuous ones. The king of vows is inexhaustible and will surely be accomplished. How gladly I rejoice in it! How gladly I delight in it!
Written on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month of the dingmao year by the Beggar of Caoxi at Nanhua Monastery, in the year he turned eighty.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: all is made by mind alone.’ The Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life likewise instructs us: ‘This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.’ Therefore when the mind is that of a buddha or a bodhisattva, one becomes a buddha or a bodhisattva; when the mind is that of a human being, one becomes human; when the mind is that of a bird or a beast, one becomes a bird or a beast. Long ago Master Lianchi once ascended the seat to perform the yoga of feeding the hungry ghosts, and all who saw him beheld the majestic marks of a Buddha — a clear proof of this. Among the beings of the six paths there are those who, without waiting for the consciousness to be reborn after death, change their form in this very body; the Fayuan Zhulin and the Twenty-Four Histories contain no few such records. All of these come about because their karmic power has ripened, and so they change their form in this very body.

The Pure Land dharma-gate covers all three capacities alike and carries one across the three realms sideways; it is supremely special and transcendent, and inconceivable. Those who devote themselves to its practice, even before they relinquish this karmic body, have already placed their spirits in the lotus flower. Thus Yang Jie and Ma Wei of the Song dynasty, both of whom cultivated the pure karma with diligence, were still alive in the world; yet the wife of the Prince of Jing (the uncle of Emperor Zhezong of Song), the Lady of Yue, traveling in spirit through the Pure Land, had already seen them! The lady and Yang and Ma had never known one another, nor even known of one another’s existence — and still she met them in the Pure Land. Such is the wonder of sympathetic response.

Tracing back to Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin, who founded the White Lotus Society, those who attained rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss have gathered like clouds and raced like the wind; yet of those whose names are recorded in the texts, scarcely one or two in a thousand. Though many attained rebirth, few wrote them down, and the occasional records that were made circulated but rarely. So it is that the fine words and noble deeds of the sages of old have often sunk into oblivion — a great pity. To compile the biographies of those who attained rebirth is not only to honor the sages of old but also to spur on those who come after. This work, then, could not be left undone. In the books compiled by the worthies of old — the Records of Rebirth, the Records of Pure Land Saints and Worthies, and others — the methods of practice and the auspicious signs of rebirth that they set forth are indeed enough to stir us and to spur us on; yet the fragrant footprints they recall were accomplished in ages long past. And in recent times the monks and laity who have gone to the lotus pond tread one upon another’s heels; if they are not gathered up, they will surely be lost and scattered. I have therefore begged the good and faithful of every quarter to collect the accounts of recent rebirths; the layman Fan Yuqin of Suzhou made the first draft, the layman Yu Wenqin of Zhenhai compiled it into a book, and I have once more revised and arranged it. In all we have more than a hundred persons, and the title is given as ‘A Record of Recent Rebirths, As Heard on Occasion.’ As for the old dragons of the sea of teaching and the true lions of the Chan caves — men whose lofty wind covered strange lands and whose Dharma rain fell upon gods and men — if they have no part in the Pure Land, they are not recorded. Thus the biographies of the patriarchs of the Pure Land school do not include Zhiyi, Cien, Qingliang, or Caoxi: it is not that they are not revered, but that the household arrangements of the school are so.

Karma exhausted, one takes leave of the Saha world to wait upon Amitābha in the land of purity; the lotus opens its petals, and one is companion to the good and virtuous in the precious pool. I deeply hope that those of like vow will not grow slack in their first resolve. Seeing the fragrant footprints, let them rouse themselves; spurring on the pure karma, let them advance in practice. To continue and prosper the Buddha-seed, to carry on the marching steps of those before, to hand on the torch of fire so that the lamp of wisdom is not extinguished — this is what the two laymen Yu and Fan and this unworthy one bow their heads and pray for.
In the jiwei year, the 2523rd year of the Buddhist era, written by Chen Hailiang of Tiantai.

This compilation was originally entitled ‘The Fourth Collection of the Records of Pure Land Saints and Worthies’; it has now been renamed ‘A Record of Recent Rebirths, As Heard on Occasion,’ for I dare not be so free with the term. Only those above the first abiding of the Perfect Teaching, or above the first ground of the Separate Teaching, may be called ‘sages’; only those of the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching, or the three worthies of the Separate Teaching, may be called ‘worthies.’ Those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land today, apart from a very few great beings who appear in transformation, are all ordinary people; and the land they are born into is the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together! How could they hastily be called sages and worthies?

The Pure Land dharma-gate covers all three capacities and takes in the whole of the nine realms. Those who practice according to the teaching all attain rebirth. ‘In the Dharma-ending age, though millions upon millions practice, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation does one cross over birth and death.’ Not to speak of ancient times, but of recent times alone: those who attained rebirth by reciting the Buddha’s name are as numerous as rice and hemp and bamboo — beyond all reckoning. What is recorded here is no more than a drop of the great ocean, a speck of dust on Mount Sumeru; it is taken only for what may suffice to urge people onward, so why must all be recorded? Thus there is no fear of the reproach that in grasping one I have let ten thousand slip.

This compilation takes as its purpose the urging of people to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. It shows forth the fragrant tracks of those before and spurs later students to diligent practice, so as to warn the obstinate and awaken the deluded and bring them to advance together in the Way. It is not like composing a eulogy of praise or attaching oneself to a famous name; may every reader understand this purpose.

This compilation takes the exclusive propagation of the Pure Land as its aim. If a person has no part in the Pure Land teaching, then though he be an honored elder of the dharma-gates, a great master of the Chan school, whose Way is spread throughout the world and whose renown weighs upon the heavens, he is not recorded. For the purport of a school may not be mixed and confused; this is not a sectarian view.

The Pure Land reveres only exclusive practice and does not prize mixed practice. Master Shandao said: ‘For the exclusive practitioner, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred; for the mixed practitioner, one or two in a hundred, three or five in a thousand.’ Those who practice both Pure Land and Esoteric, or both Chan and Pure Land, are in principle not recorded. Master Lianchi said: ‘To have a foot on each of two boats is indeed not permissible; but a round and penetrating non-obstruction — why should it not be possible?’ A round and penetrating non-obstruction — how easy is that to speak of! What people today call ‘both’ is the ‘both’ of a foot on each of two boats. Examining their minds, it truly comes of faith that is not firm and a vow that is not keen, and so their practice is not single.

Buddhism regards false speech as a grave precept. To say of one who did not truly attain rebirth that he attained it is to deceive oneself and others, and becomes a great falsehood. This record is compiled to awaken people’s right faith; if I were to commit a great falsehood and so deceive myself and others, it would be better not to have done it at all. Then what was meant to spread the Dharma would turn into slander of the Dharma — how could one fail to be cautious here? Yet this too is difficult!

The principle of sympathetic response has its root in the mind-nature. Thus to see the Buddha in samadhi, or to have a lotus grow from the tongue — such things are recorded in the texts and may be relied on with certainty. Yet one must have practiced diligently at ordinary times, with body and mind both purified, before one can elicit such auspicious signs. If one speaks extravagantly of the miraculous and is infatuated with the strange, one will instead lead practitioners onto a wrong road — this is greatly to be avoided.

Biographies of those who attained rebirth have been compiled by men of the past, and there are already many kinds — why add this volume? It is precisely because what was recorded before concerns only eminent monks, great worthies, wise scholars, and famous men, whose pure wind has grown distant and whose fragrant tracks recede ever further. The deluded therefore say: in the age of the true Dharma many attained the Way; in the age of the semblance Dharma many still understood and awakened, so those who attained rebirth by Buddha-recitation followed heel to heel. But now we are further still from the sages and people’s capacities are duller: even if they cultivate the karma of the Way, few attain anything. Seeing the worthy, they have no mind to equal them; hearing of their example, they lack the will to rouse themselves. Therefore this compilation has been made, to serve as a spur. Among those recorded here, some were our own teachers and friends, some were our own kin; the impression is near at hand and the spur to advance is easy. ‘He was a true man, and so am I; how can I belittle myself and draw back?’ Practitioners of the pure karma, take heart!

Yinguang, whose name was Shengliang, was also known as the Ever-Ashamed Monk. His lay surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Zhaochen Village, Taiyang, Shaanxi. At twenty-one he went to Lianhua Cave Monastery on Mount Zhongnan and received the tonsure from the monk Daochun; it was the seventh year of the Guangxu reign. The next year he received the full precepts at Shuangxi Monastery in Xing’an. Reading Longshu’s Essays on the Pure Land, he came to know that the Pure Land dharma-gate is the essential path to Buddhahood. Hearing that Zifu Monastery on Mount Hongluo was a practice-ground devoted to the Pure Land, he went there, entered the hall and recited the Buddha’s name, cultivating the pure karma diligently. In his spare time he studied the Mahayana scriptures, and so entered deeply into the treasury of the sutras, his wisdom like the sea. In the nineteenth year of Guangxu, the monk Huawen of Fayu Monastery on Mount Putuo went to the capital to request the canon and asked the Master to assist him, and so invited him to come south with him; he then stayed at Fayu Monastery. Twice he sealed himself in retreat, six years in all, and his learning and practice advanced twofold. With the founding of the Republic the Master was fifty-two. Gao Henian saw his writings and published them in the Shanghai Buddhist Review. Xu Weiru then edited and printed them under the title The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, which became popular at home and abroad. The Master led people by the Pure Land dharma-gate, with special attention to sincerity and reverence. He said: ‘The Pure Land dharma-gate covers all three capacities and takes in both the sharp and the dull; it is the great dharma by which the Tathagata universally provides for all, sages above and ordinary beings below, enabling them to end birth and death in this very life. Not to believe it and not to practice it — is that not lamentable! This dharma-gate takes faith, vow, and practice as its three essentials: by faith, one believes that this world is suffering and that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is bliss; one believes that I am an ordinary being of karmic power, who certainly cannot rely on my own strength to cut off delusion, realize the truth, and escape birth and death; and one believes that Amitābha Buddha has made great vows, so that if there are beings who recite his name and seek birth in his Buddha-land, then at the end of their lives the Buddha will surely extend compassion and receive them, causing them to be born in the West. By vow, one vows quickly to leave this world of suffering and quickly to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. By practice, one sincerely and earnestly constantly recites ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha,’ never for a moment forgetting it. Morning and evening one bows and recites before the Buddha, setting up a daily course according to whether one is busy or at leisure. Beyond this, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and while doing tasks that need no thought, one may recite. When sleeping one should recite silently, not aloud, and it is best to recite only the four characters ‘Amitābha Buddha,’ lest the many characters be hard to recite. If one’s clothes are not in order, or when bathing or relieving oneself, or in unclean places, one must recite silently; silent recitation earns the same merit, while reciting aloud would be improper for the occasion. Whether reciting loudly, softly, in the diamond recitation, or silently in the mind, one must have the mind reciting clearly, the mouth reciting clearly, and the ear hearing clearly. In this way the mind does not run outside, false thoughts gradually cease, and the Buddha-recitation gradually becomes pure — the merit is greatest.’ He also said: ‘I have often said that if one would obtain the benefits of the Buddha-dharma, one must seek them in reverence. With one part of reverence one erases one part of karmic offense and increases one part of blessing and wisdom; with ten parts of reverence one erases ten parts of offense and increases ten parts of blessing and wisdom. If one has no reverence but instead is disrespectful and arrogant, then offenses increase daily and blessing and wisdom decrease the more.’ He also said: ‘The one practice of Buddha-recitation is the simplest and easiest, the broadest and greatest of dharmas. One must be utterly earnest and sincere before one can be in sympathetic accord and obtain real benefit in this life. If one is lazy and slack, with no reverence at all, then though one plants a distant cause, the offense of disrespect is beyond imagining. As for Buddha images, one should look upon them as the true Buddha, not as earth, wood, copper, or iron. The scriptures are the teachers of the Buddhas of the three times, the dharma-body relics of the Tathagata; one should look upon them as the true Buddha, not as paper and ink. Toward scriptures and images one should be as a loyal minister before his sage sovereign, as a filial son reading a parent’s testament: if one can be so, then there is no karmic obstruction that is not dissolved, no blessing and wisdom that is not increased.’ He also said: ‘Sincerity and reverence — these words are known to all the world, and this way is dark to all the world. It is because I sought out the noble examples of the worthies of old that I came to know that sincerity and reverence are in truth the most wondrous secret for transcending the ordinary and entering the sage, for ending birth and death.’ The Master held the principle of cause and effect to be of the utmost importance. From ordinary being up to Buddhahood, nothing lies outside cause and effect, and so he was forever earnestly speaking of it. He once said: ‘Bodhisattvas fear the cause; ordinary beings fear the fruit. The bodhisattva, dreading the evil fruit, cuts off evil causes beforehand, and so his karmic obstructions are dissolved and his merit and virtue perfected. Ordinary beings constantly create evil causes and yet wish to escape the evil fruit; it is like trying to shun one’s shadow while standing in the sun — a vain running about. One often sees ignorant fools who, having done some trifling good, expect a great reward; and when adversity comes they say that doing good brings disaster and that there is no cause and effect; and from there they draw back and regret their first resolve, and even slander the Buddha-dharma. Do they not know the profound truth that retribution reaches through the three times and that transformation comes from the mind? Retribution reaching through the three times means: doing good or evil now and receiving blessing or disaster in this life is called present retribution; doing good or evil in this life and receiving blessing or disaster in the next is called next-life retribution; doing good or evil in this life and receiving blessing or disaster in the third, the fourth, or the tenth, hundredth, or thousandth life is called later retribution. Later retribution is uncertain in its earliness or lateness. Whatever karma is made, there is certainly nothing that is not repaid. Transformation comes from the mind: suppose a man has committed offenses deserving of falling forever into hell and suffering for long kalpas. If he afterwards gives rise to great shame and remorse, arouses the great bodhi-mind, reforms evil and cultivates good, recites the scriptures and the Buddha’s name, practices himself and transforms others, and seeks birth in the West — then for this reason, in this very life he may be slighted by others, or suffer a little illness, or bear a little poverty and every kind of unpleasantness; and the karma by which he was to fall forever into hell and suffer for long kalpas is at once dissolved, and he may even escape birth and death and transcend the ordinary to enter the sage. What the Diamond Sutra says — “If someone receives and upholds this sutra and is slighted by others, it is because of offenses committed in former lives that he should have fallen into evil paths; but because in this life he is slighted, those former offenses are dissolved, and he shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi” — this is the meaning of transformation coming from the mind.’ A disciple fell ill and worried that he had not recited the Buddha’s name well, and feared he could not attain rebirth. The Master instructed him: ‘If you think that way, you cannot go to the West! What is called reciting well? Know that even ten recitations can attain rebirth; but that you doubt you can attain rebirth — that very thought is itself an obstruction, and you cannot attain rebirth. In the practice of Buddha-recitation the weight lies in faith and vow. So long as faith and vow are true and keen, even though the mind is not yet pure, one may still attain rebirth. It is like the water of rivers and seas: though it cannot be utterly without movement, yet if there is no fierce wind and great wave, then the bright moon at mid-heaven is clearly reflected in it.’

In 1928 the Master left Putuo and lived at Baoguo Monastery in Suzhou. In 1930 he went to Lingyan Mountain. In teaching people to study Buddhism he insisted only on reverence and sincerity, on deep faith in cause and effect, and on reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land. His words were like cloth and grain, not to be done without for a single day. In the tenth lunar month of 1940 he said to the assembly: ‘I am old! The abbotship of Lingyan should not long remain vacant.’ The assembly proposed Miaozhen, and a day was chosen for his installation. The ninth of the eleventh month was first chosen; the Master said, ‘Too late!’ The fourth of the eleventh month was then chosen, and the Master said that on that day ‘I have my own affair.’ Another choice was made, the first of the eleventh month, and the Master said, ‘That will do!’ On the first day the Master himself led the assembled officers in installing Miaozhen. When the ceremony had been performed according to the rite, he showed a slight illness. At half past one in the morning of the fourth day he sat up in bed and said, ‘Reciting the Buddha’s name, one sees the Buddha; I shall certainly be born in the West.’ He called for water to wash his hands, then stood up and said, ‘Amitābha Buddha has come to receive me; I am going!’ and stepped from the edge of the bed to sit in a chair. The attendant said, ‘He is not sitting straight.’ The Master rose again, sat upright, and recited the Buddha’s name in a low voice. When Miaozhen came, the Master charged him: ‘You must maintain the practice-place and spread the Pure Land; do not learn the ways of the great establishments.’ After that he spoke no more, only his lips moving in recitation. It went on until the fifth hour, when, as if entered into samadhi, with a smile on his face, amid the sound of the assembly’s recitation, he passed away peacefully. He was eighty years old and had been a monk for fifty-nine years. At the cremation all thirty-two teeth remained, and several thousand five-colored relics were found; a stupa was built for him at Lingyan. The Master founded the Honghua Society and printed and distributed more than five million volumes of Buddhist books and more than a million Buddha images; his surviving writings, the Collected Writings, run to nearly a million words, and his refuge disciples numbered in the hundreds of thousands. The world honors him as the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school.

Hongyi, whose dharma name was Yanyin, was from Pinghu in Zhejiang. His lay surname was Li and his courtesy name Shutong. His forebears had carried on the salt trade in Tianjin, and so the family took up residence there. In his early years he studied in Japan, specializing in music and fine arts. After returning home he taught at the Beiyang Higher Industrial College and directed the editorial policy of the Shanghai Pacific Times. He then accepted a post at the Zhejiang Normal School, where he directed the teaching of music and painting for seven years. In 1918 he left home at Hupao Monastery in Hangzhou, at the age of thirty-nine. He received the full precepts at Lingyin. Grieved that the study of the Vinaya had long declined, he made the vow to spread the Vinaya and to continue and prosper the seed of the Sangha. He made it his constant aim to spread the precepts in life and to return to the Land of Peace in death. In expounding the Dharma he sought only what was practical, stressing cause and effect and prizing no abstruse talk. In ‘Dream Shadows of Ten Years in Southern Fujian’ he said: ‘The basic principle of Buddhism is deep faith in the truth of the retribution of good and evil causes. Good deeds bring good reward, evil deeds bring evil reward. One must also deeply believe in the spiritual responses of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Though the truth of the retribution of good and evil causes and the spiritual responses of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas is easy to understand, those who can thoroughly believe it are few. This so-called faith is not faith spoken with the mouth, but faith held truly within the mind. This principle, so easy to understand, is not easy to believe with true firmness. In my view one must at all costs deeply believe in the retribution of good and evil causes and in the spiritual responses of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; only then does one have the qualifications of a Buddhist. Know that good deeds bring good reward and evil deeds bring evil reward; this karmic retribution is not the least bit off. Know too that every deed of ours, every movement, even every arising of a thought, is seen clearly by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. If a person can believe this with utter certainty, his character and morals will naturally rise day by day.’

The Master always urged people to practice the Pure Land exclusively, and once taught: ‘The Buddha spoke of many dharma-gates, deep and shallow, difficult and easy, each different. If the dharma-gate one practices does not accord with one’s capacity, one puts in much effort and reaps little. If it accords with one’s capacity, one puts in little effort and reaps much. With which dharma-gate do the capacities of most living beings best accord? When all is said, only the Pure Land school. If one devotes oneself exclusively to the Pure Land dharma-gate, then relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, one is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, and quickly realizes bodhi — this is much easier.’ His exposition of the Dharma was like a family member speaking to his own, understandable to all. His life’s work was concentrated on spreading the Vinaya. His greatest work was The Table of the Precepts and Marks of the Bhiksu of the Four-Part Vinaya, which took five years to complete. His writings, several dozen in all, were gathered as The Nanshan Vinaya Garden Series. The Master was thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist texts, his practice according with his understanding, yet he always regarded himself as insufficient. In writing and speaking he transmitted but did not create. He lived in southern Fujian for a very long time.

On the fourth day of the ninth month of 1942 he passed away at Kaiyuan Monastery in Quanzhou, Fujian. At the point of death he wrote to Xia Mianzun to take leave of him, appending two verses to the letter: ‘The bond of noble friends is plain, / as water, free of gloss or stain. / To seek it by a sign, a trace, / makes of one foot a thousand-league space.’ ‘You ask me whither I shall fare — / in boundless hush, no words to spare. / The flowering bough with spring is crowned; / at heaven’s heart the moon rides round.’ At the cremation some eighteen hundred relics were found, red and white and brilliant, round and smooth and dazzling. He was sixty-four, and had been a monk for twenty-four years.

Xingci, whose name was Wuyun, was styled Guanyue and also Zhanfengzi. His lay surname was Chen, and he was a native of Xinchang in Zhejiang. His family for generations practiced Confucian learning and reverently believed in the Three Jewels. From his grandfather and father down, eight members of the family in all left home one after another. When Ci was four his mother left home to become a nun under the name Changguang. His elder sister, then eight, also left home, taking her mother as her teacher and receiving the name Mianchi. His father Zhaoshan entered Fangguang Monastery on Mount Tiantai and became a monk. Before his father left home he had gone to Tiantai to pray before the Sangharama for a son, and at night dreamed of a young child sitting cross-legged on his knee; overjoyed, he embraced it. A year later Ci was born — it was the xinsi year of the Guangxu reign. In his early years Ci was raised by his mother and grew up in the convent. At seven he went to study with his father in the mountains. At fourteen he left home under his father. The next spring he took the monk Congjing as his teacher and received the full precepts at Guoqing Monastery. Soon after he returned to Shiliang to practice Chan contemplation. At twenty-one, at Zhongfangguang Monastery, he heard Master Tonghuan lecture on the Surangama Sutra, and his wisdom from former lives suddenly broke forth, and he resolved to devote himself to the scriptures and the teachings, without a break through heat and cold for several years. At twenty-seven, invited by Gaoming Monastery, he lectured on the Diamond Sutra, setting forth its wondrous meaning and astonishing the whole assembly, and every honored elder in the mountains praised him. From then on he responded to invitations from all quarters, spreading the scriptures and lecturing widely, so that his Dharma seats covered the whole southeast. In turn he lectured on the Surangama, Lotus, Ksitigarbha, and Amitābha sutras. In 1913 he returned to Tiantai and restored the Zhongfangguang and Xiafangguang monasteries. In 1918 he founded the Fazang Lecture Monastery in Shanghai, establishing a study society and creating a practice-place. In teaching he spread the Tiantai school; in practice he devoted himself to the Pure Land. He strictly drew up the monastery rules and had them carved in stone so that they might be handed down far into the future. And to make it convenient for the sons of Shanghai to study, he planned and established the Xingci Middle School, guiding the world and pitying all creatures, attentive to the smallest detail.

In 1931, at the invitation of the elders of the Tiantai monasteries, he took charge of Huading Monastery and restored its affairs on a grand scale. Unfortunately the war came and the work was not fully completed. For thirty years he spread the school and expounded the teaching, and his Dharma connections were exceedingly abundant. He taught without wearying, and those who took refuge under him numbered no less than several hundred thousand. He was strict with himself and usually reticent, sparing of speech and laughter. Though he lived in a bustling city, he did not change his plain resolve from the mountains. He held to simplicity and detachment, standing firm and apart. Winter and summer he wore one robe; he ate without tasting. He used simplicity to master complexity and virtue to overcome authority. Inwardly he cut off love and hate; outwardly he knew neither kin nor stranger; he did not change his mind for the noble or the base, but met all with an equal compassionate mind. This was rarely seen among the Buddhist circles of Shanghai. He wrote the Combined Explanation of the Two Chanting Services and the Easy-to-Know Commentary on the Diamond Sutra, and had several dozen kinds of ancient commentaries printed and circulated. In the spring of 1950 he showed slight signs of decline, and concerning the unfinished affairs of Huading and Fazang monasteries he charged his disciple Huikai to complete them. On the seventeenth day of the fourth lunar month, knowing his hour had come, he bathed and changed his clothes and sat upright facing west, and amid the sound of the assembly’s recitation he passed away quietly. He was seventy years old. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Huading. A dragon-elephant of his generation, he may still be revered in the depths of the white clouds.

Desen, of the Yang family, was a native of Xingguo in Jiangxi. At thirty-one he left home at Bao’en Monastery in Fujian. He received the full precepts at Dacheng Monastery in Zhantian, Ningdu, Jiangxi. He was sincere and plain by nature. Sen had seen with his own eyes his teacher, the monk Jincai, pass away while seated in Buddha-recitation, and was deeply moved; and so he too recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. All his life he spread the Pure Land, sparing no effort. He would often say: ‘The key to the Buddha-dharma lies only in cutting off evil, cultivating good, and saving living beings. Outside these three things there is no other dharma. When all three are brought to their utmost, one naturally perfects the Buddha-way.’ His refuge disciples were very many, reaching as far as Southeast Asia. He formerly lived at the Fabao Hall in Shanghai. In 1937 he took up residence at Lingyan in Suzhou, sealing himself in retreat in the East Retreat House on the mountain, and for more than twenty years he did not step outside the door. When Master Yinguang founded the Honghua Society to print and distribute Buddhist books, he received much help from him. The gazetteers of the Four Great Sacred Mountains and the three parts of the Records of Pure Land Saints and Worthies were arranged and printed entirely through his effort. A few months before his passing he printed and distributed four thousand copies of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life. At that time paper and printing were both extremely difficult, yet Sen by his perseverance completed the work. In November 1962, a week before his death, he wrote to his disciples: ‘I have not long in this world,’ and arranged all the affairs after his death. At the time he felt a slight illness. On the sixteenth, at the point of death, he had himself propped upright and cried out three times, ‘I shall certainly become a Buddha!’ and passed away peacefully. A rare fragrance filled the room and did not disperse for several days. His body was placed in a seated coffin and his face looked as in life. At the cremation very many relics were found, and his disciples took them back to make offerings. He was eighty, had been a monk for fifty years, and a stupa was built for him at Lingyan.

Huixing was a man of Xixi Huawu in the suburbs of Hangzhou. After the age of twenty he left home at Dachongfu Monastery in Liangzhu. Having received the full precepts, he built himself a thatched hermitage at Huawu and lived there for more than thirty years, never going out the hermitage gate unless there was some matter. Morning and evening he performed the services, without a break through cold and heat, constantly holding to the sacred name of Amitābha. On the morning of the eighth day of the third month in 1924 he said to his disciple Ruimao: ‘I am not well today; bring me a basin of water to wash my feet.’ When he had washed, he sat cross-legged and upright, and passed away reciting the Buddha’s name. He was eighty-six.

Jidong was a native of Anhui, of commanding appearance and bold, generous nature. He had once been a soldier, serving as a regimental commander. Three months after his marriage his wife died. Awakening to the impermanence of the world, he left home. After receiving the full precepts he became abbot of Linggu Monastery in Nanjing. When a powerful man came to visit, the attendant monk prepared new clothes for him and asked him to receive the guest the next day. Dong refused. He went alone to Southeast Asia and took up residence in Penang. People saw that his countenance was ancient and his spirit clear, his samadhi and wisdom beyond the ordinary, his words few but his meaning transcendent, and very many took refuge with him; they built the Jile Monastery for him, and its incense has been abundant. Dong wearied of the commotion and returned to China. With the help of a benefactor he found a hermitage in the Huangshan mountains of Anhui and lived there ten years. Later he planned to revisit Penang, and came to Shanghai to wait for a ship. But because the 9

18 Incident broke out, blocking the way, he lodged at the Shanghai Buddhist Lay Society. In the society a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat was begun, and Dong was asked to give instruction; he lectured on the essential meaning of the Heart Sutra, and all who heard were filled with admiration. One day he said to his friend at the society, Shao Lian’e: ‘Lend me your office to stay in for three days; I am going to be reborn in the Western Pure Land.’ Lian’e did not believe it and asked: ‘Master, are you sure?’ Dong said: ‘I do not deceive you.’ He then had the door locked from the outside and asked that no food be sent for three days, and Lian’e obeyed. On the second day he peeked through the crack of the door and saw that he was still breathing. When he peeked again at four in the afternoon of the third day, he had passed away in the auspicious posture. The next day they felt the crown of his head, and it was as if scorched by fire.

Juezhao was a native of Xianju in Zhejiang, and left home in middle age at Guoqing Monastery on Mount Tiantai. His wife also became a nun. Zhao always wore a torn robe and broken sandals and never troubled to wash, and everyone disliked his slovenliness and kept away from him. He constantly held the Diamond Sutra and recited the Buddha’s name, practicing esoteric disciplines without letting others know, and no one knew of it. He was friendly only with the mountain-watching Dharma friend Yinhuo. When benefactors came to the monastery to feed the monks, he would slip away. One day in the spring of 1938 he brought out the two hundred and fifty-five silver dollars he had saved and gave them to the community for food. He said to people: ‘In three days I shall be gone!’ and gave away an antique teacup, a pair of crystal spectacles, and a sword to his Dharma friends. He shaved his head and bathed, waiting for his passing. He asked the monastery officers for a coffin. Two days later he said to his friends Yukai and Yinhuo: ‘When the fourth board is struck tomorrow morning, come to my room and call me.’ At the hour they came and called. Zhao was wearing his haiqing robe and had donned his kashaya, his cap and shoes in order; a rare fragrance overflowed, and all who saw him were solemn. The two accompanied Zhao at a brisk pace to the great hall, where he joined the assembly in the morning service; when it was done he bowed before all the images of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats in every hall of the monastery, and before the Sangharama he bowed down and did not rise. When they lifted him, he had already passed away. He was seventy-six.

Xiangen was a native of Wenling in Zhejiang. He was illiterate and left home in middle age. At first he was fond of tobacco and wine, but afterwards he purified his conduct of the precepts. He lived at Lingfeng Hermitage on Mount Tiantai. Whenever the great monasteries of Guoqing, Huading, and Gaoming had sutra-chanting or repentance services, they always asked Gen to take part. People knew only that he was skilled in chanting, and did not know that he was a strict cultivator of the pure life. Whenever Gen met anyone, he would say only a single phrase, ‘Amitābha Buddha.’ In the spring of 1939 he suddenly took leave of the monks of the various hermitages in the mountain, saying: ‘I am going to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West.’ It happened that the abbot of Guoqing Monastery, Xianlian, was staying at Biming Hermitage, and asked him: ‘Are you sure of being born in the West? Do not make yourself a laughingstock.’ Gen answered: ‘With one phrase of Amitābha, rebirth in the West is beyond doubt. I packed my bundle long ago; the Buddha will not deceive me.’ At first Gen was forever pacing about in front of the hermitage and behind the mountain; after taking leave he did not go out the hermitage gate, but sat cross-legged all day, reciting the Buddha’s name without cease. On the fifteenth day of the second month a novice monk came to Lingfeng Hermitage and saw Gen outside the hermitage gate, sitting cross-legged facing west, his palms joined at his breast. The hermitage door was locked, and the key was stuck slantwise in the right lapel of his robe. When the novice called, there was no answer and no breath at all; only the crown of his head was still warm. The novice ran about crying out in alarm, and the four assemblies of all the hermitages gathered, praising him with one voice and filled with reverence. He was seventy-five.

Qinglang was a native of Zhongxiang County, Anlu Prefecture, Hubei. His lay surname was Yan. At nineteen he was shaved as a youth of pure body, receiving the dharma name Jixiao. He paid homage at famous mountains everywhere, traveling as far as India to request relics at the stupa of Śākyamuni. Coming to Mount West Tianmu, he took up residence at Chanyuan Monastery and became its first seat, reading the canon for seven years. He built a relic hall to the left of the monastery and lived in the retirement home. In 1931 the assembly elected him abbot, but he declined. Day and night he recited scriptures and sat in meditation. When the four assemblies came to ask for instruction his seat was always full, and none went away without having his wish fulfilled. In 1937, when the war of resistance broke out, the West Zhejiang Administrative Office was set up in the monastery, and Lang moved to the upper Luo family of Fengling Township, asking Luo Youxiang to build him a hermitage. Lang was versed in both the Chan and the doctrinal schools, and perfectly clear in nature and characteristics, but he took the Pure Land as his final refuge. His practice was lofty and his eloquence unobstructed, and he was the great good knowing one of West Zhejiang since the founding of the Republic. He wrote the Explanation of the Verses on the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses and Random Notes from Reading the Canon. In the spring of 1944 his refuge disciples Shi Youyan and Fang Youzhuang came together to pay their respects, and Lang foretold that he would pass away at noon on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month of that year. When the day came he had them bring a brush and composed a verse: ‘This going is no common road; / both body and mind have both let go. / The pure light’s mercy holds me fast — / this very moment is the West.’ At the exact hour of noon he asked for recitation to aid him, faced west, and passed away sitting cross-legged. His body was soft as cotton, and the crown of his head was still warm a day and a night later. He was seventy-one. A stupa was built for him beside the Great Tree King on Mount West Tianmu.

Chengzhou was of the Jin family of Huanggang, Raoping, Guangdong, and lost his father young. When he was a little older he conceived the will to leave the world and kept the precept against killing. Again and again he asked his mother to let him leave home, and she consented on condition that he support her to the end of her life. In the spring of 1935, when his mother’s funeral rites were completed, he sailed to Dieshi Rock in Nan’ao and asked the monk Chuanji to let him shave his head. The monk Ji saw that Zhou was sincere and plain and able to endure hardship, and in the autumn of the following year had him shaved. In the eleventh month of winter he went to Kaiyuan Monastery in Chaozhou to receive the full precepts. In the first month of spring in 1937 he returned south to Dieshi Rock. Gathering firewood, drawing water, cooking, and pounding rice he took on himself alone, and for several years never slackened in the least. In his spare time he sat cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name. Whatever was given him he offered to the Buddha, or else distributed to the poor and suffering. He kept no money, and his clothes were patched a hundred times over; though his life was hard, it was sweet to him. All his life he did not speak falsely, was free of greed, and was never troubled by illness. He once said to people: ‘Those who leave home do so for the sake of birth and death. I am dull-witted and ashamed that I cannot benefit others. But my longing for the Land of Peace is keen; to attain rebirth is enough!’ In the mid-autumn of the gengchen year he went from Dieshi Rock to Huanggang to nurse the monk Ji in his illness. For a full month he did not lay his side to a mat. On the ninth day of the ninth month the monk Ji passed away to the West, and Zhou too fell ill from accumulated toil, and it was more than a month before he recovered. He deeply awakened to the suffering of the Saha world, and his vow for rebirth in the West became keener still; each day he recited the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times. In the renwu year he made the vow to make pilgrimage to Caoxi and Nanhua and to place himself under Chan Master Xuyun for a year. The Master, seeing his honesty, made him hall master; twice he was appointed and twice he declined, and when pressed he asked to serve as night watchman. So it was for more than a year. The lamp oil he received he offered entirely before the Buddha’s lamp, not daring to keep a single drop for himself. His fellow practitioners held him in high regard. At the end of spring in the bingwu year he returned from Shaoguan to Kaiyuan Monastery, and on the way caught a slight chill. After arriving in Chaozhou, though his illness was grave, he still recited the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times a day without cease. One evening at the beginning of the last month of summer he saw Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva appear three times, and knew that his hour for rebirth in the West had come, and recited the Buddha’s name with even greater effort. He said to Hongjia, whom he knew well: ‘I beg you to invite the assembled masters on the morning of the thirteenth to recite the Buddha’s name and aid my rebirth.’ When pressed again and again, he told of what he had seen that evening and warned him not to reveal it. He then arranged all he had: besides what was needed for his rebirth, every needle and thread he gave away to the assembly to form karmic bonds. He also wrote a verse: ‘Twelve years within the gate, / I ever bowed to Amitābha. / Now the karma is fulfilled: / I go to see Amitābha.’ When the day came, at seven in the morning the assembly gathered in Zhou’s room to recite in aid. Zhou rose and sat cross-legged, his spirit radiant, as if he had no illness at all. When some congratulated him on his rebirth in the West, he would join his palms in thanks and agree with the assembly to meet in the West. At noon he still took food. Toward evening he suddenly gazed toward the west and said that Avalokiteshvara had come. He recited the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara aloud, and the assembly joined him. After about the time of a meal he bowed to the assembly and said: ‘Zhou is going!’ and passed away sitting upright. At eight in the evening he was placed in the coffin; his limbs were soft and the crown of his head still warm. It was the thirteenth day of the sixth month of 1946. He was thirty-seven, and had been a monk for ten years.

Song Yue, given name Renhe, was a native of Tongcheng, Anhui. He received the tonsure beneath the seat of Nengfa at Nanquan Pagoda in Guichi County of his own province. In the spring of 1929 he went to Baohua Mountain in Nanjing to receive the precepts. Afterwards he wandered about in search of learning, and journeyed to Tiantong, where he drew near to Yuanying and practiced meditation, but found no accord. Admiring the Buddha-recitation practice-ground at Lingyan, he came to the mountain in the first month of 1933. The abbot Miaozhen permitted him to enter the hall for Buddha-recitation. Before long he was instructed to take charge of the incense lamp of the Ruyi Quarters and to look after the sick monks. Yue did not refuse toil, and strove diligently in his service. Whoever entered the quarters to recuperate, whether near or distant, thick or thin, he treated all alike and attended to them with great care. Seeing those in financial difficulty, when the sum was large he would devise means for them; when small, he gave of his own accord. When he met patients soiled and unclean, he washed them one by one. If he saw the illness grave and hopeless, he would from time to time instruct and encourage them, so they would let go of all attachments and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. If the mind were clouded and they knew not how to recite, he would from the side go on calling the sacred name to aid them. Sometimes the patients were many, and Yue would wait upon them day and night without leisure for sleep, so that both his eyes turned red, yet he still did not rest. In the summer a long drought dried the temple wells, and Yue would daily draw water from elsewhere to supply the community. While carrying the water, he recited the Buddha’s name as he walked. Miaozhen, mindful that he had labored long and that he suffered from a lung ailment, in the first month of 1946 asked him to serve as the chief clerk and bade him rest and cultivate in quiet, without joining the community in its duties. Yue accordingly recited the Buddha’s name silently, praying for an early rebirth. In the ninth and tenth months of the old calendar he told the sealed-cultivation monk Liaoran that he was about to be reborn. By the eleventh day of the eleventh month, he again took leave of Liaoran, saying, ‘Having seen you today, I fear we shall meet no more; at most I shall remain another seven days.’ All his possessions he had arranged and distributed. On the sixteenth day a fellow devotee came to ask after his illness and offered him noodles. Yue tasted a little and said, ‘This is my last meal.’ Asked, ‘Do you suffer any pain?’ he answered, ‘No.’ ‘Can you recite the Buddha’s name?’ he replied, ‘Clearly and distinctly. Tomorrow is the Buddha’s birthday; I shall be reborn.’ Asked, ‘Have you any assurance?’ he answered, ‘I myself know. When the breath of the former thought breaks, the latter thought is born.’ He added, ‘Effort must be made in ordinary times. Like a set clock, close and continuous, never interrupted. With deep faith and earnest vows, at death one is certain to be reborn in the Land of Bliss.’ On the morning of the seventeenth day, Cihai, the keeper of the storehouse, arrived. Yue pressed his palms together and said, ‘Today I am reborn; we shall meet again in the West.’ He added, ‘The abbot has gone out and will not return today; I will not wait longer. Please convey my thanks to him on my behalf.’ Then he lay on his right side and spoke no more; in a little while he passed away peacefully. At the moment of his death he could still open his mouth to recite the Buddha’s name. He had usually had much phlegm, but at the end there was none at all. The next day he was placed in the shrine, his lips had turned red, his countenance was a living smile, his hands and feet were soft, and his skin was smooth and lustrous beyond the ordinary. He was forty-six in age and seventeen years in the monastic life.

Jie Chen, secular surname Qiu, style name Diwu, was a native of Hanchuan, Hubei, and left home to become a monk at nineteen. He formed a bond of meditation companionship with Master Xuyun, dwelling in a thatched hut on Mount Zhongnan, with his heart resting in the joy of meditation. He once fell ill. Dreaming that ceaselessly he recited the Rebirth Mantra, he suddenly saw the thatched hut all turned to gold, and light shone everywhere. When he woke, his illness wholly vanished, and he knew then that his affinity lay in the Pure Land, and so he devoted himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. At the end of the Guangxu reign of the Qing, he went to Mount Jizu in Yunnan and entered a three-year retreat, practicing the Pratyutpanna samadhi until both his feet were swollen, yet he persisted without giving way. Soon he went to Hangzhou and entered the Avatamsaka College, penetrating deeply into its teaching. He wrote the ‘Drop of the Avatamsaka’ and the ‘Diagram of the Five Weeks and Four Divisions, Seven Places and Nine Assemblies of the Avatamsaka.’ He further went to Foyuan Temple in Changshu and entered a three-year retreat, firmly resolved upon the Pure Land karma. He compiled works such as the ‘Clear Instruction of the Lotus Society’ and the ‘Essential Words of the Pure Land School.’ Returning to Yunnan, he established the Pure Karma Lotus Society. Chen was of a solid and sincere nature, strict in the rules of the precepts, and thoroughly versed in the scriptural canon. Whoever came to seek guidance, his answers always gave them satisfaction. Those who took refuge in him numbered tens of thousands. The ancient Qiongzhu temple in that region had long fallen into ruin. Chen became abbot and led the community in labor, without ever declining hardship, until the temple was renovated anew. Soon he went to Yunqi (in Yunnan) to lecture on the Four-Part Vinaya. One morning as he rose early he suddenly fell, and so lay ill. His attendant brought him gruel, but Chen said, ‘The sun is already past noon. I have observed the precepts for decades; how could I break them at the very last? You should at once assist me with the recitation.’ By evening his breath gradually grew faint, and he passed into stillness. The time was the twenty-first day of the fifth month of 1948, and his age was seventy. Placed in the shrine, his countenance was as though living. Seven days later he was cremated; the fourfold assembly gathered together, and the sound of the Buddha-recitation shook the mountain valley. When the firewood was spent, more than a hundred relics were obtained and stored, by his last instruction, within the Haihui Pagoda.

Ming Da, a native of Huzhou, Zhejiang, left home at eighteen to become a monk at Haichao Temple in Hangzhou. He wandered among the famous mountains and visited good-knowing teachers. Through the introduction of Wang Yiting, he took up lodging in the Transformation Furnace at the Dharma Storehouse Temple in Shanghai. Inspired by the keeper of the furnace, Manyue, he set his mind wholly upon Buddha-recitation. In 1949, when Da was already a great age of eighty, he suddenly said to people, ‘I am about to be gone,’ but they answered him carelessly. After breakfast on the twenty-third day of the eighth month, he bade farewell to Manyue and his fellow cultivators, saying, ‘I am going away!’ They asked, ‘Where are you going?’ He answered, ‘To the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West.’ They all said, ‘Say not such a thing! You are as healthy as ever, without the slightest ailment; how can you go?’ Da replied, ‘My karmic retribution is exhausted; when I wish to go, I go.’ And to Manyue he said, ‘I thank you, Master, for awakening me to the Buddha-recitation. That I now attain rebirth is your gift. I have four silver dollars to meet the needs of my cremation after death; now I give them to you.’ Manyue said, ‘This matter is in my charge; do not worry. But since I left home, I have never yet witnessed anyone attain rebirth. Today I am fortunate to meet with you, Master — this may be called a karmic affinity. I only pray that you will return to the Sahā world and universally deliver sentient beings.’ Da said, ‘Yes!’ Then again he told Manyue, ‘There is a refuge disciple surnamed Cao who has gone to the Great World; pray, Master, summon him quickly, for if he is late we shall not catch sight of him.’ Manyue then raced by car to fetch Cao, who arrived only when Da had already sat cross-legged, palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name, about to pass away. Seeing Cao come, he nodded and smiled, and so passed away.

Nian Xing, a native of Xiangtan, left home while still a child. He once made a pilgrimage to pay reverence to Master Yinguang at Putuo. Every day he recited the Diamond Sutra. In the intervals of meditating he studied the great Mahāyāna sutras such as the Brahma Net Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Sutra, and the Lotus Sutra. He dwelt at Tiantong for more than fifty years, lodging in the idle quarters and silently cultivating together with his companions. He delved into the Vinaya division, and his pure conduct was lofty and undefiled. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of 1950, knowing that his worldly affinity was drawing to its end, he bade the incense-lamp keeper to invite Changxiu, and gave him the copy of the ‘Transmission of the Precepts Liturgy’ that he treasured, telling him that next spring he would return home, and asking him to distribute on his behalf the robes and articles he left behind to form karmic bonds. On the fourth day of the new year he felt slightly unwell. In the afternoon he again had Changxiu come, and asked on what day Changxiu would descend the mountain. Changxiu answered that it would be about the eighth or ninth. He then kept Changxiu to remain until after the twelfth day before going. On the night of the eleventh, Changxiu again came to enquire; Xing urged him to do his utmost to maintain the monastery. And he said, ‘At the second watch of the night I shall be reborn in the Pure Land.’ At midnight Xing asked the assembly to assist him in reciting the sacred name of Amitābha, and calmly donned his robe and sat upon the bed. Exactly at the second watch, he passed away with a smile, and a warm vapor rose from the crown of his head. He was eighty-two years of age.

Dao Cong, chief clerk of Tiantong Temple in Ningbo, was a native of Fujian. At the end of the Qing dynasty he went to Tiantong to seek the precepts. At that time Master Jichan was abbot, stern and severe in his blows and shouts. Cong served as his attendant and attained considerable insight. He then remained at the temple to study and cultivate, and went nowhere else. In guarding and maintaining the monastery he revealed a wholehearted sincerity. For scores of years, whatever he received by way of offerings he gave entirely to the community. In his daily practice he recited the Great Compassion Mantra, the Lotus Sutra, and the sacred name of Amitābha most diligently. In the early winter of 1951, at sixty-nine, he knew that his bodily strength was failing and his worldly affinity near its end. On the night of the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month he went to the quarters of his fellow cultivator Changxiu to ask leave and to entrust to him his affairs after death. The next day, which was the Beginning of Winter, he again sent word and invited his fellow cultivator Hai’an, and face to face entrusted to him the arrangements with Changxiu for his cremation and the distribution of his relics to form karmic bonds, and he bade farewell to each of his fellow practitioners. He then lay quietly awaiting his end. By the morning of the first day of the eleventh month, when the fourth board sounded, he rose, washed, and burned incense and bowed to the Buddha, then displayed the auspicious lion’s posture, lying on his right side. He asked the assembly to assist him in the recitation, and after about an hour passed away peacefully.

Jin Da, a native of Hubei, lived at Tiantong in Ningbo for more than thirty years. He was strenuous and industrious, and in daily life not a single word passed from him. In the winter of 1951 he caught a slight cold, asked leave for three days, and in his own quarters applied himself diligently to the Buddha-recitation. On the third day, as the setting sun was about to sink, he took leave of the community with deep affection, and sitting at ease passed away. He was seventy-two in age.

Hong Lin, a native of Shandong, lived at Tiantong Temple in Ningbo for more than twenty years and held the various posts in turn. Morning and evening he followed the community and never failed the chanting of the liturgy. Through the night he sat in stillness, his side never touching the mat. In his later years he applied himself with even greater vigor. After the Liberation he helped to organize production and took the lead in labor. At the beginning of the eleventh month of 1952 he chanced to catch a chill, and his food grew less. In his illness he sat cross-legged and would not lie down. A week later, at midnight, he straightened his robes and sat upright facing the West, and with a smile bade farewell to his friends, passing away peacefully in rebirth. He was fifty-nine.

Bian He, surname Xie, was a native of Xinjin County, Sichuan. He was not quite four chǐ in height, of bizarre ugliness, with limpid blue eyes and lame feet, so that walking was hard for him. His garments were tattered and his whole body was covered with dust and grime. From childhood both his parents had died. In 1912, at twenty-four, he went to the Elder’s Plain on Mount Emei and took the tonsure under Master Puxiong. After two years he received the full precepts, and from then on he traveled on foot to pay homage at the four great mountains. In 1926 he reached Shanghai, where he served as keeper of the incense lamp for many years at Baohua Temple in Dachang and at Haihui Temple in the southern city. After 1942 he dwelt within the Transformation Furnace at the Dharma Storehouse Temple, Number 765, South Zhongshan First Road, and there lived in seclusion, cultivating in quiet. In ordinary life he disliked to talk, and all day long he held the vast name of Amitābha Buddha and recited the sacred names of the Seven Tathāgatas without pause. He delighted in waiting upon sick monks, without shrinking from toil or loathing the foul. Every night he took part in the Mount Meng food-offering. In 1954 he was sixty-six. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month of that year he suddenly bathed and changed his robes, shaved his head and donned his cassock, and told Manyue, the caretaker of the Transformation Furnace, ‘Before long I must leave the temple and go elsewhere.’ By the second day of the fourth month he again arranged his robes and respectfully took leave of Manyue, and brought out the savings of a lifetime, asking him to hold a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat. He also invited in advance seven fellow practitioners he knew well to take part in the Dharma assembly. The remainder of the money he gave to supply the food of Mount Wutai and of Tiantong Temple, and to provide gruel and rice to the community at both the Dharma Storehouse Temple and the Diamond (Vajra) Practice-Ground. All his robes and articles he divided and gave to others, arranging every matter with the greatest care. On the morning of the fourteenth day of the fourth month he again said to Manyue, ‘In three days I am determined to go.’ He then cleaned his robes and his quarters. And indeed on the eighteenth day of the fourth month, at half past eleven in the morning, he passed into rebirth. Everything was as usual, without any pain of illness. Just before his death he gave a great ho ho laugh, and passed away freely.

Zhao Ci, born in the Lǚ family at Nanxiang, Shanghai, was by nature open-handed in giving. Even as a child he could share his fruit and sweets with the neighboring children. As he grew up, whenever he met relatives or friends in difficulty he would open his purse and help them, without the least look of reluctance. At sixteen he took up a trade in a certain transport firm. At twenty-six he was promoted to be the head of that firm. The next year, the shop owner’s son died at the prime of life; in his last moments he cried out in a shrill and pitiable voice, and all who heard were saddened to the heart. Moved by this, Ci turned his mind to the question of life and death. It happened that Master Yinguang was then spreading the Dharma in Shanghai, and Ci heard the Pure Land teaching and was filled with joy, rejoicing greatly. He then made the resolve to hold the name and seek rebirth in the West. Whenever he met relatives or friends, he urged upon them the Pure Land method. At twenty-six he married; after six years his wife died of illness, and because there were no children to be a burden, he abandoned business and left home to become a monk. Alone he went to Hangzhou. First he went to the Ladle Stone at Chenghuang Mountain, and in the end he settled at the Fushou Nunnery on Mount Ziyin, where he practiced exclusively the Pure Land karma, right down to the Liberation. During this time he drew in good people to cultivate the Pure Land together, and many turned to his teaching, his Dharma affinity being exceedingly flourishing. From February 1974 his stomach no longer took food; he suffered from dropsy, grew thin as a skeleton, his limbs ached, and he needed constant massage. It went on to the early autumn, when he could take neither rice nor wheat, but only fluids. On the day he passed into stillness, he suddenly discharged the congealed accumulations, and the dropsy of his whole body vanished at once. That day was the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month of the lunar calendar, exactly the birthday of Kṣitigarbha. That night at nine fifty-five he passed into rebirth. Five minutes before he relinquished his body, his disciples held up the image of the Three Sages for him to behold, aiding him to press his palms together in reverence. Afterwards he used all his remaining strength to move the prayer beads, silently holding the sacred name. After his death, his countenance was as in life, and his limbs were soft. In his daily life Ci always exhorted people to cut off evil and cultivate goodness; besides the Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth, he especially valued the release of life. The creatures he released ran to tens of millions. The strength of his study of Buddhism lay in his earnest, unsullied, and diligent sincerity. Even when ill, his mind was clear, and he would from time to time expound the essential Dharma to those who visited him. Right up to his final moments he taught without weariness, and was ever praised by his many disciples.

Liao Yuan, secular surname Chen, was a native of Huanggang County, Hubei. He had once been a Taoist wearing the yellow cap, but soon realized that this teaching was not final, and at nineteen left home to become a monk. His father, seeing his son renounce the world, also left the homelife; in daily life he followed the community in the sitting meditation, and silently recited the Buddha’s name; and at the end, knowing the time beforehand, with no pain of illness and going about his work as usual, he passed away peacefully in sitting posture. Yuan, seeing that his father had practiced the Buddha-recitation diligently and had such a destination, was deeply moved. For this reason he prayed earnestly and held the name, and made it his constant rule to recite ten or twenty thousand each day. He had traveled on foot to visit the four great mountains, and to such places as Zhongnan and Tiantai. Later he went to Putuo to pay his respects to the elder Yinguang, asking for instruction in the essential teaching of Chan and the Pure Land. Yuan had deep attainments in both meditation and doctrine, yet he set his heart upon the Pure Land. He successively served for more than ten years as first-seat of Gaomin Temple in Yangzhou, and as abbot of Lingshan Temple and Longhua Temple in Shanghai. In such places as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou, and Changzhou he propagated the Dharma for more than thirty years. After the Liberation he lived in Shanghai. He once lectured on such great Mahāyāna sutras as the Śūraṅgama Sutra and the Amitābha Sutra, and the rain of the Dharma was shed over the two provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, so that many good people took refuge. In dealing with people he was kind and approachable. All who came to call on him, he universally exhorted to eat no flesh and to recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land. In his later years he lived at the Garden of the Buddha’s Son, and at all times of the day and night he held the sacred name without pause. During the Cultural Revolution he suddenly suffered a stroke; his speech became impeded and his hands and feet cramped, but after medical treatment he somewhat recovered. Before the Winter Solstice he chanced to catch a chill and, weary and worn, wished to lie down. He said to his disciples, ‘I have already seen Amitābha Buddha with my own eyes. My body has no pain of illness, my mind is not confused; I shall certainly be reborn in the Land of Bliss.’ By midnight he again said, ‘The Buddha has come!’ Then he recited the Buddha’s name aloud. Gradually his voice grew low, but his lips still moved faintly, and he passed away peacefully. The time was the morning of the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of 1975, and he was eighty-six.

Jin Yang, style name Rúyú, was a native of Chengtan Town, Xinchang County, Zhejiang; his father was Zhang Genyu, and of the six brothers Yang was the third. Because his family was poor, his father could not support him and wished to sell him to the keeper of the Zhanyuan Nunnery to be a monk. The abbess Xianhua at first would not consent. But seeing that Yang was honest and simple, she took him in and gave him to her disciple Liaoming. At the time of his tonsure he was only eleven years old. At the beginning, while in the nunnery, he had to attend to the worldly chanting of sutras and repentance services, and to suit himself to his circumstances, Yang could only go along with them. When he had grown a little older, he declined such engagements and devoted himself wholly to pure cultivation. At sixteen he went to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai to receive the full precepts. When the precept period was complete, he went out on foot to visit Tiantong and the Aśoka Temple. At the Dharma Storehouse Temple in Shanghai he drew near to the elder Xingci and heard him lecture on scripture and teaching for many years. In the end he returned to the Great Buddha Temple in Xinchang to nurture the Way, remaining there until he passed into stillness. In his daily practice he took the Pure Land method as his chief. Besides the two periods of chanting, he also recited the Kṣitigarbha Sutra and performed the Great Compassion Repentance, without break through cold and heat, for decades as one day. His master’s master Xianhua was quite skilled in acupuncture. Yang received her transmission and, in the intervals of his studies, treated people’s ailments, in most cases restoring them to health. The offerings of the faithful, apart from their proper uses, he would turn to other meritorious deeds and to the release of life. He often said, ‘A single grain of rice from a benefactor is as great as Mount Sumeru. If you eat it and do not realize the Way, you shall return wearing fur and horns.’ In childhood he loved to study ancient books. In his ordinary dealings with people he was single-hearted in sincerity, preaching the Dharma to benefit living beings with great earnestness, so that he won the deep respect of the local people. When he was eighty, he gradually felt his spirits sink. At the beginning of the tenth month of that year his illness grew daily more serious; he could take no food, yet his mind remained clear, and he would always recite sutras and the Buddha’s name from his bed as usual. He passed into rebirth on the seventh day of the tenth month of the Gregorian calendar in 1976, shortly after the second hour of the morning. His nephew Zhang Bohua and his pure friend Kang Zhijing happened to be at his side. Seeing him gaze upward with both eyes and press his palms together in salutation, as though marking something, they at once recited the Buddha’s name to aid his rebirth. He then lay in the auspicious posture facing the West, and amid the sound of the Buddha-recitation passed away all at once. After his death his whole body was cold, but his four limbs were soft. Three hours later he was placed in the coffin, and the crown of his head was still warm. The whole room was filled with a rare fragrance that lingered long and did not fade.

Han Ye, a son of the Ye family of Yixian, Anhui, had at one time studied at Aurora University in Shanghai. By nature gentle, he studied Confucian learning in his youth and understood the way of self-cultivation, the ordering of the family, the governance of the state, and the peace of the world. Skilled in poetry, he was broadly learned in the outer classics. He floated and sank in the sea of officialdom for twenty years, keeping both sleeves clear and remaining his own self. Having been deeply immersed in the world, the latent causes of his former lives arose, and he went to the Mist-and-Water Nunnery by Gantang Lake in Jiujiang to shave his head and leave the world, at the age of forty-one. The next year he received the full precepts at the Great Storehouse Temple in Guangji, Hubei. Thereafter he traveled on foot to visit masters and study, investigating the teaching and practicing Chan, a single bowl and a lone body, drifting like the clouds and water. In March 1950 he came to the Gaoming Temple on Mount Tiantai. The temple was the practice-place of the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui, and in the Ming dynasty it was revived by Master Chuandeng of Youxi. The teacher dwelt here in seclusion for nearly thirty years; he did not care to visit the families of the great, and read through the Great Treasury three times, being deeply versed in its mysterious profundities and thoroughly understanding the truth of the realities. He cultivated the Pure Land in all earnestness, rising early and retiring late, bowing in repentance and holding the sacred name, without break through cold or heat. After the Liberation the incense of the temple withered and most of the monks scattered; the teacher held fast in his own cultivation. Though beset by hardship and difficulty, he was unmoved in his determination. Every night he made the Amitābha Repentance his constant lesson, never forgoing it. When the Japanese friendship delegation visited the temple, the teacher presented them with poems, saying:
‘The One-Vehicle’s wondrous Dharma rose at Tiantai;
After a thousand years the same school comes across the seas.
Surely at Vulture Peak we shared one assembly;
A lone sail comes visiting from afar, how many times again?’
And again:
‘The autumn light is gorgeous, the days of the chrysanthemum;
Just now it is a year of rich abundance.
To wish our friendly neighbors many splendid deeds,
Know that the Buddha-Dharma is itself without bound.’
In his later years he had a slight illness. Before his stillness he knew beforehand that the time of his rebirth was at hand; he distributed his robes and articles and took leave of the community. On the morning of the sixth day of the third month of 1978, the temple community was reciting the Universal Buddha, and at that time Ye was still pacing in meditation in his room, reciting the Buddha’s name. When the recitation was finished and the assembly went to look, he had already passed away, facing the West and lying on his right side. He was seventy-four in age and thirty-four in the Dharma-life.

Liao Dao, style name Xinhui, was a native of Chongming, Jiangsu. He left home in early youth and had made pilgrimage to all the famous mountains. At Chongming he initiated the establishment of the Chongming Lotus Society and the Qidong Buddhist Association, and renovated the Yunlin Lecture Temple. Having worn himself into illness by accumulated toil, he closed himself in retreat at Yunlin to recover. Dao had at first lived at Lingyan, where he was held in esteem by Master Yinguang. Afterwards, at the earnest invitation of Miaozhen, he again went to Lingyan and took up the post of chief supervisor. With the single resource of a plan he rendered no small meritorious service. Before long, finding his strength could not bear up, he returned with his disciple Guruo to Yunlin. Worn by the toil of boat and carriage, his illness broke out. Dao wished to take no medicine, but his disciples urgently begged him; unable to refuse, he took a single dose, without effect. He then said to Guruo, ‘Life is but this; my vow may be accomplished.’ Three days later his illness had much improved.
