By the third month (the twenty-fifth day of the third month), when he rose in the morning, he suddenly said, ‘Three watches from now I shall return to the West. Cultivate well, all of you, and make no worldly show.’ Presently he ordered an incense table set up in his sleeping-place and bade them hang the image of the Three Sages, and told his disciples to recite the Buddha’s name together. Until ten thirty-five, with palms joined and a smile, amid the sound of the Buddha-recitation, he passed away peacefully.

Ming Yuan had originally lived at the Release of Life Temple by the Tiger-Sounding Lotus Pond in Suzhou, and was brought to Lingyan by Master Miaozhen. During the Cultural Revolution he moved to the Paradise Orchard work area at Tianping, which was the former site of the Lingyan farm. Yuan was by nature taciturn, and devoutly cultivated the Pure Land. He single-mindedly held the vast name of myriad virtues, striving without slackness. At ninety-one, he passed into rebirth in the winter of that year. Three days before his rebirth he himself cleaned his bed and took leave of the monks who lodged with him. Seeing that he was without illness, they would none of them believe him. Three days later, Yuan, upon his bed, asked someone to help him rise into an upright sitting position. With no pain of illness and his mind not confused, his two palms joined, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed into rebirth.

Xia Ming, a native of Hubei, left home at the Yongquan Temple on Mount Gu in Fujian. He investigated that which goes up and beyond, and attained considerable insight. Though an elder of the Chan school, he cultivated the Pure Land in secret, single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-recitation. For decades he traveled on foot, a free cloud and a wild crane, with no fixed abode. He paid homage at each of the great mountains, and wherever he went he never lingered. Passing a temple he would ask for a lodging; hearing the bell he would enter the hall, and at the set times sit in meditation. In bowing, reciting, and burning incense in worship he was diligent and never idle. At the Gold Mountain (Jinshan) Temple in Zhenjiang he was honored as first-seat, and there he spent his last years. Ming was strict in the precepts and extraordinarily plain in his way of life. He loved to give; whatever he had beyond his body, if anyone needed it, he would present it as a gift, never showing the least reluctance. Fine food he offered to the community; the coarse husks he kept for himself. When he met with offerings, he passed them on to the monastery, never enjoying them privately. When he saw a fellow cultivator lying sick, he would tend him with the utmost care, never shirking the toil. His refuge disciples were very many. His age was eighty-five. A week before his rebirth he knew the time beforehand. He sent letters to his several disciples, telling them that he was soon to return to the West. The remaining robes and articles he gave all away to others. When the time came, he bathed and changed his robes, and with no pain of illness passed away sitting cross-legged.

Qing Feng lived at the Nianhua Nunnery in the Village of Yellow Bean Sprouts in the suburbs of Suzhou. His whole life he devoted to ascetic practice, bowing and reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra, and setting his mind upon the Pure Land. By day he would do nothing but sit cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name; by night he only sat and never lay down, for decades as one day, and never once exchanged idle chat with anyone. Whoever came to call on him, he exhorted with the impermanence of the world, telling them to recite the Buddha’s name honestly and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. His refuge disciples were very many. He accepted no incense-offering, and received no gifts. Where he was firmly unable to refuse, he would pass them on to others rather than use them for himself. Before his rebirth he knew the time beforehand; he bathed and changed his robes, and sitting upright passed away. His age was over eighty. On the day of his cremation his disciples all gathered. When the fire was lit, the assembly saw Feng’s body hovering in the sky, seated upon a jeweled lotus, with children standing in attendance on either side; after a moment it vanished. All who saw and heard were filled with joy and praise, and because of this awakened to the bodhi mind. In the suburbs of Suzhou there are still those who can tell of the matter.

Jing Quan, a native of Xianju, Zhejiang, when still a boy heard the sound of the temple monks reciting sutras, and at once conceived the resolve to leave the world. At twenty-seven he served as a kitchen head at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. Through this he was able to draw near to the venerable elders of the Tiantai school, such as the teachers Yongzhi and Minxi. In his early years the teacher studied diligently; at night he would read the sutras by moonlight, and on moonless evenings he gave himself wholly to bowing, so that he came to understand all the sutras and commentaries. He served as chief lecturer under Master Dixian for several years. He founded a Buddhist Studies Institute to train young monks; he established the Wondrous Dharma Hall to guide the practice of calming and insight; and he created the Nurture Hall to shelter the aged and the weak. Every night the teacher performed the Mount Meng food-offering. In great and small Buddhist services alike he made sincerity and reverence the rule. He once instructed his disciples, ‘Rely upon the incense and flowers of benefactors to cultivate your own merit and wisdom.’ His daily life was hard and plain. For more than forty years he propagated the sutras and protected the Dharma without sparing his strength. In teaching he expounded the doctrine of the Tiantai (Lotus) school; in practice he returned to the Pure Land — in the morning he cultivated the ten recitations, and in the evening he held the Contemplation Sutra. At seventy-nine, suddenly showing the marks of age and illness amid the assembly’s sound of the Buddha-recitation, he passed away with a smile.

Dan Yun, secular surname Zhu, was born on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of 1901, in the village of Baiyang, Dajing, in Yueqing, Zhejiang. He lost his father in childhood. At twelve he left home under Master Yuetan at the Changlè Temple in Wenling. At nineteen he received the full precepts. At twenty he went to Guanzong Temple in Ningbo, drew near to the elder Master Dixian, and studied the Tiantai doctrine. Later he also drew near to Master Yinguang. At thirty-six he served as abbot of Mingyin Temple in Wenling County. At forty-four he served as head of the Buddhist Institute at Guanzong Temple. At forty-six he traveled in many directions. At forty-nine he became abbot of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, holding the post for twenty-six years. Since the Liberation he had been elected a deputy to the provincial people’s congress, a member of the provincial committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, and a council member of the Buddhist Association of China. Tiantai is a celebrated beauty of the Southeast, with its monasteries standing in forest-like array, and Guoqing Temple is the foremost of all the Tiantai monasteries. Ever since the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui dynasty opened the mountain, generation after generation there were eminent monks, and the stream of the Dharma never ceased. When Dan Yun took office, reform had but just begun and the source of donors’ alms was cut off from without. He led the community, following the legacy of Baizhang, in farming so as to be self-sufficient. He thereby caused the whole assembly to be without lack in the four needs, and the pure atmosphere not to be cut off. During the Cultural Revolution the whole temple was ruined and Dan Yun himself was cast into prison. Yet he was able to be at ease as though in his customary conditions, unbending and unyielding; such was his perfection of patience. Dan Yun once compiled by hand a single volume of lectures on the Tiantai school for the use of beginning students. He composed twenty-eight verses in praise of the Lotus Sutra and sent them to Japan, where they were received with great admiration. He was a close friend of Master Han Ye of Youxi. Morning and evening he never neglected the six recollections; amid busyness he never failed in collecting the mind; his side never touched the mat, and he was content with coarse herbs — such were his understanding and his practice. In the autumn of 1975, in the ninth month, he fell ill, yet he could still receive visitors despite his sickness. On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, in the hai watch, he entered stillness. Three days before, he had given instructions for his affairs after death. All the affairs of the monastery he entrusted to Master Jinghui to take charge. At the time there was no pain of illness; with palms joined he bade farewell to the assembly, and reciting the Buddha’s name he passed away. He was seventy-five in age and fifty-six years in the monastic life.

Fo Cheng, secular surname Peng, was a native of Guiyang, Hunan. From childhood he left home at a small local temple. When he had grown a little older, hearing that the way of Qishan was flourishing greatly, he went there to visit. Before long he went again to the sandalwood grove of the Arhat Temple at Hengzhou and entered a seven-day retreat; there he gained some awakening. Later he met Master Daojie, who bade him go to the Southern Peak to draw near to the elder Mo’an. The elder, on seeing him, held him in deep esteem, and taught him orally the doctrine of Consciousness-Only. The teacher attended him personally for years, and came to be thoroughly versed in both the doors of nature and characteristics, so that he was much praised by his fellow practitioners. The teacher often said that the Buddha’s grace is hard to repay, and so burned one of his fingers to require the Buddha’s grace. Once, invited by Tiantong, he lectured on the Śūraṅgama Sutra. Thereafter he abode where there was no constancy, following conditions to guide and transform beings. In 1922 he presided over the Zhusheng Temple on the Southern Peak; those who received the precepts from him numbered more than three hundred, and he initiated a monks’ institute and a Dharma lecture-study school. The next year he handed over the affairs of the monastery, retired to Fuyan Temple for quiet recuperation, and suddenly showed signs of illness. On the twelfth day of the tenth month he bathed, changed his robes, and sat cross-legged facing the West. His fellow cultivator, the teacher Ande, asked, ‘Old Master is a great workman of this age; now you meet the last move. You ought to spur yourself on vigorously, and leave a model for those who come after.’ The teacher answered, ‘Yes!’ Then, palms joined, he recited the Buddha’s name once and entered stillness. He was fifty-one. In accordance with his last will, his bones were laid in the common pagoda at Fuyan Temple.

Chuan Xin, style name Qinghua, was a native of Santai County, Sichuan, and took the tonsure under Master Haifu at the Golden Summit of Mount Emei. In 1916, during the winter precept session at Baoguang Temple, he received the full precepts. In 1922 he applied for lodging at the Qizhen Temple in the Chixi township, twenty lǐ north of Jiaxing city, Zhejiang. The temple was the place of the pagoda-shrine of the Chan master Yungu of the Ming dynasty, a celebrated monastery of the locality, first built in the Song dynasty and undergoing alternate rise and decline. In the twenty-sixth year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing, Master Lianren was abbot of the temple and rebuilt the Mahāvīra (Great Hero) Hall, the Thousand-Buddha Pavilion, and the Western Hall. Within the temple there was established a Buddha-recitation hall; in the pure course of that hall each day there were four periods of contemplation, two periods of chanting, and two periods of repentance, preserving the old rules of Hongluo and Yunqi, so that the ocean-like multitude gathered from all the ten directions and took refuge in great numbers. The year after the teacher arrived at the temple, he again asked leave to make pilgrimage to Mount Wutai. Returning from Mount Wutai, he entered the Buddha-recitation hall and devoutly practiced the Pure Land karma. On the morning of the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the lunar calendar of 1924, sitting while reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away, at the age of fifty-five. More than a month before his rebirth he told the guest-master of the temple that he would be going on a distant journey. The guest-master asked where he was going; the teacher said he had a place to go. The guest-master said to him by way of illustration, ‘To be able to go to the Western Pure Land is the best of all!’ The teacher replied, ‘Yes!’ On the day of his rebirth, when the morning chanting was finished, the teacher first spread his mat before the Buddha and bowed with his head to the ground. Then he went to the abbot’s quarters, took leave of Master Lianren, bowed deeply and knelt long, asking for instruction. The abbot asked him why. The teacher said, ‘The karmic opportunity is ripe; I must be going.’ The abbot thereupon instructed him, saying, ‘Strive hard in the Buddha-recitation, and surely it shall be as you wish — you will be reborn in the West and see Amitābha.’ The teacher bowed in thanks and rose, returned to the hall, sat cross-legged and recited the Buddha’s name, changing nothing of his usual demeanor. The assembly saw a vapor rising in heat from the crown of the teacher’s head, and drawing near to look, they found he had already passed away placidly.

Xiu Wu, a native of Yingkou, came of a bricklayer’s and tiler’s stock. Feeling that life is full of suffering, he many times thought of a way to escape it. Later he heard people say that reciting the Buddha’s name enables one to leave suffering and attain bliss, and so he made the resolve to recite the Buddha’s name. After leaving home, his mind of the Buddha-recitation became ever more earnest, and whenever he met anyone he would surely urge them to recite the Buddha’s name. In 1929 Master Dixian transmitted the precepts at the Land of Bliss Temple in Harbin. The teacher made the resolve to wait upon the sick during the precept period. He had lodged at the temple only a dozen days when he suddenly said he must go. The proctor asked, ‘Where are you going?’ The teacher said, ‘I am not going anywhere else; I am going to be reborn. Pray, Proctor, in your compassion prepare me several hundred catties of firewood to be burned after my death.’ The proctor asked, ‘When will you go?’ The teacher replied, ‘Within ten days, I think.’ The next day he again said to the proctor, ‘Take leave for me to the Master. I am going today. Please give me a room, and find a few people to recite the Buddha’s name to see me off.’ Those who saw him off asked him to leave a verse as a remembrance. He said, ‘I came of hard labor and cannot compose poems and verses. But I have one word of what I have myself experienced to tell you all — that “to be able to speak and not to act is not true wisdom.”’ Thereupon the whole assembly recited the Buddha’s name in unison. The teacher sat cross-legged facing the West, reciting the Buddha’s name along with the assembly. In less than a quarter of an hour he had already passed into rebirth. Placed in the shrine, his face was as in life. Master Dixian saw the matter with his own eyes and sighed that it was rare.

Xiu Hang, a son of the Zhang family of Baiquan County, Heilongjiang, was known in his youth in the countryside for both character and learning, and served as a primary-school teacher. At forty he suddenly thought of leaving the world. He took the teacher Zhiru of Yongan Temple in Shenyang as his teacher, and received the Dharma name Renhe. In 1935 he received the full precepts under Master Tanxu at the Pure Land Temple in Hulan. That year he went to Qingdao and studied the perfect and sudden calming and insight of the Tiantai. Reading the ‘Comments on the Lotus Sutra,’ he penetrated deeply and gained an awakening. In 1937 he studied the Vinaya under Master Hongyi, vowing to protect the Nanshan school for the whole of his life. When he heard that Master Hong had entered extinction, his grief was past bearing. He then took up the master’s verse on chrysanthemums and inscribed it beside his seat. The verse runs: ‘A single chrysanthemum stands so tall, whose lofty standard holds the late season. Why is its color so deep red? For the teaching it should shed its blood.’ The heart with which he served the Dharma may be seen from this. He ate one meal a day and always sat without lying down, imitating Master Lingfeng in bowing the Zhancha Repentance, and obtained the pure and clear wheel-signs. He was professor of the precept studies at Zhanshan; upright and stern in his personal conduct, he walked the path according to the four mindfulnesses, not allowing worldly concerns to disturb his mind, and was content in worn clothes and grass sandals. In dealing with people he spoke plainly without reserve; when some reproached him for not knowing the ways of the world, he paid them no mind and answered, ‘I would rather suffer a hot iron wheel whirling on my head than ever use the Buddha-Dharma to do a personal favor.’ Once caught by a slight illness and knowing he would not recover, he took the twenty-one Vinaya texts he himself had punctuated and gave them to the Sutra Repository; the remaining fifty-odd he numbered, drew lots among them, and distributed to form karmic bonds with the assembly. Whatever money for medicine monks or laity sent him, he gave to the refectory to provide for the community. At his end he bade his students to chant the ‘Chapter on the Vows of the Universal Worthy and to dedicate the merit toward the West. Composing his mind to contemplate the Buddha, his right mindfulness clear and distinct, he passed away in auspicious manner. It was the middle of the night on the twelfth day of the third month of the bǐngxū year (1946); hours later the crown of his head was still warm. He was fifty-two in age and twelve years in the monastic life.

Tong Li, secular surname Cao, was a native of Suzhou, Jiangsu, and practiced as a physician of traditional Chinese medicine. Only at fifty-nine did he first hear of the Buddha-Dharma. Reading Master Yinguang’s collected writings, he conceived a deep faith in the Pure Land method, and went to Mount Tiantai in Zhejiang to bow before Master Huilian and shave his head. In 1940, when he was already sixty-two, admiring the Pure Land practice-ground of Lingyan, he went up the mountain to join the community in the Buddha-recitation. Before long, with the permission of Master Miaozhen, he took up residence in the Common Pagoda Court. After he moved into the pagoda court, he let go of every condition with not the slightest attachment, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the West. In the summer of 1946 he gradually felt his body weaken and his food grow less; he lodged in the Ruyi Quarters to recuperate, still fingering his prayer beads and reciting the Buddha’s name without pause. On the night of the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the bell had sounded the ninth stroke, he was still sitting on the steps before the courtyard to enjoy the cool while reciting the Buddha’s name, when he suddenly said to the incense-lamp keeper, ‘I must return to my room.’ The incense-lamp keeper helped him into the room, and the teacher said, ‘Tonight I am going to be reborn in the West; make haste and light the lamps.’ Having said this, he lay down to rest, silently holding the sacred name, until at the eleventh hour the incense-lamp keeper called him and got no answer, and hastily invited the teachers to assist the recitation. After only a moment the teacher had already passed away peacefully in sitting posture. The next day he was placed in the shrine; the crown of his head was still warm, his countenance as in life, its smoothness and luster beyond the ordinary.

Hong Ci, style name Miaojue, original name Xisheng, secular surname Zhang, was a native of Ankang in southern Shaanxi, a descendant of Zhang Liang, the Marquis of Liu of the Han. As a child the teacher was unlike other children; by nature he was silent and did not love idle play, and cherished a resolve to transcend the world. When a little older, he went to the Southern Mountain and took the venerable Dàxíng as his teacher, shaving his head and leaving the world. In the spring of the rénwǔ year (1942) he went to the Reclining Dragon Temple in Xi’an and received the full precepts from Master Langzhao. Having heard the instruction of good-knowing teachers, he believed deeply in the Pure Land method, which gathers in all three capacities of beings, to which all the nine realms alike return, which suddenly transcends all existences, and which is accomplished in a single lifetime. He then went to the Pure Karma Court on Cuìhuà Mountain and practiced exclusively the method of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Day and night he strove ardently, working without letup; some five years passed, and of the many who came to him for guidance he answered according to their capacities, the essential words being few and never vexatious. Though the teacher was admired by the multitude, in his daily life he kept himself low and humble, without any look of pride. In the summer of the dīnghài year (1947), knowing that the time of impermanence had come, he began a zealous seven-day retreat, observed silence and did not sleep, devoting himself wholly to reciting the Great Compassion Mantra. On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month the Buddha-recitation week was complete. That afternoon, when he had finished reciting the Great Compassion Mantra and made the dedication of merit, he faced the West, closed his eyes and sat cross-legged, as though entering meditation-concentration. The assembly saw the teacher’s face like the morning clouds and his lips like cinnabar; when they felt him, his whole body was ice-cold, but the crown of his head was hot as though boiling. So the assembly gathered together and praised the sacred name, assisting the teacher’s recitation. After his stillness, according to the Dharma he was cremated, and among the ashes were found more than two hundred firm relics in the seven colors of gold, red, purple, white, blue, green, and gray. The period of the teacher’s passing into stillness was the ninth month of 1948.

Mi Gao, secular surname Zhong, was a native of the Qijiazhuang in the northern countryside of Rugao, Jiangsu; three brothers all left the homelife to become monks. At nineteen the teacher shaved his head at the Guanyin Nunnery in Xichang town, Rugao; the nunnery was a subordinate cloister of Dinghui Temple in Rugao, and Dinghui Temple was a renowned monastery of Rugao. When the teacher was over fifty he came to Dinghui Temple, and while in his sixties he was chosen as abbot, residing at the temple for more than thirty years in all. He propagated the Dharma and benefited living beings without sparing his strength, and was praised by the local people. In his daily practice he recited wholly the Lotus Sutra. On the nineteenth day of the sixth month of the old calendar in 1958, the birthday of Guanyin, reciting the Buddha’s name while sitting, he passed away, at the age of eighty-four.

Ji Lian, secular surname Huang, was a native of Huangyan, Zhejiang, and left home at sixteen. Master Jing Quan of Mount Tiantai was his elder Dharma-brother. The teacher later went to the Longqing Temple in Cangmi Lane of Suzhou, and under the seat of Master Jingguang succeeded to his robe and bowl, becoming abbot of Longqing Temple for a period of several decades. He opened the great precepts three times, the last being in 1934. The teacher was upright and compassionate; he often urged people to recite the Buddha’s name honestly, and to hold and recite the Diamond Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, and the Universal Gate Chapter, never forgoing these throughout. On the tenth day of the tenth month of the lunar calendar in 1956, at nine in the morning, without any pain of illness, reciting the Buddha’s name while sitting, he passed away, at the age of eighty-six.

Qian Fa was from Anhui. At the age of forty he received full ordination at Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo. For more than forty years he gave himself warmly to the work of the resident community, living plainly and enduring hardship. He applied himself with diligence and recited the Buddha's name with simple honesty. In turn he served as rice cook, garden keeper, and in other posts. The Master deeply believed in the Pure Land; for the sake of birth and death he truly aroused the bodhi mind. On August 20, 1981 (the twenty-first day of the seventh lunar month), he announced before everyone, "I shall pass away within three days." With his own hand he wrote in advance on a small wooden board the day of his rebirth in the West. On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh lunar month (August 23), he instructed the monk in charge of the storeroom to carry every article of the resident community's property out of his quarters. The Master no longer let his ribs touch a mat, resting only seated on a chair, day and night alike. On August 22, that is, the evening of the twenty-third day of the seventh lunar month at seven o'clock, several young novices of the monastery recited the Buddha's name to assist him. The next morning the Master was clear in mind and spirit, took a little boiled water, and asked, "What time is it now?" It happened to be exactly eight o'clock. At about ten he waved his hand, signaling those who were reciting to go to their midday meal, and the assembly took turns reciting. By five minutes past one in the afternoon, free of bodily suffering, he passed away serenely while seated amid the sound of Buddha-recitation. He was eighty-four.

Pin Xing was first named Qing Fu; his secular surname was Zheng, and he was from Qianqi Commune in Fuding, Fujian. In 1929, when he was twenty-four, he went to Ruiyun Monastery on Mount Feng in Xiamen Town, Fuding, and took the monk Jianshan as his teacher. He then went to Mount Putuo to study, serving as garden keeper and rice cook, and so three years passed. At twenty-seven he received full ordination at Puji Monastery. That same year he made pilgrimage to Biyun Monastery on Mount Wutai, where he held the posts of hall server and kitchen fire-tender. In 1950, when the Master was forty-five, he returned to Fuding and took the Elder Monk Bude of Baiyun Monastery on Mount Taimal as his second teacher, changing his name to the present one. At fifty-eight he took up residence at Macao Hut in Nanxi, and later went on to Zhaoming Monastery at Aoling and Qilin Monastery at Kuling. In every monastery he shrank from no toil, rising early and working in the dark, setting out under the stars and returning under the moon, laboring for the resident community. At fifty-nine he came to Pingxing Monastery. There he became a mainstay of production, opening waste land and planting tea, bearing hardship and complaint alike without resentment, loving the monastery as his own home, equal toward foe and friend; through all his exhausting diligence the great assembly of monasteries in Fuding called him a fine model of production and practice in this Dharma-ending age. All his life the Master revered the Pure Land method, following the instructions of the old Master Yinguang, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. He would not serve as abbot, would not perform repentance and funeral rites for hire, and would not gather disciples in numbers. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down his recitation never ceased. In 1983, on the first day of the seventh lunar month, he rose feeling unwell. On the tenth he took leave of the whole monastery, saying, "At five o'clock this morning I saw Amitābha come in person to instruct me. Five days from now, at eight in the morning, I shall be reborn in Ultimate Bliss." He then handed over his ordinary savings and clothing to the abbot, Master Shixing, to be given as karmic bonds to the monks of the monastery. He had someone telephone Qianqi Commune in his home district to say that on the fifteenth of the seventh month, at eight o'clock, he would be reborn in the West. At about three in the afternoon of the fourteenth he asked for a basin of clear water, bathed and changed his clothes, and sat upright reciting the Buddha's name. At eight in the morning of the fifteenth he passed away serenely, exactly on time. His worldly age was seventy-eight, his monastic seniority fifty-one. After cremation, from his ashes more than a few relics were found, brilliant and dazzling to the eye. In accordance with his will they were scattered into the great sea, to form karmic bonds with the water-dwelling creatures.
Xing Ji's secular surname was Guan. He was from Liaoning and a graduate of the foreign languages department of Northeastern University. After the September

18 Incident he came south and called upon Master Yinguang. Receiving his instruction, he at once resolved to leave home, being then twenty-six. Thereafter, for more than fifty years, he dwelt at Lingyan Mountain, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name with unbroken diligence. In 1983, on the eighth day of the tenth lunar month, he took to bed with a chill, slept four days together, and his strength gradually failed and his food and drink diminished. When the layman Zhu Zhichao came to visit, he asked, "Would you like us to ask the community to recite for you? Or use a recording of Buddha-recitation?" He answered, "No need. I have my own certainty." From then on he shut his door and received no visitors, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name. On the seventh day, that is, at eight minutes past eleven in the morning of the fourteenth day of the tenth month, he lay down in the auspicious posture, free of illness and suffering, his heart without clinging, his mind without confusion, and passed serenely to the West. He was seventy-seven, with monastic seniority of fifty-one. After his rebirth, matters were handled according to the Lingyan regulations for the dying: the resident community appointed eight monks to recite the Buddha's name in shifts day and night, and at four in the afternoon of the next day he was placed in the casket, his face as if alive and his four limbs supple. Before his illness ended, the Master gave his lifetime savings of three hundred yuan to help print the Ten Essentials of the Pure Land, the remainder being offered to the community to form karmic bonds. He also wrote four letters of farewell in advance, asking that they be sent to relatives and friends after his death. In one of them he said, "The state has appeared before me; I am going." After cremation, from his ashes were picked out several dozen relics, śarīra flowers, and crystal beads of various sizes and colors, some as large as a peanut.

Miao Jing's secular surname was Wang; she was the stepmother of the Monk Xuyun. The Venerable Yun's birth mother died early, and Jing raised him to manhood. Yun's father wished him to inherit both branches of the family and so married him to two wives. After Yun left home, in the third year of the Tongzhi reign (1864) his father died of illness, and Jing at once led her two daughters-in-law into the Buddhist fold as nuns. All the family wealth she gave away in charity, single-mindedly turning toward the Way. For more than forty years after leaving home she devoted herself wholly to the Pure Land. On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month of the first year of the Xuantong reign (1909), the day of the Buddha's enlightenment, she showed a slight illness and, reciting the Buddha's name, passed to the West. As she lay dying she sat cross-legged and spoke these verses: "Because of love and grace I clung to the red dust; / For greed and delusion I lost my true nature. / More than eighty years, a dream and an illusion; / Where all conditions are empty, no person was ever there." "Today I am freed from the burdens of this life, / And gain instead a pure and wondrous body in the Land of Lotuses. / Let those with the karmic bond recite the Buddha and go to the West; / Do not long sink and drift in the sea of suffering." After her death a rare fragrance lingered for several days, and she sat upright, solemn as if alive.

Guang Hua's secular surname was Xie and her given name Caidi. At her parents' bidding she was married at seventeen to a man of the Chen family. Before a year had passed her husband died, and she forthwith shaved her head and left home, taking the old bhikṣuṇī of Tanhua Hut in Taohua Village, Wuyang Lane, Mount Xiang, Suzhou, as her teacher. Seeing her sincerity, the Master handed the hut over to Hua and went elsewhere. Hua was thus able to dwell alone in the hut in quiet practice. The hut stood among mountains on every side, a place few people ever reached. On the summit there was a stone-carved image of Guanyin with four faces, and every morning without fail Hua climbed to the summit, burned incense and lit lamps, and bowed in reverence. She recited one scroll of the Amitābha Sutra and three rounds of the Rebirth Mantra as her daily lesson, and for the rest held the holy name of Amitābha with diligence. By day she went up the mountain to gather firewood, and what she sold it for she spent on incense, candles, and lamp oil as offerings to the Buddha. For herself she ate only the fruit she planted with her own hands, or wild grasses and leaves she gathered to stave off hunger. Though good believers came up the mountain to reverence Guanyin, whatever offerings came to Hua she gave away to others as she pleased, never keeping them for herself. If firewood, grass, or food was stolen, she did not take account of it or pursue the matter. At fifty-eight she went to Xiyuan Jiezhuang Monastery in Suzhou to receive the greater precepts. Thereafter her practice grew more diligent still. At seventy-four she went to Lingyan to join the memorial for the placing of Master Yinguang's relics in the stupa, and there bought a place in the columbarium for her own ashes. On the very next morning, wholly free of illness, she lay down at peace and attained rebirth. At that time good believers from near and far were gathered at the mountain in great numbers; witnessing the sight, they all recited the Amitābha Sutra and the holy name of the Buddha. After her death, as the hours passed, her face grew ruddy and her limbs supple. They raised her into the casket seated cross-legged, just like a living person. After cremation, more than ten white relics were obtained, and several śarīra flowers, all white as crystal, bright, smooth, and lustrous; those who saw them praised without cease.

Guo Song was from Yancheng in northern Jiangsu; nothing is known of her family background. She left home at the age of three, entering the Tianfei Palace nunnery in that place and taking the old bhikṣuṇī Changde as her teacher. From childhood Song knew to recite the Buddha's name diligently, and she also practiced Chan concentration. Her teacher wished her to manage the affairs of the nunnery and urged her, "Past fifty, it will not be too late to apply yourself." Song answered, "In this turbid world all is impermanent, and the stream of time runs swift. Suppose my lifespan does not reach fifty; would I not have missed this whole life?" So she did not follow her teacher's command, and recited the Buddha's name diligently as before. At nineteen she went to Xiyuan Jiezhuang Monastery in Suzhou and sought the greater precepts. In 1947 war broke out in northern Jiangsu, and the three generations of teacher, disciple, and grand-disciple abandoned the nunnery and came to Suzhou. Just when they had nowhere to shelter and could neither advance nor retreat, they met on the road the bhikṣuṇī Cheng Hui, abbess of Wunan Hut in the alley of the Small Wooden Bridge at Xumen. Cheng Hui inquired into their situation and, pitying them for drifting with no place to rest, took them back to the hut to live, providing them with board and lodging. Song dwelt in that nunnery for several years. In 1956 Song was thirty-nine. On the sixth day of the ninth lunar month, free of bodily suffering and with right mindfulness clear, she passed away serenely. Three days earlier she had said to Cheng Hui, "Three days from now I shall return to the West. Please recite the Buddha's name to see me off." She also said, "Do you know how the Buddha's name should be recited? Let me teach you." Cheng Hui asked her to instruct her. Song said, "Hold the six-character great name, neither fast nor slow, with utmost sincerity and earnestness, reciting one character at a time. The recitation must rise from the mind, the sound must come from the mouth, and the sound must enter the ear. Recite so that you are perfectly clear, and listen so that you are perfectly clear; do not slur over it in a muddle. Recite too fast and you cannot keep up; recite too slowly and the mind scatters." Cheng Hui followed her instructions, one character at a time, neither tense nor slack, holding the holy name; and Song recited along with her. Thus three days passed, until nine in the evening of the sixth day, when Song rose, straightened her robe, and took the cross-legged posture. Reciting the Buddha's name, she passed her hand over her head in the manner of bestowing a prediction, making three circles. She paused, then did it again, and so three times in all. At eleven she said to Cheng Hui, "Farewell! Farewell!" and calmly passed away seated.

Miao Xing was from Wujin in Jiangsu; her surname and family background are unknown. She once served as abbess of Rulai Nunnery inside the Chang Gate of Suzhou. In the spring of 1920 she received the greater precepts at Tianning Monastery in Changzhou, the precept master being the Elder Zhikai. In heart Xing was kind and compassionate, strictly upheld the precepts, and took no pleasure in seeking connections. The work of her whole life was simply to uphold and recite the Avataṃsaka Sutra, recite the Buddha's name diligently, and transfer the merit to the Pure Land. In the third month of 1956 she fell ill, yet her recitation never stopped. At two in the afternoon on the thirteenth day of the ninth month she sat cross-legged facing west, bade farewell to her disciple Yixing, joined her palms, and loudly called the great name, passing away serenely. Her worldly age was fifty-seven.

Ming Chang's secular surname was Li; in middle age she believed in the Buddha and received the refuges and precepts. At fifty-eight she lived with her daughter Ming Fu in Xiaotao Nunnery in the town of Mudu, Suzhou. Later she was tonsured under Master Yuanying and received the full precepts at Xiyuan Jiezhuang Monastery in Suzhou. All her life she devoted herself wholly to the Pure Land, reciting the six-character great name day and night. On the morning of the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh lunar month of 1966, knowing beforehand that her time had come, she bathed and changed her clothes, sat upright cross-legged, formed the Amitābha mudrā with her hands, and held the holy name. Her daughter Ming Fu urged her mother to lie down, and before long she sat up again. She said of herself, "The wondrous realm of the West has already appeared; the Buddha's words are not false." She urgently recited Namo Amitābha Buddha without stopping. By nine o'clock her voice grew faint, a smile came to her face, and she passed away serenely while seated. After cremation, a great many śarīra flowers were found, of three colors, yellow, white, and green. Her last words were: "No weeping is permitted, no mourning dress allowed, no stupa to be built; make my ashes into steamed buns and give them to the water-dwelling creatures, to form a bond with the West." Her worldly age was eighty, her monastic seniority twenty-two.

Miao Sheng's secular surname was Zhu; she was from Qingpu County in Jiangsu and was married to a wealthy merchant named Zhao. At forty-four, meeting with some unhappy turn of events, she saw through the ways of the world and was tonsured at Xilin Nunnery in Suzhou. The abbess was Master Yanshi, who conferred the greater precepts on her alone in that nunnery, inviting the old Master Yingci to be the precept master. Sheng began by studying the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and in the end took refuge in the Pure Land. She was versed in both the doctrinal and the meditative schools, and her eloquence was unobstructed. Compassionate, joyful, and giving, she delighted in goodness. With the savings of her whole life she had images made and gilded, and rebuilt Xilin Nunnery, making it wholly new. At sixty-one she fell ill and knew her time had come. There was an old teacher, Min of Yunlin Nunnery, long acquainted with Sheng, who one night dreamed he saw Sheng give him a roll of white paper on which four lines of verse were written: "Where now is the glory of former days? / In the Pure Land of the West it was long ago arranged. / Today I can truly leave the sea of suffering, / At ease and free, ascending the lotus terrace." Min woke and forgot it, then fell asleep again. Once more he saw Sheng show him the verse, charging him again and again, "Do not forget; you must show it to Master Cihui." The next day, when Min met Cihui, he learned that Sheng had attained rebirth the night before! It was the thirteenth of October, 1969. Her worldly age was sixty-one.

Yong Bao's secular surname was Luo; she was from Huangyan County in Zhejiang. Her mother, née Chen, dreamed that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva came bearing a little girl and gave her to her, saying, "This girl has great good roots; you must have her leave home." She woke and gave birth to Bao. When Bao was twelve, her mother sent her to Utpala Nunnery in Huangyan, where she was tonsured under the old nun Shidong and given the Dharma name Wentong. She dwelt in that nunnery for more than thirty years. She took part in agricultural labor and, besides the community's morning and evening lessons, single-mindedly held the holy name of Amitābha. The nunnery had been the only community of nuns in Huangyan, and afterwards, under the pressure of the times, it declined. So she moved to Jixiang Nunnery in Cixi, then to Dingxiang Nunnery at the head of Yingluo River; and ten years later she came to No. 4, Lane 961, Chengdu North Road in Shanghai, where she built Dingxin Nunnery. Her heart rested in the Pure Land, and her recitation never stopped. In dealing with people she took compassion as her foundation. Strict and meticulous in the precepts, she was famed far and near. She had a great many disciples who took refuge with her. Her instructions were keen and to the point; she urged only this: "Recite the Buddha's name with simple honesty and seek the West. If you let this slip past in a blink, there will be no day of deliverance." Seven days before her passing she knew beforehand that her time had come. She said to the disciples who recited for her, "I have already seen Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; my rebirth is certain." In the evening of the twenty-fourth day of the fifth lunar month of the Western year 1976, amid the sound of the assembly's Buddha-recitation, she passed away serenely. Her worldly age was ninety-three.

Yuan Xin was the eldest daughter of Wang Jieyu. She was married to a man named Cao and bore a daughter, who died of illness in adulthood. Awakened to the impermanence of human life, she then left home. She dwelt at Lengyan Nunnery at Xiaocangkou in Suzhou. She constantly upheld and recited the Śūraṅgama Sutra, and her Buddha-recitation never ceased. Her resolve for the Way was firm, the same for decades as for a single day. In the autumn of 1976 she felt unwell and took to her bed, never to rise. When her illness became critical, a fellow practitioner said to Xin, "Rebirth in the West is what matters most." Xin smiled and nodded, joined her palms, and thanked her. To the very end her right mindfulness was clear, and she passed away serenely. Her face was as if alive, ruddy and lustrous. It was eight in the evening of the twenty-ninth day of the eighth lunar month of 1976; her worldly age was seventy-nine.

Zong Ru's secular surname was Huang and her given name Zhixue; she was from Wujin in Jiangsu and left home in middle age. In her early years she took refuge with Master Yuanying. She was tonsured at Zizhu Nunnery in Suzhou, taking the nun Lianjing as her teacher. At sixty she went to Longchang Monastery on Mount Bao and sought the greater precepts. All her life she cultivated the Pure Land method with diligence, was strict and meticulous in the precepts, and delighted in giving. She passed away on February 19, 1977. Though ill, her right mindfulness was clear and she knew beforehand that her time had come. Until her rebirth her recitation never stopped. Her countenance was moist and radiant, more so than in life. Her worldly age was eighty.

Dao Yin's secular surname was Guo; she was from Shuojiang County in Yangzhou and lived at No. 625 Lannidu Road in Pudong, Shanghai. From childhood she ate vegetarian food, took refuge with the Elder Laiguo of Gaomin Monastery, practiced the pure karma, and also took part in inquiry. In middle age her husband died, and she saw through worldly ties, left home, and received the śrāmaṇerikā precepts, dwelling in a small nunnery on Magang Mountain at Shanren Bridge in Suzhou. During the Cultural Revolution she moved to Shanghai. Because she had once received from the old Master Xuyun instruction in the rules of practice, he urged her to cultivate the Pure Land, and from then on she followed it faithfully without wavering. Bold and diligent, she single-mindedly held the name. Before her rebirth she felt a slight illness and knew she would not recover, and she arranged all her affairs after death. At the end she saw with her own eyes Amitābha Buddha send forth light to receive her; right mindfulness came before her, and she passed away serenely. Her worldly age was seventy-one. She died on the second day of the fifth lunar month of 1975.

Ru Lian's secular surname was Xu; she was from Tiantai County in Zhejiang. After her marriage she bore a son and a daughter. At twenty-two her husband died. An elder uncle of the clan conspired with others, intending to sell Lian. An old woman of the neighborhood who recited the Buddha's name was on very good terms with Lian; learning of the plot, she secretly told her. Lian hid in the old woman's house. The old woman taught Lian to recite in silence the holy name of the Great Being, praying for her protection, and so she escaped being seized. Some days later she planned to go to Sheng County, but the road was long and she did not know which way to turn. Reaching Xinchang, she saw a boat passing and asked for passage. Arriving at Sheng, she saw a young nun washing clothes by the river, and Lian at once asked to stay one night in her nunnery. The nun gladly agreed and brought her to see her teacher. Because Lian was young and dignified in bearing, the teacher told her to stay in the nunnery, help with the chores, and study the lessons. Before long the teacher passed away, and her disciple, the young nun, also left the nunnery, so Lian inherited the incense and fire. She dwelt in the nunnery for seven years. When the war of resistance broke out, Lian took refuge in Hangzhou, living in a nunnery by the side of Xiangfu Bridge. After Liberation the nunnery was turned into a school, and she moved to Daxian Nunnery, where she lived more than ten years. Though Lian never received the greater precepts, she was careful in body and conduct, purer than ice and frost. Her practice was diligent and her longing and loathing were keen; morning and evening lessons were never interrupted. If illness left her unable to hold up, she would always take leave before the Buddha. Each day she recited three scrolls of the Diamond Sutra, five thousand recitations of Amitābha's holy name, and five hundred rounds of the Rebirth Mantra. On the ten fasting days she recited the Kṣitigarbha Sutra. Whatever offerings she received, after providing for her own sustenance she would use the rest to relieve the poor and needy. A year before her rebirth she said to people, "I shall remain in this world only a little more than a year!" In 1965 she was eighty-four. One night in the first lunar month she dreamed of two monks who said to her, "In the second month of this year you will die." Then they wrote on the table the character for "death" and showed it to her. At the sight Lian was overjoyed. On the night of the fifteenth of the second month she again dreamed of two monks who came and said, "On the eighteenth you will die." When she woke, she summoned her nephew and made her will, entrusting her affairs after death. On the eighteenth she bathed in fragrant water; she asked Master Haishan to arrange the seated casket and the cremation. When all was done, she sat upright, formed the Amitābha mudrā with her hands, single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name, and asked her fellow practitioners to recite for her. All saw that Lian wore a smile and showed no sign of illness. At noon she passed serenely to the West.

Liao Chun's secular surname was Zhang; he was from Lin'an County in Zhejiang and left home at the age of four in a small nunnery at Dingtian in that district. In the seventh year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing (1881), at twenty-seven, he received the full precepts at Guoqing Monastery on Mount Tiantai, and after the precept ceremony returned to the nunnery. Because the nunnery was small and the people many, he moved to Xianglin Monastery in Pingyang. The monastery buildings were cramped and low, unable to hold the assembly, so the Master threw himself into managing and building, raising the great hall and the side chambers on both wings, and thus the community was able to dwell in peace and walk the Way. The sound of the wooden fish, drum, bell, and chime never ceased, and he was revered by believers far and near. The Master was sparing in his own living and generous and kind to others, and all his life he maintained seven places for lecturing on the sutras. Through the six periods of the day, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, he never parted from a single utterance of the Buddha's name, the same for decades as for a single day. In the year of his rebirth, in the first days of the second lunar month, he felt a slight illness and instructed his disciples not to call a doctor or give him medicine. He especially invited great virtuous ones to the monastery to hold a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat to aid his rebirth. At about eleven at night on the eighteenth of that month, the Master saw with his own eyes the thousand-armed Guanyin appear in the sky, and his joy was extraordinary. At midnight on the twentieth he asked his great-grandson Pinglian, "What time is it now?" The answer was, "Twelve o'clock." The Master said gladly, "Good; at this moment I can go." He sat up in bed, joined both palms, and said to the assembly, "I have seen lotus flowers covering the ground in this room." At that time the sound of Buddha-recitation from his mouth still came, now breaking off, now continuing. Before long he closed his eyes and passed away. His worldly age was seventy-five, his monastic seniority forty-eight.

Zheng Chi's secular surname was Wang; she was from Changshu in Jiangsu. Of peasant family, she kept her chastity and never married. In her twenties she went to White Robe Nunnery in the outskirts of Suzhou and was tonsured under the old bhikṣuṇī Huizhi, receiving the Dharma name Zhengchi. White Robe Nunnery stood north of the village of Yellow Bean Sprout, and had originally been the ancient White Robe Temple, always presided over by monks. At the end of the Qing it was destroyed in the flames of war and lay waste for a full sixty years. The bhikṣuṇī Huizhi raised funds by begging and rebuilt it, changing the name to White Robe Nunnery. In 1928 the Master went to Mount Bao in Nanjing to receive the greater precepts, the precept master being the old monk De. From the age of thirty-six she closed a three-year Huayan retreat. Her daily lessons were never once neglected, and in her spare time she recited the Buddha's name. After the bhikṣuṇī Huizhi passed away, the Master succeeded her as abbess. She was always known for strictness in the precepts, warning her disciples that on entering the Buddha hall they must not chatter or talk at random and must not wear their robes untidy. Ordinary believers admired the Master's practice and often gave in charity at the nunnery to form karmic bonds; the Master spared no effort in protecting the Three Jewels, and the five great halls of the nunnery she repaired and made new. On the twenty-ninth day of the third lunar month of 1949 she passed away seated, without illness, at the age of fifty-one. Shortly before her rebirth she had a slight cold. She told her disciple's disciple Huide, "In three more days I shall attain rebirth." The disciple's disciple said, "We hope the Master will live some years more, to teach us." The Master said, "People must go in the end; why keep me? I go first; I hope you will come after. Recite the Buddha's name well for me, and do not disturb me. After my rebirth, do not come near my bed, do not touch my body; only recite the Buddha's name. The small bell is to be struck only an hour after my rebirth, and softly when it is struck." Having spoken, she sat cross-legged on the bed reciting the Buddha's name. She said of herself that Amitābha Buddha had come, and with these words she closed her eyes and passed away serenely. At the time more than a hundred people knelt on the ground reciting the Buddha's name to see her off. A hundred days later her body was sent to Lingyan for cremation, and a great many five-colored relics were found: some red as vermilion pearls, some green as kingfisher jade, with blue, yellow, white, and purple all present.

You Kong's secular surname was Zhu. She was from Erhui Town in Qidong County, Jiangsu. Her father was a carpenter by trade and had two daughters, Kong and her elder sister. In childhood Kong and her sister already ate vegetarian food with their mother, gladdening their parents' hearts, and vowed never to marry. Kong then received the five precepts at Shouan Monastery in Chongming. Afterwards her father and mother died one after the other. One summer, at the place of Master Yechen in Chongming, Kong heard a lecture on the Brahmā Net Sutra and resolved to leave home; she and her sister together went to Zhulin Nunnery in their own town and had their hair shaved under a certain bhikṣuṇī. In the spring of 1955 the two sisters went together to Mount Bao in Nanjing to receive the full precepts. When they came out of the precept hall they returned to Zhulin Nunnery as before, cultivating the pure karma with diligence, their whole purpose set on the West. In the winter of 1958 she showed illness, yet still sat cross-legged day and night, her recitation never ceasing. On the fourth day of the first lunar month of the Jihai year, 1959, she said to her sister and her disciples, "All within the world is suffering, not worth clinging to. I beg you to recite the Buddha's name with me and help me to be reborn in the West." On that day at the hour of you, amid the sound of the assembly's Buddha-recitation, she sat facing west and passed away. A day and a night later her whole body was supple, and the crown of her head was still warm. Her casket stood three days, her countenance as if alive, and she was cremated according to the Dharma; countless relics were obtained, all clear and lustrous as gems, brilliant as pearls and jade. Her skull was split into several pieces, and the cracks took the shape of bodhi leaves; on one piece the cracks seemed to form the four characters "the mind creates, the mind is." Truly this is strange! Master Yuanche once wrote a long song on the matter.

Yuan Song was from Wuxi in Jiangsu, born in 1886. Her secular surname was Shi, and her husband's surname Wang. In 1928, because her husband kept a mistress in secret, she resolutely saw through worldly ties, left her home, and became a nun under Master Canxia of Xilin Nunnery. All her secular relatives she avoided and refused to acknowledge. In 1934 she received the full precepts. Master Xia kept strict rules and earnestly instructed her, guiding her to leave the sea of suffering quickly. The Master herself truly reflected that the bitter courses of human life are boundless and without limit; therefore she strictly kept the precepts, resolved to escape, single-mindedly recited Guanyin's holy name, and closed two retreats. When she was abbess of Xilin Nunnery the income from incense and offerings was quite ample, yet she herself lived in extraordinary austerity. At times she ate bean dregs with her food, and even the grains left in the water when washing the pot she would eat rather than pour out carelessly. In the early years of the war of resistance, when Japanese planes bombed Wuxi, the Master did not avoid the danger but made a vow to suffer in place of living beings. It happened then that a bomb fell beside her and destroyed the house; nearby stood a round barrel, shaken by the blast so that it rolled wildly over the ground. Yet the Master devoutly recited Guanyin's holy name as if nothing were happening, and came through wholly unharmed. In 1968, to settle the last of her worldly ties, the Master did not leave her meditation room for three years, single-mindedly reciting the holy name of the Seven Tathāgatas. On the morning of April 11, 1971, she told her disciples to ask for leave from their work units, and said, "Today I am going." Hearing this, the disciples all wept in silence with tears in their eyes as they arranged everything, attending on her left and right and joining in the recitation of the Tathāgata's holy name. At about three in the afternoon the Master changed her clothes and sat quietly. At about four she joined her palms, bowed toward the sky, and said, "Amitābha Buddha has come to receive me!" and at once passed away serenely, aged eighty-five. The Master was humane and forgiving, upright and true, kind and good; whenever she saw people in poverty and hardship she spared no effort to help them, and she was praised by all.

Tian Ci's secular surname was Sun; her ancestral home was Wuzuo Town in the southern district of Yancheng, northern Jiangsu. At twenty-four she was tonsured under the old Master Huishan and received the full precepts at a monastery in Yangzhou. After that she came to Suzhou and served three years as a guest monk at Xiaoputuo Monastery at Huqiu; then she went to Baofu Nunnery at Zhabei in Shanghai, again as a guest monk, for three years. Afterwards she returned to Suzhou and dwelt at Erlang Nunnery at the Feng Gate. When the Master first entered the nunnery there were only three broken rooms amid a stretch of wilderness. She vowed to restore the Dharma site; for several years she cut back on food and clothing, labored hard, accumulated funds, and built three great halls, in a moment turning shattered tiles and crumbling walls into a solemn place of practice. In ordinary times the Master recited the Great Compassion Mantra and the great name of myriad virtues, her ascetic practice outstanding, and she was praised with admiration by the assembly. In the early autumn of 1977 her strength gradually failed. In the winter of 1978 she suffered from dropsy, yet body and mind were at peace and she felt no pain; though ill and confined to bed she recited the Buddha's name without cease. On May 5, 1979 (the tenth day of the fourth lunar month), at fifteen minutes past four in the afternoon, with right mindfulness clear, she passed away serenely. At that time the nuns of Wenshan Monastery and many laymen and laywomen gathered to recite the Buddha's name and see her off. In the very last instant before her rebirth the Master said to herself, "Amitābha Buddha has come! He has come!" With these words she closed her eyes and passed away. Her worldly age was eighty-seven. After cremation, a number of śarīra flowers were found.

Miao Xing's secular surname was Zhou; she was from Nanxun in Huzhou, Zhejiang, of poor peasant stock. Her husband died young, leaving a son and a daughter, and these too died one after the other. Knowing herself to be heavy in karma and thin in fate, at twenty-four she resolved to leave home and went to Hangzhou, where she was tonsured as a śrāmaṇerikā under a certain old nun of Dabei Nunnery, receiving the Dharma name Miaoxing. Later she went to Mount Qixia in Nanjing to receive the precepts. By nature the Master was kind and compassionate, and ordinarily cultivated the Pure Land exclusively. She once closed a retreat in the Zhenjing Retreat at Zhonglou Tou in Suzhou. Three years later she became abbess of Tianlong Nunnery in the Northern Garden. At seventy-five she suffered from dropsy. Bedridden for more than twenty days, knowing she would not recover, she would not seek a doctor or take medicine, but single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name and sought the West. Three days before her rebirth she said to her disciple, "Three more days and I shall attain rebirth." On the third day her right mindfulness was still clear and she held the Buddha's name. Unwittingly she sighed, "It is already the third day; why has the Buddha not yet come to receive me?" Even as she spoke she suddenly felt light filling her eyes, and beckoning to her disciple she said, "The light is too bright; put out the lamp for me, quickly." The assembly said, "No lamp has been lit." Then the Master joined her palms with the others, called the holy name, and passed away seated. After her death the crown of her head was warm and her limbs supple, the auspicious signs plain to see. It was eleven o'clock at noon on June 16, 1974.

Yuan Changjing's maiden name was Jiang; her family lived in Hankou, Hubei. At thirty-six she resolved to recite the Buddha's name and took refuge under Master Deqing, receiving the Dharma name Changjing. She received the five precepts at Yuanzhao Monastery in Hankou. She kept a long vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha's name for thirty-three years, attaining rebirth at sixty-nine. In ordinary times the laywoman was diligent in practice; winter and summer, cold and heat alike, she rose at four o'clock every day to recite the Buddha's name, and by day she devoted herself to bowing to the Buddha. Whenever the weather was hot and her robe grew wet with sweat, she kept several robes ready for changing, taking care that her deportment be dignified and that she never bow to the Buddha in everyday clothes. When she saw people in rags begging at her door, she took off her own clothes and gave them away without a sign of reluctance. If someone stole articles from her maiden home, once she noticed she not only did not stop them, but went to the kitchen, filled a bowl to the brim with rice, let them eat their fill, and then let them go. In the first month of 1944 she suddenly felt a slight illness. By the tenth day of the fourth month she saw with her own eyes the Three Saints of the West come. On the morning of the seventeenth she said to her family, "I want my head shaved. Go quickly to Guiyuan Monastery and ask the chief seat to come and give me the precepts." She also had sandalwood incense burned and bathed. When the bathing and change of clothes were done the chief seat arrived, shaved her head, and conferred the śrāmaṇerikā precepts. On the morning of the twentieth she told her family, "Today I am going home to the West. Go quickly to Guiyuan Monastery and invite the chief seat and the other masters to come and recite the Buddha's name, to help me to be reborn in the West." At about eight, when the chief seat of Guiyuan Monastery arrived with the assembly of monks, the laywoman had already had herself raised up and sat cross-legged in a chair. With her precept certificate hung on her breast and her counting beads in her hand, she said, "Amitābha Buddha and all the holy assembly have long since come. Do not weep; recite the Buddha's name for me." With these words she herself called the Buddha's name several times, while the assembly around her joined in the holy name. At ten o'clock she quietly passed into stillness, as if entering samādhi. At ten the next day, when she was placed in the casket, she sat upright as before. On the day of cremation a thousand people recited the Buddha's name and followed the funeral. After cremation her ashes turned golden yellow, and seven relics, pale white in color, large and small, were obtained.

Fan Gunong, style name Jidong, was from Yueli in Jiaxing, Zhejiang. His father, Mr. Wenzhi, kept the family in farming and letters. Gunong was bright from childhood. At fifteen he entered the imperial academy as the top candidate. At eighteen he studied at Nanyang Public School in Shanghai, where he always stood at the head of his fellows. He once carried his books to Qiushi Academy in Hangzhou. Among his schoolmates was one Jiang Baiqi, whose father, Zhiyou, ran a daily newspaper in Tianjin and constantly instructed Baiqi in Eastern and Western philosophy, greatly praising the unique supremacy of Buddhist truth. From this Gunong first came to know of Buddhism. At first he read the "Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment"; though he could not fully grasp its meaning, his heart greatly loved it. At that time he was studying the "Elements of Geometry," a book whose notes said, "He who studies this book should merely follow the principles laid down to solve the problems; he must not doubt, nor may he invent." From this he understood that in reading Buddhist sutras one should do likewise: accept the Buddha's words in faith, not interpret them willfully, not doubt them. In his early twenties he married Qi Jinliang. Soon after he founded the Yuxiu Girls' School, the first women's school in Jiaxing. At twenty-seven he went to Japan to study in Tokyo. He studied under such gentlemen as Gui Bohua and Zhang Taiyan, and came to hear of the Laṅkāvatāra and Consciousness-Only teachings. In a bookshop he found the "Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna" and its "Record of Meaning" and read them, and his faith grew firmer still. At twenty-nine he returned to China and served as principal of the Second Provincial Middle School of Zhejiang, reading Buddhist books in his spare time. The next year he went to Baoben Monastery in Pinghu to hear Master Huashan lecture on the Amitābha Sutra with its commentary. With the founding of the Republic he established a Buddhist study society in his home district and served as its lecturer himself. Young students turned to him in great numbers. In every winter and summer vacation he spread the Dharma in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Songjiang, and Shaoxing. The sound of the Dharma spread far, and all quarters followed; Buddhist groups sprang up throughout Jiangsu and Zhejiang. In 1917 he received the refuges and precepts from Master Dixian at Guanzong Monastery in Ningbo, receiving the Dharma name Huanxiu. In January 1929 he was engaged by the Shanghai Buddhist Bookstore as chief editor, and also presided over the "Buddhist Questions and Answers" column of the Buddhist Fortnightly. Whenever there was a question, he answered as a drum answers the stick, analyzing with precision and fairness, and no questioner failed to be delighted and convinced. From this his Dharma connections spread throughout the world. In April 1935 the monks and laity of Shanghai organized the Buddhist Daily News and chose Gunong to direct its editorial policy, which lasted three years. Then, because of the war of resistance, the daily ceased publication. He went to Mount Tianmu and dwelt seven months at Chanyuan Monastery. Sheltering among forests and ravines, he devoted himself wholly to the pure karma. Afterwards he returned to Shanghai and lectured on the Awakening of Faith at the Shengxin Lotus Society, established a Buddhist study class, and expounded the three Pure Land sutras and the Treatise on Rebirth. He then turned to the Dharma characteristics, lecturing on the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only and the Cheng Weishi Lun and others. Gunong understood the doctrinal school of Dharma characteristics and in practice took refuge in the Pure Land. In the thirty-fourth year of the Republic (1945) he returned to Jiaxing, being then already sixty-five and declining in years. Yet still he shrank from no weariness and went again and again to Pinghu, Songjiang, and Suzhou to expound the Dharma. Pitying the children of his home district who had no schooling, he gave over his own house as the Fan Family Primary School to nurture them. In the thirty-seventh year (1948) his fellow practitioners in Shanghai, longing for Gunong as children for a lost mother and yearning after him most earnestly, invited him to Shanghai, where he stayed at the Shengxin Lotus Society. By then Gunong's hair and beard were all white, yet his spirit was remarkably vigorous and his resolve to spread the Dharma grew keener with age. He founded the "Dharma Characteristics Study Society" and expounded the treatises on Dharma characteristics and consciousness-only. When the World Buddhist Laymen's Grove was reorganized he was elected its sixth president. In the spring of 1951, having finished lecturing on the Treatise on the Manifestation of the Sacred Teaching, he showed a slight illness the next day, March 22. On April 12 (the seventh day of the third lunar month) he passed away in hospital. At the end his mind was clear, his recitation of the Buddha's name unbroken, and with a smile he was gone. Ten days later he was cremated, and his remains were placed at Lingyan Mountain. Counting from his birth on the tenth day of the tenth month of the seventh year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing, he lived seventy-one years. Gunong was broadly versed in the three baskets and devoted himself to spreading the Dharma for forty years. He encouraged and lifted up those who came after as though he could not do enough. His compassion was deep and earnest, rare in his generation. He was the author of the Life of Śākyamuni, An Anthology of the Mahāyāna Teaching of Emptiness, A Stringed Explanation of the Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses, A Textbook of Dharma Characteristics, A Structural Analysis of the Cheng Weishi Lun, Selections from the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Birthday Commemorations, Buddhist Questions and Answers, and the Collected Works of Huan'an, all extant in the world.

Jiang Weinong, given name Zhongye, Dharma name Miaoxu. In the books he wrote he sometimes signed himself Huanzhu, sometimes Shengguan. He was from Lingge Village in Jiangning, Jiangsu. His grandfather Lefeng held office in Hubei and settled there. In childhood Nong already followed his grandfather in reciting the Diamond Sutra, and to the end of his life never let it lapse. His father Jinwu spent decades in official travel, from Jiangxi to Sichuan, and Nong attended and assisted him throughout. In the renyin year of the Guangxu reign (1902) Nong passed the provincial examination; he nourished his parents' hearts and gladdened them, taking no pleasure in advancement. In the autumn of the xinhai year (1911) he came to Shanghai. On his father's death, amid his grief, he seized the occasion to urge his mother, née Guo, to keep a long vegetarian fast and recite the Buddha's name. At that time a drought in five northern provinces brought terrible famine, and Nong, entrusted by Jian Zhaonan, carried funds north and joined the Buddhist relief committee, disbursing a hundred thousand in loans and saving a great many lives. In the gengshen year (1920) he returned to Shanghai, and his mother showed signs of illness; Nong recited the Great Compassion Mantra for her and had the family devoutly recite the Buddha's name to empower her. At the end his mother sat up, faced west, joined her palms, and passed away reciting the Buddha's name. By this Nong's faith grew firmer still. With the Jian brothers Zhaonan and Yujie he founded the Gongdelin Buddhist Sutra Circulation Office in Shanghai, gathering scriptures from the northern and southern woodblock printing offices and from the various famous mountains and circulating them throughout the country, spreading the Buddha Dharma widely. In the summer of the xinyou year (1921) the laymen of Nanyuan in Shanghai initiated a lecture society, and Nong proposed inviting Master Dixian to lecture on the Mahāyāna Calming and Contemplation. Nong took notes every day, and where the meaning was deep and subtle he used winding parables and similes to make it clear; the work was titled "Narrated Record." In the summer of the yichou year (1925) the Venerable Baipuren came south to preside over the Golden Light Dharma Assembly, and Nong was unanimously chosen to assist in its propagation; thus from Shanghai to Hangzhou, to Hunan, to Hubei, to Nanjing, he traveled several thousand li, attending to the affairs of the assembly in person with perfect order. In the autumn of the jisi year (1929), at the invitation of good believers in Fujian, he went to Fuzhou to expound the Buddha Dharma, returning only after three months. In the autumn of the gengwu year (1930) he began lecturing in Shanghai on the "Narrated Record of Mahāyāna Calming and Contemplation," finishing only after more than a year. When the Shengxin Lotus Society was established he was elected its president. Thus he often lectured on Mahāyāna sutras in the society and led its members in reciting the Buddha's name and bowing in repentance. In the summer of the jiaxu year (1934) he began lecturing on the Diamond Sutra, and when the Dharma assembly concluded the lectures filled three thick volumes. In the early summer of the wuyin year (1938) he showed illness, his stomach unable to digest. When a friend inquired after him, Nong said, "Once the yellow plum season passes, the illness will clear up of itself." His disciples recited the Buddha's name for him in the Buddha hall next door, the sound of the name unbroken all day. Nong also lay at peace reciting silently, his mind perfectly clear. By the middle of the fifth lunar month his illness had worsened slightly; he lay in bed unable to rise, yet his mind grew clearer still. On the night of the eighteenth he said of himself, "Golden light shines everywhere; the Buddha has come to receive me." He then invited his fellow practitioners to gather, but Cai Jiping, being detained by business, arrived only at midnight; Nong still instructed him, saying, "In practice, the 'Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows' is the most essential." Then he joined his palms and spoke no more, and amid the sound of the Buddha's name from his fellow practitioners and his family, he passed away seated. He was sixty-seven.

Xu Zhijing, given name Yehu, was born in Pengze, Jiangxi. In the Guichen year of the Guangxu reign he won the jinshi degree and served at the Hanlin Academy for eight years, retiring into seclusion after the restoration. In 1917 he turned his heart to the Buddhas and devoted himself wholly to the Pure Land. In 1922 he went to Putuo to pay homage to the Bodhisattva and called upon Master Yinguang, seeking refuge and receiving the Dharma name Zhijing. From that time he kept a long vegetarian fast. He resolved to compile three works, the "Eulogy on the Spiritual Responses of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva," "A General Record of Karmic Response in History," and "A Buddhist Discourse for Deliverance from Calamity," completing and circulating them in turn; all among monks and laity who held right understanding marveled that his Buddhist insight was profound and his literary craft refined. In 1936 he again asked Master Yinguang to bestow the bodhisattva precepts. Though Zhijing was broadly versed in scripture and doctrine, he was in all things like the simplest man or woman, earnestly reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. He bowed to every monk he met and paid homage to every Buddha image he saw. Zhijing was frail and often unwell. In May 1938 he took refuge amid the troubles at Huanglong Temple on Guling, Mount Lu, and lay sick. By the intercalary seventh month his condition had somewhat healed. On the first day of the ninth month he summoned Yao Banseng, who lodged with him in the temple, and entrusted him with his affairs after death. Then he smiled and said, "This morning I dreamed that the Buddha came, adorned all about with jeweled netting, radiant with the marks of perfection and light. He said to me, I have come to see you. I at once bowed to him. After a while I woke. Was it not the World-Honored One's compassion, coming especially to comfort me? If he would only manifest his welcome and allow me to be reborn by virtue of past karma, what great good fortune that would be!" Having spoken he joined his palms and said, "We shall meet again in the West!" From then on he made no further sound, only single-mindedly and silently reciting the Buddha's name. At seven o'clock on the morning of the third day he passed serenely to the West. His whole body grew cold, yet the crown of his head remained warm. When placed in the coffin his whole body was soft as cotton, exactly like an old monk settled in meditation. His countenance was radiant, more so than in life. This is what is meant by the faculties at ease, right mindfulness clear, the relinquishing of life serene, as though entering samadhi. His body was kept in the temple and the Buddha's name recited for seven days, then cremated in accordance with the Dharma; his ashes were preserved at Huanglong Temple. He was sixty-three.

Xia Lianju was eager to learn from youth and broadly versed in the whole of the canon. He deeply probed the principle of mind and was accomplished in many arts. In mid-life he quietly studied the Buddhist scriptures. From the doctrinal schools to the teaching, from the exoteric to the esoteric, he penetrated them all without obstruction, gathering everything into the Pure Land. In the Yichou year, when the warlord Zhang Zongchang governed Shandong, he was charged with a fabricated crime, his property was confiscated, and an order was issued for his arrest, so he fled to Japan to escape the calamity. Returning after a year, he closed himself in retreat at Tianjin. His small room held only an image of Amitābha Buddha; with single mind he devoutly held the sacred name, stilling thought and cutting off deliberation, applying himself to the Way with utmost dedication. Thus he passed ten years. Through the union of his practice and the Buddha's power, auspicious signs appeared again and again; he saw the Buddha and saw light, yet never revealed this to others. He had a verse: "One scroll of the six-character sutra / Breaks open ten years of darkness. / People say that I recite the Buddha; / I say the Buddha is reciting me. / Through clouds of delusion and fog of dust passing on, / In a clear pool I see the round moon's reflection a perfect circle." In the September

18 Incident broke out, and the national crisis was at its height. The monks and laity of Beijing repeatedly and earnestly invited him, so he came to the capital and settled beside the Drum Tower. He pursued the Way with keen resolve and gave himself wholly to teaching, widely praising the Mahayana and proclaiming the Pure Land school, tireless in instructing others, the same decade after decade.
