Those seeking the Way and inquiring into doctrine filled his courtyard day by day; those obtaining the benefit of the Dharma were beyond counting. Some attained clear realization and saw their own nature; some at rebirth stood and departed; some showed auspicious signs at rebirth; some left the world and became monastics. As for those who, on hearing the teaching, awakened faith and cleansed their hearts toward goodness, they were more than could be reckoned. In deep winter of the Yisi year, aged eighty-three, he said one day to those about him, "My great matter is accomplished; I am resolved to leave this defiled world." At that time his spirit was vigorous. The essential Dharma he taught and the states revealed in his practice were for the most part things he had never before spoken of. Ten days later he showed a slight illness. At night his family attended him and heard him reciting the Buddha's name without break. Suddenly they heard a single ringing utterance; startled, they looked, and in that very name of myriad virtues he passed serenely to rebirth. Right mindfulness was clear, and he went as soon as he said he would. He entered the sea of Amitābha's vow, a model for students; how true it is! Several verses on mindful recitation from his retreat years survive in transmission.

Chen Wuwo, style name Faxiang, lived in Shanghai though his ancestral home was Qiantang. He served as editor of the "Pacific News" and the "Republic Daily" among other publications. Deeply learned in Chinese letters, he founded the New World News Agency and acted as its head. The layman Chen Baixu guided him to faith in Buddhism. On reading the "Protection of Life Picture Book" he resolved to become a vegetarian. To spread the Buddha Dharma he opened the Great Dharma Wheel Bookstore, circulating Buddhist books. He also compiled and printed the monthly "Awakened Sentience." The monthly's contents were substantial and lively, and the editing and selection of manuscripts Chen Wuwo personally undertook. It was published for more than ten years, with subscribers at home and abroad. He also wrote "All Are Rejoicing" and "Strange Dreams of Rebirth," works that accord with principle and with the capacity of beings, much favored by readers. At forty-two he lost his wife and never married again. Wuwo firmly believed in the Pure Land. He once told his friend Dou Cunwo, "I have read the Master Zhongfeng's

Three Rites of Mind and found it deeply effective." Every dawn at cockcrow he rose, and his worship and recitation were diligent. In dealing with the world he was honest toward others, a kindly elder. On November 3, 1967 he passed away in illness while reciting the Buddha's name, aged eighty-four. His son Xinchun, style name Nianci, was also versed in the Dharma and wrote "Nianci's Essays." Resolute in the Pure Land, he passed away early of a frail body.

Zhang Dalang, of Dapan Village, Huaiyuan, Anhui, was illiterate but most filial to his mother, earning his living as a stone mason. He received the practice of reciting the Buddha's name from Xu Benxiao, a man of his district; his wife tried hard to stop him, but he was not moved. Before long his wife died, and he applied himself with single mind, bowing and reciting day and night without rest. He did this for seven years. In the year 1920, as the Mid-Autumn Festival approached, he showed a slight illness. He said to his mother, "After I leave I shall surely come first to deliver you; do not grieve." His mother, who already kept a vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha's name, also urged her son: "Recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and seek rebirth." At noon on the thirteenth day of the eighth month he instructed his younger brother Genlang: "From now on you must serve our old mother well. I am about to go. The heavenly music of the West has come to welcome me; do you hear it?" Having spoken, he lit incense, sat cross-legged, joined his palms, and passed away. At that moment heavenly music suddenly sounded in the sky, like a small trumpet, its tone so sweet as to be beyond description. Besides the heavenly music there were two lamps as large as basins, waving and rippling, seen by all the assembled people for about two hours before they disappeared. People outside the village all heard the sound of the heavenly music above Dapan Village, and several hundred came to watch. Yet the moment they entered the village the sound ceased, while the villagers still heard it. Not one of the onlookers failed to sigh in wonder. Dalang was then thirty years old. Years later his mother lay ill and said to those around her, "My son Dalang has come to welcome me," and so passed away. Wang Kunru of Dama Works in Yujiao County, Anhui, wrote to Master Yinguang about Dalang's affair. The master replied, "A matter as extraordinary as mason Zhang's must mean there are people in that place who earnestly recite the Buddha's name. You should go and inquire and confirm it, in order to encourage faith." Wang Kunru then wrote to Huaiyuan to ask, and received replies from four gentlemen of the village, Pan Weisheng, Hu Jiachun, Zheng Guangyi, and Pan Fuyi, testifying that they had all seen and heard it together and that it was indeed beyond doubt. The mason Zhang was a man who could not read a single character, yet the moment he heard the practice of reciting the Buddha's name he believed, accepted, and practiced it. Though he met with setbacks, his resolve was never weakened. With the three requisites of faith, vow, and practice complete, after seven years of diligent practice he left the burning house. The entry is easy and the success swift, all the more confirming that the Pure Land method answers the capacity of these times.

Zhou Zishan, named Yuying, was the eldest grandson of the great merchant Zhou Fujiu of Ji'an, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was raised by his grandmother, Lady Tan. Naturally clever and fond of learning, he was kind and gentle, his heart empty as a valley. Though born into a wealthy house he had not the slightest trace of arrogance or extravagance. In office he was known for uprightness and loyalty. When colleagues, relatives, friends, and even servants erred, he never turned a harsh word or angry look on them. When he retired into seclusion he closed his door and nurtured his own virtue. On casually reading the Buddhist canon he knew that the Buddha Dharma is the root of all things in the world, and that the welfare of society and the deliverance of all beings rest upon it. Thereupon he took refuge under Master Dixian and received the Dharma name Zhizang. From then on he kept a long fast and recited the Buddha's name, refraining from killing and nurturing life, frugal in his own living. To friends and relations who asked for help he never tired of responding. He relieved the hungry and cold as a matter of course, generously aiding every good undertaking. All the worldly good he did he dedicated, with a great bodhi-mind, toward the West. In 1932, the Renshen year, he reached the age of knowing his mandate. On the eighth day of the fourth month, which fell on the Buddha's birthday, at seven in the morning he showed a slight illness. Feeling pain in his back and waist, he asked someone to pat him gently for relief. He himself sat cross-legged facing west, single-mindedly reciting "Amitābha Buddha" in a clear voice. After a long time his voice gradually lowered, and he passed away. The person patting his back, seeing him long still and silent, felt for his breath and knew he had already relinquished his body and gone to rebirth. A rare fragrance filled the room and did not disperse for five days.

Fu Chunpu, given name Chuan, was from Dongguo Village, Qingjiang County, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was educated by his mother, Lady Nie, who in her hardship kept her honor and raised him. He studied law, government, and police science, and served in posts as county-office clerk and school principal. His mother had long served the Bodhisattva Guanyin, keeping a vegetarian fast and reciting the Buddha's name. In 1928, because of his mother's illness, he vowed to make a pilgrimage to Putuo; his mother's illness soon healed. So in the ninth month of 1931 he went to Putuo to fulfill his vow. Paying homage at the Cave of the Dharma Sound, he felt the Bodhisattva appear in a white robe holding a pure vase and a willow branch. He further sought to know his past lives and saw a mendicant in tattered clothing, and so understood that the wheel of rebirth was no illusion. He called upon Master Yinguang at Baoguo Temple in Suzhou and first heard the essentials of the Pure Land teaching. From then on he believed, vowed, and recited, advancing without slack. He also took refuge under Master Desen and received the Dharma name Chuanchuan. In 1933 he served as lecturer-in-chief of the Lujiang Recitation Grove, guiding and encouraging many followers. His family had long been poor and he was frail and often ill. That spring he dreamed that the Bodhisattva Guanyin spoke to him, setting the time in the seventh month. After the Ullambana assembly he fell ill and, with single mind, recited the Buddha's name, forgetting his suffering. On the twenty-third, relatives and friends aided his recitation; he lost consciousness, then revived after a while. He invited Master Daren and entrusted him with his cremation. On the twenty-sixth he lapsed again and the family wept around him. The layman smiled and stopped them, saying, "Why do you weep? I shall be reborn on the festival day of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva." At the appointed time, sitting upright in a chair, he formed the Amitābha mudra, gazed fixedly on the Buddha image, and passed away peacefully. His whole body was cold yet the crown of his head alone was warm, his face lovely and radiant beyond his living looks. On the second day of the intercalary seventh month the abbot Dasong of Tonghui Temple in Zhangshu Town and Master Daren came to attend to his encoffining; he sat cross-legged with palms joined, exactly like a living man. The day before had been great wind and rain, yet when at the hour of Zi the fire was lit the sky suddenly brightened, and a rare fragrance filled the air, neither orchid nor sandalwood. A beam of white light issued from the coffin and shot toward the West. He was forty-eight.

Bei Zushan, styled Youwei, was a native of Suzhou. Naturally quick, he was filial to his mother. She was blind, and he licked her eyes and restored her sight. His elder sister married into the Yan family, but both husband and wife died young, leaving one son and two daughters, small and helpless. Zushan raised and supported them all, even seeing them through their higher schooling. Among his brothers and friends any who met sudden hardship he helped with all he had, never a grudging look. In his prime he drifted through officialdom, serving as head of the Nanjing Electric Works, confidential secretary to Song Ziwen, and customs director. In his forties, differing in opinion from those in power, he retired home and gave himself to the study of body and mind, life and nature. He first practiced the Daoist arts of breathing and guidance, then studied the esoteric school. Nearing the age of knowing his mandate he at last heard from a teacher the Pure Land method of holding the name, rejoiced to have found his true home, and cast aside all his former learning and practice. One phrase, "Amitābha," he held single-mindedly. Even when distant guests came or pressing matters arose, he would not come out to respond until his daily recitation was complete. In the autumn of 1936 he suddenly fell ill. Knowing the affinity with the Pure Land had ripened, he arranged in advance all the matters of his final moments. Fearing that his wife's deep worldly love would bring tears, he had already moved her to another room and let her know nothing. Besides inviting several Dharma friends to lead the assisting recitation, he kept only his eldest daughter beside him to attend to him, and earnestly charged the household, "You must not weep or make a disturbance. For eight hours after my death you must not touch the body. Everything must be done as the book "Companion for the Final Journey" prescribes." All other relatives, friends, and his children were refused seeing him. With single mind he recited the Buddha's name, resolved on rebirth. When his illness was grave, his brother-in-law Zhao came to see him and, seeing him so ill, could not hold back his tears. Zushan laughed and consoled him instead, "All our lives you and I have recited the Buddha's name and cultivated the Pure Land precisely for rebirth at a time like this. This is a great and joyous matter; how can we act like worldly sons and daughters?" Throughout the illness his mind remained clear. On the twelfth day of the ninth month at the hour of Hai, he joined his palms, sat cross-legged upon his bed, and passed away reciting the Buddha's name. He was fifty-two.

Nie Yunsheng, named Chuanceng, was a native of Qingjiang, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was raised by his mother, grave and fond of learning. He passed the jinshi examination in the Guichen year of the Guangxu reign and took office in Hubei. Soon after the death of his eldest brother he returned home and was elected a member of the provincial assembly. He fully discharged his duty of remonstrance, fearing no one in power. Before long he flung up his sleeve and withdrew. In life he loved classical prose, yet would never write carelessly unless it served the world. In later years he studied the Buddhist canon, taking up the Lotus, Shurangama, Diamond, and Perfect Enlightenment scriptures and reciting them in turn, while gathering all into the five Pure Land sutras. He kept a long fast and a fixed daily recitation. In the Dingchou year he established the Gaoyu Recitation Grove, and often went to other recitation groves to speak, transforming many. In the summer of Jihai he was troubled by repeated diarrhea. Set resolutely on returning to the West, he no longer sought the help of medicine. By the tenth month his decline was graver still. Knowing his time had come, he dictated his last will and invited monks, relatives, and friends, leading his children and grandchildren in reciting the Buddha's name. As he sank ever weaker he still recited silently through clenched teeth. Without any pain, right mindfulness clear, he relinquished his life serenely as though entering samadhi, his features as if living. Yunsheng was born in the Jisi year of the eighth year of the Tongzhi reign and returned to the West on the first day of the eleventh month of the Jimao year, 1939, at the age of seventy-one. His work "Poems, Essays and Diary from the Hall of Mending Prajna" much clarifies the meaning of the Pure Land teaching, and is kept in his home.

Zhao Xiude, of Xingtai city in Hebei, was most filial to his mother, honest with all men, and of a pure, thickhearted nature. He took refuge in the Three Jewels and strictly kept the five precepts. In midwinter of 1938 his mother fell gravely ill and the whole family recited the Buddha's name. At her end she charged Xiude with great earnestness, "Recite the Buddha's name well. Within three years, do not let your recitation stop." Having given this charge, she lay in the auspicious posture and passed away serenely. Three hours later her body was soft, the crown of her head warm, and her face suffused with radiance. After his mother's death Xiude did all things in accordance with the rites. He also obeyed his mother's command: for three years, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, he never ceased reciting. Every dawn at cockcrow he rose and went beneath the pagoda of Perfect Light, walking around it to the right while reciting the Buddha's name. When he walked, if bricks or stones blocked the road he would kick them clean away so as not to hinder travelers. When a fast day came he went to the Buddha hall of Kaiyuan Temple and struck the bell and lit the lamps, tending the incense. Whoever he met he urged to recite the Buddha's name. His word of exhortation ran, "Recite the Buddha's name! Recite the Buddha's name! The Land of Bliss is our own home." In holding the Buddha's name he was utterly diligent; in keeping his mother's command he was wholly sincere and careful. By November 1941 he said repeatedly, "My mother's command is fulfilled; I shall soon return. But because my past karma cannot be escaped, I must suffer the pain of illness." Presently he showed a slight ailment, and when it came on his chest and back ached, just as he had said. One day, rousing himself despite his illness, he went to Kaiyuan Temple to bow before the Buddha. On finishing he returned home, closed his eyes and mouth, and neither looked nor spoke. Smiling alone, he sat upright in a chair, his left hand making the gesture of counting beads while reciting the Buddha's name, and passed away. Four hours later the crown of his head was still warm, and a strange fragrance lingered for days. It was the first day of the twelfth month of 1941. He was fifty-six.

Yu Mingsheng, of Gaoting on Daishan, Zhejiang, was a farmer, simple and goodhearted. Whenever a dispute arose in his village he would come forward and settle it. To aid the imperiled, relieve the afflicted, and bring things to a good end he took pleasure as his own duty. Yet he did not know what the Buddha Dharma might be. His son Dingyong, who from youth embraced the Buddhas, took refuge under Master Yuanying, devoted himself to the Pure Land, and founded a lay Buddhist association in the countryside to guide the people in reciting the Buddha's name. Though Mingsheng was influenced by this, his practice was not yet earnest. On the twenty-third day of the first month of 1942 he fell slightly ill. After seven days the illness grew worse. Dingyong then gathered fellow lay devotees and led the family in devout assisting recitation. After a day and a night the illness improved and his mind cleared. Dingyong consoled him kindly and told him of the excellence of rebirth through the Buddha-name. Mingsheng came to understanding with joy, let go of everything, and with single mind recited the Buddha's name. He also told the assembly, "Recite the four-character name." The people did as he said. On the morning of the second day of the second month he said to his son, "I want my hair cut, a bath, and fresh clothes." Dingyong asked, "Father, can you be reborn in the West?" He answered, "Yes!" — the words firm and forceful. The assembly continued their aiding recitation, the Buddha's name unbroken. At midnight of the next day Mingsheng told the company, "I have already seen Amitābha Buddha, a lotus in his hand." On saying this he began to rise as if to seat himself on the lotus throne, and himself struck the small bell and recited the Buddha's name loudly. After an hour his voice gradually faded; his younger brother Mingmao and others recited at his side. They told him, "The ten final recitations at death surely attain rebirth." Mingsheng gathered his spirit again, joined his palms, and recited "Namo Amitābha Buddha." At the eighth utterance his voice suddenly fell and his breath stopped. A quarter of an hour later he revived, laughed aloud before the company, and said again and again, "I am overjoyed!" Then he passed away serenely. At the encoffining the next day his limbs were soft and his face rosy as in life. He was forty-nine.

Zhu Shiseng, given name Qi. In his early years he took refuge under Master Dixian and received the Dharma name Xianjia. Later he took refuge under Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Zhirui. His father was a farmer; his mother, Lady Yang, was fond of helping others. Shiseng, schooled in his youth by his family, was kind, honest, and plain. He served long as stationmaster of Wusong on the Shanghai-Nanjing Railway. In 1922 he took the lead in establishing the World Buddhist Lay Association and served as vice-chairman. He oversaw the expansion of the association's main hall and quarters, planning and rushing about at great pains. In 1931, the July

7 Incident broke out, and there were many refugees in Shanghai, in hunger and cold. Shiseng, in consultation with Dharma friends, raised funds to set up a Buddhist society for relieving the cold and did his utmost in relief works. For all the cold, destitute, and hidden poor he made thorough investigation and dispensed monthly aid. In protecting the Dharma and relieving beings he exhausted his heart's blood. In later years, worn by overwork, he was often afflicted with illness. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the old calendar, 1942, when Master Miaozhen of Lingyan heard that Shiseng was gravely ill, he came personally to his sickbed and gave detailed instruction, charging him to "let go all ties, raise right mindfulness, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and seek rebirth in the West." Shiseng was deeply moved and put it earnestly into practice. By nine in the morning of the eleventh, as fellow members of the association were aiding his recitation, his son Yongjun asked his father, "Can you still recite the Buddha's name in your heart?" He nodded and said, "Yes! My heart has long since reached the West; the Buddha-name recitation truly does not come to nothing." He then asked for a pen and wrote the few characters "Your father is surely bound for the West." He fingered his beads, his lips and teeth moving faintly, reciting the Buddha's name without ceasing. By the hour of noon he passed serenely into rebirth in the West.

Gu Yunqing, of Xiaohai Town, Nantong. Losing his father in childhood, he was most filial to his mother. In business he honored his word. In managing local public welfare he spared himself no toil. In later years he took refuge in the Three Jewels and devoted himself wholly to the Pure Land. In bowing to the Buddha and holding the scriptures he was diligent without slack, even in bitter cold and scorching heat. At the year's end of the Renwu year he was troubled by a cough. By the second day of the new year, Guiwei, he said to his family, "I am all day in a bamboo grove, and see the holy host releasing great light. We have but three days together!" He also charged them that at his passing the whole house must not weep but should aid his recitation to send him to the West. As it fell out, at the appointed time he sat and passed away. On the crown of his head the gathered warmth long would not disperse, and his face was bright and clear. The whole countryside, one and all, sighed in admiration.

Wu Lichen, named Bin, was a native of Kaifeng, Henan. Of straightforward nature, he excelled in painting and calligraphy. He took part in the revolution for more than ten years, his footprints across all of China, holding high posts in Guangdong and Yunnan. Meeting a capable colleague he would yield his position to him without a moment's regret. Whoever sought relief he aided from his purse, without a trace of stinginess. In 1920 he met Chan Master Xuyun at Kunming and heard the Buddha Dharma. In 1925 he returned to Kaifeng and met the Vinaya Master Cizhou, receiving the Three Refuges and the five precepts. Thereupon he devoted his mind to the Way. Later his family died and his wealth scattered, leaving him alone, his years drawing toward the evening, a hundred feelings crowding upon him. In 1934 he went north to the Yan capital and, through a friend's introduction, went to Mile Temple to draw near Chan Master Zhenkong and investigate the highest matter. Later, old and ill, he gave up the investigation and cultivated the Pure Land, single-mindedly dwelling in the Land of Peace. Two days before the Mid-Autumn Festival of 1943 he first caught a cold, took little note of it, and it ended in a grave illness. His whole body grew stiff, turning was hard, and in food, drink, and relief he needed help on every side. After twenty days the condition worsened. A pure friend came and asked, "Do you feel the pain of illness?" "Yes," he said. "I wish to recite the scriptures for you; would you care to hear?" "I would," he said. He asked again, "I wish to recite the Buddha's name for you; would you wish to hear it?" "I would dearly like to," he said. The friend further told him, "The merit of the Earth Store Sutra is most vast. If your lifespan is not yet spent, it can wipe away past karma and free you from the pain of illness; if your lifespan is ended, it can help you be reborn in the Land of Bliss and be guided by the Buddha. I shall recite it aloud; listen with a still mind, and you may gain its response." The friend then recited the Earth Store Sutra once. That night Lichen's breath grew even fainter. The friend again instructed him, "This body is the root of all suffering; you should at once put it down and recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, seeking rebirth in the West." He added, "You have practiced for many years, precisely to have its use at this hour. Be sure to raise right mindfulness, recite the Buddha's name along with me, and fly single-mindedly westward. To end birth and death lies in this very moment; under no circumstances may a second thought arise." At the time Lichen's expression was clear, his face without a look of pain, his lips and teeth moving faintly with the sound of the bell. After about an hour his lips stilled and his breath stopped; he passed away serenely. His whole body was cold, but the crown of his head remained warm.

Mao Aitang, of Meiyuan Township, Shaoxing, Zhejiang. In youth he studied at the Hangzhou Zhaohui Silk Factory. The owner, taking a liking to the young man, gave him his daughter in marriage. Aitang, ever mindful of his father-in-law's kindness in recognizing him, labored with all his thought to expand the business. Unfortunately he had a lung ailment and coughed blood often, his strength sharply declining. Still he hurried between Shanghai and Hangzhou, working diligently. Generous by nature and fond of giving, frugal in his own living, he wore plain clothes and ate coarse food, never altering his resolve with the prosperity of his lot. When the war of resistance broke out he moved west into Sichuan. After repeated upheavals his old illness returned, and he recuperated at the Great Sage Compassionate Temple in Chengdu. The abbot, Master Chang'en, knowing he had planted good roots in former lives, gave him many scriptures, among them the collected writings of Master Yinguang. On seeing the collection Aitang felt as though he had found a rare treasure and read it constantly. He once said, "Toward the Pure Land method I seem to have a bond from former lives; I vow to serve it my whole life." Before long his illness gradually healed. He then went to Chongqing and resumed his old trade, reciting the Buddha's name whenever he had leisure. In 1944, aged forty-one, on the sixteenth day of the ninth month by the old calendar his old ailment suddenly flared and he lost his voice. He charged the family to aid his recitation of the Buddha's name and invited four monks to recite in shifts day and night. He himself went on silently reciting with them. He raised his hand again and again, pressing thumb and forefinger together. At first the family did not grasp what he meant; then, seeing him make the gesture of pressing his palms together in reverence, they realized he wanted his prayer beads. They handed them to him, and he took up the beads and counted with faint stirrings of his mouth. On the nineteenth he could suddenly speak. He said, "I shall be reborn on the twenty-first, for the old master has already come to tell me." The family answered casually and took no great heed. That evening, as his wife sat by his bed, in a daze she saw him rise from the bed, take up his robe and put it on, and stride briskly out the door. Much alarmed, she followed. When he reached the door she saw a Buddha body sixteen feet tall standing in the air, radiant with such blazing light as cannot be described. She then saw the Buddha lower his hand in welcome and bear him away. With a start she woke. The next day Aitang was comfortable as ever and could even join the assembly in recitation without ceasing. Asked what troubled him, he only said, "A slight discomfort in the throat." It was carried on to four twenty in the afternoon of the twenty-first, and amid the great company's recitation, joining his palms and reciting, he passed serenely into rebirth. On the evening of his rebirth in the West, Master Chang'en, already lain down to rest in his quarters, suddenly saw Aitang, holding the "Collected Writings," come and say, "I thank the master for his kind gift; the benefit was beyond measure, and now I return it." Just as the master was about to answer him he started awake. The next day he sent a letter to inquire and only then learned that Aitang had passed away the day before.

Fan Xingnian lived at Guangji Bridge outside the Chang Gate of Suzhou and worked as a box-office attendant for a playhouse. In middle age, under the influence of his colleague He Guifang, he came to believe in the Buddha Dharma. Before long he took refuge under Master Yinguang. At every Buddhist observance he went up to the third-floor Buddha hall of the Gongdelin vegetarian restaurant and recited the Buddha's name with the assembly. Later he joined the Buddhist Pure Practice Society established by Chen Yiren on Shihouzi Street within the Chang Gate. At fifty he went to the Precept-Grasping Temple at West Garden and received the precepts of an upasaka, from then on keeping a vegetarian fast and reciting the Buddha's name to the end of his life. Xingnian throughout his life depended on his own labor to get by. He ever kept a compassionate heart, pitying the suffering of others; whenever he met the poor he held the wish to relieve them. When his own strength was insufficient he turned to the wealthy and virtuous, bowing to them and begging for alms in bitter earnest on another's behalf. For his own part he filled his belly with coarse greens and covered his body with ragged clothes. In the tenth month of 1945, knowing he was soon to be reborn, he held a seven-day recitation retreat in his own room, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. He also said to his daughter-in-law Quan Fude, "It would be best to be reborn on the fourth day of the eleventh month, for the old master Yinguang of Lingyan also passed into nirvana on that day." With his family and the assembled lay devotees aiding his recitation he passed away serenely, at seven in the evening of the fourth day of the eleventh month. Several days after rebirth he was taken to Lingyan for cremation. Along the way, whoever knew him joined their palms in reverence. After the cremation, many multicolored sharira were obtained.

Hu Songnian, of Shanghai. Kindhearted and benevolent, he was amiable and affable in all dealings, and made his living in the silk trade. After middle age, on hearing a master expound the scriptures and realizing the impermanence of the world, he gave up his trade and took refuge under Master Yinguang. From then on he believed deeply in the Pure Land teaching, keeping a vegetarian fast and reciting the Buddha's name. When the war of resistance broke out, the flames of war reached everywhere. The temples of Shanghai one after another held Dharma assemblies to pray for peace. Songnian labored with zeal, sustaining the sacred grounds with all his might. He dwelt for years at the Treasure of Dharma House in Jue Garden, his mind at peace in practice, spreading the Dharma and benefiting beings. Later he went to live at Lingyan in Suzhou, working with the community at their tasks and reciting the Buddha's name intently in his leisure. After Master Yinguang passed into nirvana and a pagoda-court was built, Songnian assisted in the overseeing and construction with no little pains. On the eve of his departing he showed a slight illness. In a daze he seemed to hear someone tell him "rebirth at eight," and told it to Master Miaozhen. Songnian had two sons; the elder had died young. Miaozhen therefore wired the younger son to come to the mountain, telling him his father's time had come, and likewise settled all other things. Songnian then bathed and changed his clothes, sat cross-legged, and recited the Buddha's name. Hearing the news the assembly all came to aid his recitation. When eight had passed that evening, seeing him behave as usual, they were about to scatter. Songnian said, "The evening is already over; my rebirth will be at eight tomorrow morning, and I still trouble you all to come and aid me." The next morning the great company gathered and took turns assisting recitation. When eight drew near they saw Songnian seated cross-legged reciting the Buddha's name, exactly as usual. One or two who doubted put it to him as a question; Songnian said, "Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva has already come to fetch me, but I must have Amitābha Buddha come in person to welcome me; only then will I go." No sooner had he spoken than he added, "Amitābha Buddha has come!" He smiled, closed his eyes, and passed away, just as the clock struck eight. That day was the anniversary of the completion of the pagoda-court of the old master; the monks and laity who came to the mountain saw it, and none failed to marvel at its rarity.

Li Guangxiang, originally of Anhui, had for generations lived at No. 146 Cang Street, Suzhou. Of honest and generous nature, when he was wronged by others he only examined his own faults and endured rather than contend. His mother had taken refuge in the Three Jewels and earnestly recited the Buddha's name. She bore three sons, Guangxiang the youngest. Nourished by his mother's influence, he came early to the Buddhist gate. At sixteen he purified his mouth and took a long fast. At twenty-eight he married Zou Jingming and had two daughters. Because his income was small, his livelihood was very hard. He was content in poverty and took pleasure in the Way, not much troubled by it. At forty-five he took refuge under Master Daojian of the Great Reed Hermitage on Qionglong Mountain, and resolved to ring the long bell of the hermitage for half a year in repentance of past karma. At home all day he earnestly recited the Buddha's name without once ceasing. In April 1948, at sixty-five, he was suddenly stricken with paralysis on one side. Though ill, his mind was clear and he felt no pain. At his last moment his wife and daughters waited at his side. He asked to be propped up in cross-legged sitting, and could still move his lips in recitation. Before long his eyes closed and he sat and passed away serenely.

Sun Changquan, of Tiantai, Zhejiang. While resting on Chicheng Mountain he met the lay Buddhist Chen Hailiang, who guided him to the Buddhas; he was then twenty. His faith was pure and deep and his recitation diligent. He joined with his townsmen Zhu Tianbao, Yuan Ziping, and others to found the Tiantai Buddhist Lay Association, and was chosen chairman and also lecturer. On every ninth day of the month he gathered the assembly and spoke the Dharma. Gently he exhorted and persuaded, urging people to believe deeply in karmic retribution. He once said, "Sow melons and you get melons, sow beans and you get beans; this is a clear and certain matter. The fruit arises from the cause, and the cause surely brings fruit. The karma of human affairs is exceedingly complex. To view it with a short and shallow eye is not enough to see the whole truth of karma from first to last. Karma reaches through the three times and is not confined to one lifetime. The fruit you receive in this life is the cause you made in a former life; and some of the causes you make in this life await a future life to receive their recompense. The sutra says, "Would you know the causes of your former life, look at what you receive in this life. Would you know the fruits of your life to come, look at what you do in this life." To plant good causes brings good fruits, to plant evil causes brings evil fruits; this admits of no doubt. Moreover the causes made in the past have indeed fixed your own fortune and misfortune; this is called past karma. But the power to plant causes now lies in my own hand, so I may even seize this good occasion to plant abundant good causes and turn the appointed retribution of past karma." Changquan held that for one who studies the Buddhas the greatest enemy is not the demons of heaven or the heretical teachers, but the mind-fiends of the five desires. He composed a "Gatha on the Five Desires" to spur himself: "How could the Way-mind be turned? / The five desires raise up obstacles. / A child licking honey on the knife's edge / Cuts its tongue and suffers harm. / The five desires darken the mind, / And the Way grows distant day by day. / Galloping toward the cliff's brink, / Check the horse and do not delay." The poetry he wrote was bleak and refined, waking men to deep reflection. His seven-character regulated verse "Passing by My Grandmother's Old Home South of the Ravine" reads, "Two generations' kindness, raising my mother and nurturing the child, / Thirty years of my body turned against the cold village. / The new master of the old garden wonders at the arriving guest, / An old neighbor of the ruined house speaks of heartbreak. / Red trees at the window recall my mother's white hair, / Green hills bury her bones in the cold dusk. / The autumn wind cannot exhaust an orphan's tears, / To repay her toil I bow to the World-Honored One." A work of uttermost feeling. At thirty-three he was reborn in the Pure Land. On the eve of his passing, fellow practitioners ringed his bed aiding his recitation. He then said, "At eight tomorrow morning the Buddha will come to guide me, and I shall be reborn in the Land of Bliss." At past eight the next morning he again said to all, "The Buddha has come; I am going," and, reciting the Buddha's name, passed away. It was the fifteenth day of March, 1949.

Wang Dongyuan, of Baozhuang in Yin east, Zhejiang. In youth his family was quite poor. He entered a private school, and in less than half a year gave up study for trade, becoming an apprentice in a printing house. Naturally clever, he set himself to hard study. While still young he became a teacher and had a ready tongue. He founded the Siming Daily, the Yin East Public Hospital, and village schools and other undertakings of benefit to society, and served successively as a member of the Zhejiang provincial assembly and manager of the Shanghai Tianchu Monosodium-Glutamate Works. The home-made Tianchu product was his own invention; it was welcomed by vegetarians, and at the same time recovered for the nation what was flowing away in trade. Dongyuan loved books and spent his whole salary on them; his collection was not less than tens of thousands of volumes. While in Tianjin he met Chen Zhengyou, who awakened him and turned his heart to the Buddhist gate. From then on he recited only the Buddha and sought only the Pure Land. After the age of fifty he studied the Buddhist canon with care, engraved scriptures for distribution and broadly formed ties of Dharma. At his Shanghai residence he set up a Buddha hall and recited the Buddha's name all day without slack. At sixty-three he resigned and lived in retirement, practicing recitation even more assiduously. He relieved poverty, gave grain, and aided students, the same for more than ten years; the people of his county praised his goodness. On the fourth day of the third month of 1950 by the old calendar he felt out of sorts all over and took to bed. His family hung an image of the Three Holy Ones of the West beside the bed. Dongyuan fingered his beads and recited the Buddha's name, feeling no pain. From the sixth he twice fell into long sleep, each lasting dozens of hours. On waking the family asked what he had seen, and he replied, "My body is in the West." At four in the morning of the fourteenth his breath gave forth a clear fragrance. Late at night the room suddenly grew bright as day, and among the household there were those who saw the Bodhisattva appear. At noon he passed away serenely reciting the Buddha's name. In his illness Master Yuanqing of the Changgeng Tower on Taibai and the nearby nuns came together to aid his recitation. For eleven days the sound of the Buddha's name did not cease. The whole family, believing in the Dharma, joined the assisting recitation. Dongyuan had served the Buddhas for more than twenty years, keeping a long fast and taking no life; the Practices of Samantabhadra and the Diamond Sutra he could recite from memory. In worship he was reverent, and in washing and rinsing strict, never touching a scripture or image with unclean hands. He was seventy-seven.

Wang Xinzhan, originally named Xinsan and styling himself Zhenru Layman, was a native of Shanyin, Zhejiang. In youth he was quick beyond his fellows. On coming of age, grieved that the Qing government was corrupt, he joined the Revolutionary Alliance and took part in the revolution. He gathered comrades and founded a daily paper to open the people's understanding. With Zhang Jizhi of Nantong he jointly financed a salt-reclamation enterprise, opening up several hundred thousand acres of wasteland at Rufu in northern Jiangsu, and established a match factory and a wool-felt mill in Tianjin. Whatever could invigorate industry and win back the nation's rights, he strove toward with all his might. His family was naturally wealthy, and he gave freely without sparing, gradually draining his resources. After the Republic was founded, many who had joined the revolution rose to high posts and generous salaries. Xinzhan, however, retired to Shanghai and spoke nothing of rank or emolument. With his younger brother Datong he wore plain clothes and ate simple fare; the family lived in harmony, passing quiet days. The teachers and friends of his life were for the most part the great scholars of the age. Among the laity were Zhang Taiyan, Ouyang Jingwu, and Ma Yifu; among the monkhood were Masters Dixian and Taixu, and with Master Hongyi he shared the bond of teacher and student. At the last he served Master Yinguang and took refuge in the Three Jewels. In his later years, at the Shousheng Hermitage in Shanghai, he established an Amitābha assembly. On the first and fifteenth of each month he gathered people to recite the Buddha's name; on Sundays he lectured on the scriptures, his influence spreading ever wider. In the spring of the Jichou year of the Republic he suddenly fell ill with phlegm, wheezing, and loss of voice, which neither Chinese nor Western medicine could cure. Though his body was weak, his spirit did not fail. He often said to his family, "Before long I shall be going." On the night of April 21, 1950, he said again, "I go tomorrow. On no account must you weep; rather recite the Buddha's name in unison to send me off." At five thirty the next morning he passed away serenely. He was sixty-nine. His writings were many, but regretfully never printed.

Sun Jilu, of Tianjin. Deep-rooted in past merit, he believed firmly in the Buddha Dharma. Keeping the fast and reciting the Buddha's name, brave and vigorous in practice, he was the same for more than twenty years. He joined the Tianjin Buddhist Lay Association and invited Masters Taixu, Cizhou, and Yuanying to expound the scriptures there, leading his wife and children to listen with reverence from first to last, never once absent. In 1950, at sixty-eight, even in illness his heart for protecting the Dharma did not slacken. When the illness became critical he recited the Buddha's name all the more. Many fellow members of the association and his family divided into shifts to aid his recitation, the sound of the Buddha's name rolling on. At nine in the evening of the thirteenth day of the fifth month he returned serenely to the West, and all who aided the recitation sensed a rare fragrance.

Yu Fuheng was a man of Xiaoyu Village at the North Station of Tianjin. By nature he was honest and kind, and his intelligence was beyond the common run. After finishing middle school he served as a clerk in the Beining Railway Bureau. For more than twenty years he attended to public duty with diligence and care, and never once was at fault. In the summer of 1950 he resigned his post on account of illness and rested at home. Through the instruction of Master Xikong he took refuge in Buddhism, and his faith and vow were firm. Each day, besides bowing to and reciting the holy names of Amitābha and Avalokiteshvara, he also read and recited the Mahayana scriptures. He gave special weight to the Pure Land dharma-gate, and above all revered and believed the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Amitābha Sutra, and others. In the tenth month his illness grew somewhat worse, and he recited the holy name all the more diligently. He also followed what is set out in the Guide to the Final Crossing, and instructed his family to prepare for what was to come. On the third day of the eleventh lunar month, knowing that his hour had come, he had his family recite the Buddha’s name for him and forbade them to weep. At nine in the evening he washed and changed his clothes, reciting the Buddha’s name as he did so. At half past one he lay down on his right side and passed away in peace. He was forty-four.

Ding Guiqiao, whose given name was Chuanshen, was a man of Changsha in Hunan. He was born in Chengdu, Sichuan, in the Guangxu reign of the Qing. As a child his intelligence was beyond the common run, and he never forgot what he had once read. The poetry and prose he composed were serene, elegant, and of ancient simplicity, rivalling the writers of Wei and Jin. In his early years he studied the learning of Laozi and Zhuangzi; afterwards, judging it to be empty metaphysical talk that could not save the world, he cast it aside and studied medicine, and went to Japan to study. After four years he returned home with a university degree and took up the work of education. At that time Guiqiao was still young. After the founding of the Republic he hurried north and south, throwing himself into political life, and served in office with integrity, so that people spoke of him with praise. After the age of thirty he gave up political life, settled in Shanghai, declined all social engagements, adopted a vegetarian diet and took refuge in the Buddha, devoting himself to the inner scriptures. Those he drew near to were all good knowing ones of the day. He studied and discussed the teachings, distinguished the true from the false, delved deeply into Hetuvidya and Consciousness-Only, penetrated both the exoteric and the esoteric in contemplation and practice, and wove together Yogacara and Madhyamaka, dissolving the disputes between Mahayana and Hinayana, between the empty and the existent, between exoteric and esoteric, until he took refuge in the Pure Land. His faith and vow were deep and keen, and he practiced what he professed; for several decades his recitation of the Buddha’s name was never interrupted. In his later years he had no mind for prajna texts and wrote nothing. He only brought forth the supreme mind and walked the bodhisattva path. He advocated vegetarianism and the protection of living things, and he initiated the printing of the supplementary canon; whatever pertained to spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings, there was nothing he did not do with all his strength. He entered cessation at the hour of hai on the thirteenth day of the second lunar month in 1953, at the age of sixty-seven. On the day he entered cessation he was still teaching the Dharma to his family. From the hour of xu he straightened his clothes and washed his hands. Ten minutes before the end his countenance was unchanged and his movements as usual. He said to his friend Dr. Chen Yuxiu: ‘The mind that recites the Buddha’s name is wholly free of obstruction.’ His spirit bright and clear, he recited the holy name and passed away in peace, as if entering samadhi.

Chen Yiren was a man of Xiangshan in Suzhou. He practiced medicine, and all his life took joy in doing good. He understood the teachings deeply, took refuge in the Pure Land, and recited the name with utmost sincerity. He had taken refuge with Master Dixian, who gave him the Dharma name Shengyuan. At Houshizi Street in Suzhou he founded the Buddhist Pure Practice Society and led the assembly in practice. He spread the great Mahayana Pure Land scriptures, and his eloquence was unobstructed, so that the assembly held him in esteem. Once, in his home village of Xiangshan, he lectured on the Amitābha Sutra and urged the villagers to reform. His preaching was subtle and wonderful, drawing his hearers in. The local storytelling hall, which usually did a brisk trade, now had a deserted front and fewer guests day by day, for all were flocking to Yiren’s lecture seat to reverently hear the essentials of the Dharma. Such sincerity for the Dharma and such power to move others were truly rarely seen among the laymen of his time. He passed away on the sixteenth day of the seventh lunar month in 1957. Before his death, though he suffered no grave illness, his years were advanced and his strength failing, and at last he took to his bed and could not rise. He then grew confused and lost right mindfulness. His fellow cultivators were all gathered, at a loss what to do. The old monk Qingchan of Qionglong Monastery, hearing the news, hurried over; seeing the situation, he had the assembly withdraw and shut the door, then struck the small chime at Yiren’s ear, first reciting the Amitābha Sutra, and then reciting the holy name. After some three hours Yiren began to come to himself and slightly opened his eyes. The old monk gave him further instruction, and Yiren at once sat up, joined his palms in gratitude, and passed away with a smile on his face. He was seventy-five.

Lü Huiqiao’s family had lived for generations at Qiaosikong Lane in Suzhou, and he made his living painting portraits. In middle age his wife and son died one after another, and he grieved deeply over impermanence. On the urging of a friend he began to have faith in the Buddhadharma. Not long after he took refuge with the monk Qingfeng of Nianhua Hermitage and with Master Yin. Thereafter, in his own house, he gathered fellow cultivators and founded a Pure Land aid-to-recitation society, helping people accomplish the final act of their practice. The rules he laid down for aid-to-recitation were extremely strict. The society’s expenses were borne by Huiqiao alone. On the first and fifteenth of each month, or on the birthdays of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, he gathered the assembly for Buddha-recitation and seven-day retreats. All his life his practice was diligent and never slackened. Later, together with Chi Lianbang and Pan Yanling, he jointly ran the Bao’an Buddha-Recitation Hall, holding year-round recitation and seven-day retreats. In the end it closed for lack of funds. Afterwards Huiqiao moved to a hermitage in Hong Kong, old and frail. On the evening of the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth lunar month in 1957, joining his palms and reciting the Buddha’s name, he attained rebirth in peace at the age of seventy. In his later years, though utterly destitute, he never asked anyone for help. In hardship he advanced without retreat, wholeheartedly seeking the West. His lofty character and shining integrity made the stubborn modest and the timid stand up. At the end he had the aid of his fellow cultivator Zhu Huirui, who recited for him and saw to everything. That giving and recompense never miss their mark — how could that be mere chance?

Guo Fengzao, styled Yuncen, was a man of Weiyuan County in Gansu, living on North Street within the county town. He was skilled in letters, and especially accomplished in calligraphy and painting, so that people vied to seek them of him. In his later years he quietly cultivated the Buddha-vehicle, devoted himself to the Pure Land, kept the Five Precepts, and practiced the Ten Good Deeds. He also urged his wife, of the Chai family, and his daughter-in-law, of the Wu family, to take refuge in the Buddhist fold and make their household a Buddhist one. With his pure friends Zhou Foxing and Zhang Ruiting he spread the Dharma with one heart and founded a Lay Buddhist Society. At the great temple fort by the ruined pond at the North Gate they built Fayuan Monastery and established a Buddhist branch association. The faithful turned their hearts to it, and those who recited the Buddha’s name numbered three or four hundred. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh lunar month in 1958 he showed a slight illness. On the fourteenth his family helped him into the courtyard to sit in the sun. In the afternoon he lay down on his bed and asked his Dharma friends and his family to recite the Buddha’s name for him, and Fengzao silently recited along with them. Waking in the night, he recited along with the assembly again. At seven in the evening of the fifteenth he sat up, gazed at the Buddha’s image, his spirit clear and calm and wholly free of distress, and passed away with a smile.

Lu Genlin was a man of Changzhou. In middle age he took work in a restaurant in Tianjin, and in the kitchen he killed countless living things. After 1931 he came to live in Suzhou. At that time Master Yinguang was living at Baoguo Monastery in Suzhou, and Genlin went to the monastery to seek refuge. Many people came to the Master asking for refuge, and the Master accepted them all with compassion, but Genlin alone he refused. Genlin then pleaded in bitter grief, and the Master answered: ‘You are covered in the light of blood, and therefore I do not accept you. You must first eat vegetarian for three years, and then I will permit you to take refuge.’ Genlin at once followed the teaching. Three years later he went again to Baoguo Monastery and was enrolled by the Master as his disciple. From then on he recited the Buddha’s name diligently. He also founded a lotus society at Shanxin Hermitage at Xiguan Bridge, leading the assembly in Buddha-recitation on the second and sixteenth of each month. He further invited Master Mingkai and others to the society to expound the sacred scriptures and urge people to practice diligently, so that they might attain rebirth at the end. In 1966, though troubled by asthma, he recited as before. At the end he sat upright on his bed reciting the Great Compassion Mantra, right mindfulness clear, wholly free of suffering, and passed away serenely.

Tang Rongkang was a man of Wuxi in Jiangsu, living on Jingde Road in Suzhou, and a silversmith by trade. In middle age he came to believe in the Buddhadharma. He took refuge with Master Yin and received the Dharma name Tongle. Besides practicing the Pure Land dharma-gate, Rongkang was always fond of studying the doctrinal texts. He constantly recited such Mahayana scriptures as the Surangama and the Diamond Sutra. With Ye Tonghe and others he founded a Pure Land dharma assembly in Ranxiang Hermitage on West Qilin Lane, naming it the Perfect Enlightenment Lotus Society, and they recited the Buddha’s name at fixed times each month. All the society’s expenses were borne by Rongkang and a few fellow cultivators. He also warmly supported other practice places, such as the local Huayan Monastery, Fayin Monastery on Mount Shizi, the Miaoxiang Lotus Hall, and the Buddhist Pure Practice Society. He was upright by nature and sparing of words. In doing things for others he never shirked hardship. On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth lunar month in 1969, free of illness, he attained rebirth in peace at the age of sixty-nine. On the day before his rebirth he said to his wife: ‘I am going to be reborn.’ The next day it was exactly as he had said.

Wu Rongqing was the full brother of the laywoman Wu Dewen, who lived in front of the North Temple Pagoda in Suzhou. As a child he had eight years of schooling and was not much given to letters. He was loyal and honest by nature. At twenty-eight he lost his wife, and having a son and a daughter, he did not marry again. Nearing fifty, out of work and at home, he adopted a vegetarian diet. At first he took refuge with Master Yinguang, and later received the Five Precepts under the Venerable Xuyun, taking the Pure Land as his refuge. He recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, and in his spare time chanted the sutras. Morning and evening services never stopped through cold or heat. Each day he bowed to the Buddha two hundred times, and for twenty years it was as one day. When his mother passed on to the West and he saw the auspicious signs, his heart was moved by the Buddha’s compassion and he recited the name with even greater strength. In ordinary life he gave his strength for others, and answered every request, enduring toil without complaint. On cold days, seeing people frozen, he would take off his own padded jacket and trousers and give them away. After 1966 he often sat in stillness alone. He said to his sister Dewen: ‘Do you hear it? In my ears I constantly hear the Buddha’s voice, and never once is it broken, waking or sleeping.’ Rongqing had long suffered from asthma. In May 1970 it was suddenly cured, and he no longer took medicine. On the night of his rebirth his sister rose to look in on him. Rongqing said to her: ‘Go and sleep easy; I am quite comfortable.’ His sister left, and his good friend Yuan Xinhong stayed with him. Before long Yuan saw that Rongqing’s expression had changed, and at once called his sister in. They saw his lips moving slightly, as if reciting the Buddha’s name. The two of them took turns reciting the great name aloud at his ear to aid him. In a moment they saw a smile come over Rongqing’s face twice, and at the last he seemed to break into a great laugh; his body and mind at ease and joyful, he passed away in peace.
Li Xiyuan was a man of Sichuan. Honest and amiable, fond of learning and earnest in practice, he resolved to study Buddhism and in his later years devoted himself to the Pure Land. After the July 7th

Incident of 1937, he met Xia Lianju in Yanjing and received the benefit of the Dharma, which was like drinking sweet cream; he rejoiced as he had never done in his life, and had never known its like before. He therefore gave himself wholly to him as his teacher. Xiyuan was older than Xia, yet to the end he kept the courtesy of a disciple, for decades as one day. He read widely among the scriptures and treatises and received the bodhisattva precepts. All his life he ate vegetarian and took no food after noon. Each day at dawn, while others still slept soundly, Xiyuan had long since finished his bowing and recitation. He compiled by hand the ‘Essentials of Pure Practice’ as his daily lesson. His recitation of the name and cultivation of contemplation were wholly sincere. Even in the busy market he would often recite silently and enter contemplation. After Liberation he again sealed himself in retreat for many years, devoting himself to the holy name and bending all his thought toward the West. His son, Li Xiaoyuan, likewise cultivated the pure karma earnestly, but contracted tuberculosis and died young. In his last years Xiyuan lost his son and had no means of living; when the bitter winter came, the only thing on his bed was a straw mat. Yet in hardship he had not the least thought of retreat. His resolve grew firmer and his practice more earnest. For another twenty years he recited with single-minded devotion. His merit grew purer and his virtue higher. In his later years he deeply attained the joy of the Dharma, at peace and at ease. Past eighty, he could still write in small regular script, and he often wrote Dharma words on fans to give to others. Past ninety, he could still walk briskly. In the year of his rebirth he was already ninety-four. His fasting and precepts did not slacken, and his bowing and recitation continued as ever. Before the Spring Festival of 1971, free of illness, he sat upright facing west, holding his beads and reciting the Buddha’s name. At the last he simply lifted the beads in his hand toward his daughter-in-law and the others who were reciting for him, and passed away serenely.

Chi Yiqiao, whose courtesy name was Lianbang, was a man of Zhenjiang, living on Tieping Lane in the city of Suzhou. In his early years he practiced massage in Shanghai, and after meeting Zhu Shiseng he came to believe in Buddhism. He was on friendly terms with Huang Hanzhi, Guan Jiongzhi, and others, and joined the Buddhist Lay Society. Before long he founded a vegetarian restaurant and advocated a vegetarian diet. Later, when his wife and son died one after another, he awakened to the impermanence of the world and practiced all the more diligently. In 1941 he came to Suzhou and lodged at his elder cousin’s hermitage, going often to the Xiangguang Lotus Society in the Lion Grove to join in Buddha-recitation. Later, to spread the Buddhadharma, he held his own Dharma assemblies at Fushou Hermitage in Shilin Monastery, naming it the Suzhou Buddhist Lay Society, and proposed the layman Wang Qingjiu as its head. In the winter of 1943 he borrowed Yaocao Hermitage and invited Master Haishan to expound the Lotus Sutra for three months. In the spring of 1944 he invited Master Xuexiang to expound the entire Sutra of Immeasurable Life at Lingjiu Monastery. He also invited Master Huizhou to expound the Ksitigarbha Sutra at the Wang family ancestral hall. After Liberation he invited Master Liaoyuan to expound the Diamond Sutra at Tieping Lane. He also often started intensive seven-day Buddha-recitation retreats of twenty-one days, with three shifts a day, so that the sound of recitation continued day and night without a break. Whatever pertained to spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings, there was nothing he did not strive for with all his strength. Yiqiao was sincere and honest by nature, and rich in concentration. In the assemblies he led, when the provisions sometimes fell short, he could still maintain them with all his strength, reciting the Buddha’s name in peace and wholly composed. After Liberation the Lay Society was renamed the Qingxin Lotus Society. To make things convenient for monastics and laity alike, he opened a vegetable-eating place in the East Garden on Tieping Lane. In 1973, having injured his foot, he was treated by Qian Fuyuan, a bone-setter, and in time was cured. Though often ill, he still recited the Buddha’s name without slackening. A week before the end he foreknew his hour and entrusted all his affairs after death to his pure friend Xu Jueyi. He then sat upright facing west and passed away reciting the Buddha’s name. He used often to say: ‘The West one must go to oneself.’ At the time there was no one to recite for him, and it was indeed as he had wished. It was the eleventh day of the eighth month, 1973. He was eighty.

Zhao Mengshao lived on Gunxiu Lane in Suzhou. In the early years of the Republic he graduated from Beijing Industrial University and taught in schools and colleges in various places, retiring at sixty-nine. Mengshao was loyal and honest by nature, wholly without pretence. Only at seventy did he come to believe in the Buddhadharma. Each morning he sat in meditation for two hours and read the Buddhist scriptures, and he had a fair measure of insight. At seventy-six, having contracted cholecystitis, he adopted a vegetarian diet and began reciting the Buddha’s name. Past eighty, his faith grew still more earnest. His pure friend Huang Huibang explained the Pure Land dharma-gate to him: ‘You must be able to let go of everything and not cling to anything. Recite the Buddha’s name with one heart and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. If your allotted span has come, then though you fear death, death cannot be escaped. If your span has not yet ended, then without seeking a cure the illness will cure itself. Illness arises from karma, and karma arises from the mind; reciting the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion is the best way to dissolve karma, and the suffering of illness will heal of itself.’ Mengshao deeply awakened to this purport. On the tenth of November 1973, feeling a slight pain in his gallbladder and aching in his loins, he washed and changed his clothes and bade farewell to family and friends. On the morning of the thirteenth he said: ‘The suffering of illness has ended; in two days I shall go.’ He did not stop reciting the Buddha’s name. When his son asked him questions, he told him not to disturb him. At noon he said: ‘A Buddha has come from the West to welcome me.’ At a little past one in the afternoon he attained rebirth in peace. On the eighteenth he was cremated, his face rosy, his limbs supple, as if entered into Chan samadhi.

Bao Tingfu was a man of Suzhou, living on Lindun Road. He had worked in the embroidery trade. In his early years he had faith in both Buddhism and Daoism; in the end he abandoned Daoism and took refuge in the Buddha, cultivating the Pure Land earnestly. He kept a long-term vegetarian diet and performed the services without a break through cold and heat, and he was especially fond of chanting the Avatamsaka Sutra; whenever a local lotus society held an Avatamsaka assembly, he would join in the bowing and chanting with single-minded devotion. At first he took part in the Pure Land aid-to-recitation society founded by Wu Weijiao. In 1944 he further joined the General Benevolence Buddhist Society initiated by Shi Lin’an and Tang Jinpei. He was kind-hearted, loyal, and sincere. He was sparing of words and never contended with others. Through the six periods of the day and night he held to the name, most earnestly. In 1974, already eighty-four, though his strength had failed and he lay in bed much of the time, he had no great suffering. A few days before his rebirth a neighboring old woman of the Wang family said to him: ‘You recite the Buddha’s name all day long — what good has it done?’ He answered: ‘The merit is not in vain.’ At eight in the morning on the fifth day of the sixth lunar month the old woman Wang came again. Tingfu cupped his hands to her in farewell. She asked: ‘Where are you going?’ He answered: ‘I have already seen the Buddha; the golden terrace is coming to receive me and take me to the West.’ Having spoken, he lowered his eyes, joined his palms, and passed away.

Zhang Shiren was a man of Nanxun Town in Wuxing, Zhejiang. He was sincere and kind-hearted. In his prime he studied at the Nantong Specialized Textile School. After graduating he went to work at the Nantong Dasheng Textile Mill. He was later transferred to the Dasheng No. 3 Mill at Haimen. He often released living creatures and recited the Buddha’s name, performing many meritorious deeds. He took refuge with Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Debo. His home was on Shanhaiguan Road in Shanghai, and to escape the noise of the world he moved to Suzhou in 1957 and settled at No. 13 Gaoshi Lane, the better to practice. Though his retirement pay was a comfortable income, he kept himself very frugal, eating one dish at a meal and never a second flavor. But when he asked others to copy out the Mahayana scriptures, he would not stint a heavy sum in payment. He took the Pure Land dharma-gate as his refuge, holding the Buddha’s name with deep faith and vow. He constantly recited such Mahayana scriptures as the Avatamsaka, the Surangama, and the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra. He was especially fond of reading the Avatamsaka, one scroll a day, and for forty years he never stopped. Once at a friend’s house he saw thirteen great chests of unbound pages from the photographic reprint of the Song dynasty Qisha edition of the canon, their page order in disarray, incomplete and long covered with dust. Grieving that the Dharma-treasure had been damaged, he resolved to put them in order. What was missing he supplied, what was damaged he repaired, and he had them bound into volumes; it took several years before the work was done. In his eightieth year he still recited daily from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, selecting its striking phrases and copying them out in single sheets to give away, urging people to recite the Buddha’s name. On the seventh of January 1975 he showed a slight illness and had no wish for food or drink. That night he saw Amitābha Buddha appear, and knowing that he would not recover, he urgently telegraphed his son Guoguang to come to Suzhou, and gave him his instructions for after his death. On the morning of the eighth he again saw Amitābha Buddha, and with him Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, appearing in tall and mighty forms. He joyfully told his son: ‘The Western realm is right before my eyes.’ His manner was calm and at ease, and he recited the Buddha’s name in a clear voice, telling his son to recite for him. At half past eight on the morning of the ninth, right mindfulness clear, he attained rebirth in peace, at the age of eighty.

Long Feng was a man of Fuyang County in Zhejiang, living at No. 138 Siyi Road in Hangzhou. He ran an embroidery business, and in old age retired, alone and in difficult circumstances, and was looked after by the government. All his life he had recited the Buddha’s name with some devotion, and he also recited the Heart Sutra. In December 1975, because of erysipelas in his leg, he lay ill for more than a month. On the twenty-second of February the next year (the thirteenth day of the first lunar month), Feng sent someone to No. 121 Siyi Road to fetch Chi Jinbiao, the owner of a tinfoil shop, and said to him: ‘I am going today; please change my clothes for me.’ When his affairs had been arranged, he cupped his hands in farewell to the assembled company, closed his eyes, and passed away.

Ling Bingyan was a man of the Red Guard brigade of the Tiantai county seat. Before Liberation his family was too poor to support itself, and he went to Shanghai to live with his uncle Ling Yingxi. There he came to the Buddhist Youth Association and met such laymen as Chen Hongfa and Li Wenqi, and often received their guidance, so that his faith became very earnest. After Liberation he returned home to farm. As mouths to feed multiplied, the household grew hard pressed, and he gradually forgot the Buddhadharma. One day in January 1978 his wife went to a certain Mr. Zhang, a friend of Ling’s, and said that Bingyan was gravely ill and wished to see him. Zhang suspected that he meant to entrust him with his affairs after death. When he arrived, Bingyan questioned him closely about practice and Buddha-recitation, and he told him of each in turn. From then on he recited the holy name of Amitābha with devotion. After a month or so his suffering vanished at once and his pure mindfulness was well ripened. But his food and drink dwindled day by day and his flesh wasted away. Knowing that he would not recover, he gave his instructions for after death and recited the Buddha’s name with one heart. More than two months later, one early morning, an aunt who had not visited for a long time because of a quarrel over some matter three years before came to look in on him. Seeing Bingyan still on his bed, she hesitated and stammered for a long while. Then she told his family: ‘Last night I dreamed of Bingyan in a torn jacket and worn-out shoes, his face radiant, joyfully going forward. I asked where he was going, and he pointed far off into the sky and said: They are coming to welcome me. Then I saw red light flooding the sky and wondrous music sounding in the air, and a golden stairway let down from the heavens; Bingyan climbed step by step and gradually went off to the West. I woke at once, and that is why I have come to look in on him.’ That evening Bingyan indeed passed away. So said Zhang Shanzue of Tiantai, the younger brother of Ling’s friend Mr. Zhang.

Hu Fusheng was a man of Changzhou in Jiangsu. His family had been merchants for generations. At twenty his parents and his younger brother died one after another. Feeling the emptiness and illusion of human life, he accepted his elder cousin’s urging, believed in Christianity, and was baptized. In 1923 he took a post in the Wusong engineering office of the Nanjing-Shanghai Railway. With Zhu Shiseng, the stationmaster at Wusong, he was in daily company. Shiseng repeatedly urged Fusheng to believe in Buddhism, and was always refused, and at times they contended. Shiseng advised him with patience; but though his words were earnest, Fusheng heard them lightly. Thus six years passed. One day, tidying his desk by chance, Fusheng came upon the Buddhist books Shiseng had given him, which in ordinary times he had thought beneath his notice. In them he read: ‘Human life is a dream, and a hundred years a single instant. Wealth and honor are smoke and cloud passing before the eyes. Shi Chong did not enjoy a thousand years of riches; Han Xin schemed in vain to become a king. And after all, human life has more sorrow than joy; and even if it were all joy, its hurried span is no more than a few score of cold and summer heats.’ It was to him like the midnight bell, and he awoke with a start. He therefore abandoned Christianity and took refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge with Master Dixian and receiving the Dharma name Sansheng. With Shiseng he organized the Wusong Buddhist Lay Society and founded a free elementary school. On the one hand he urged people to believe in the Buddha; on the other he did all he could for the public welfare, such as giving medicine and medical treatment. Fusheng was strict with himself, sincere and cautious. He did not smoke, drink, or gamble, and he never took a second woman. After believing in the Buddha he took the Pure Land dharma-gate as his refuge. From his retirement in 1950, Fusheng bowed to the Buddha four hundred and eighty times every day without fail, kneeling to recite one roll of the Chapter on Conduct and Vow, and holding the holy name of Amitābha, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. If there were urgent matters in the day, he made up the lesson at night, and would not rest until deep into the night. So it was for thirty years. In 1979, after the Spring Festival, he fell slightly ill, without suffering. He had no wish for food or drink, and for a week ate only two or three spoonfuls of rice gruel a day. His legs then grew weak, and he could no longer bow. He therefore took to quiet sitting and held the great name. At noon on the twentieth day of the seventh lunar month he felt slightly unwell. By eleven the next morning he had passed away in peace; the crown of his head was the last to grow cold, and his four limbs were supple as in life. He was ninety.

Zhu Ziqiao, whose given name was Qinglan, had once served as a military governor, and people called him General Zhu. He was frank and straightforward by nature, and as an official he was clean and upright, carrying nothing away but a clean pair of sleeves. In ordinary times, for any good work of local public welfare, there was nothing he did not strive to contribute to, bringing it to a happy completion. After taking refuge with Master Yinguang he cultivated the Pure Land earnestly, and in his practice he was never careless. At that time Shaanxi suffered a great drought, and many famine-stricken people died. Master Yin raised funds for relief and gave Ziqiao full authority to oversee the work. Ziqiao wore himself out in the relief work and did not disgrace his teacher’s charge, and won Master Yin’s deep approval. After seventy he suddenly contracted an intestinal abscess, and the Shanghai hospitals, because he was old and his strength failing, did not dare operate. His sons and nephews decided to send him to the Peking Union Medical College Hospital for treatment. Before setting out, all preparations were made. Ziqiao thought that on this journey north his life or death could not be known, and so he went to take leave of Master Yin and told him the reason. Master Yin would not permit it, and reproached him for not honestly reciting the Buddha’s name. And he instructed him, saying: ‘If you could recite the Buddha’s name with one heart, how could it have come to this?’ Ziqiao had always respected his teacher’s word and did not dare disobey, so he firmly refused to go to Beijing and returned the train ticket he had bought. From then on he recited the Buddha’s name with one heart. On the third day the intestinal abscess burst of itself, discharging a great bowl of pus and blood, and he turned the corner. He then recited the Buddha’s name even more diligently. On the day before the end he called his family and said: ‘All my life I have written calligraphy, yet in the house there is not a single scrap of it left behind.’ He told them to cut four scrolls in readiness. His family, thinking his spirits poor, urged him to put it off, but Ziqiao firmly refused. He then wrote out the calligraphy scrolls, and went about as usual. The next morning after breakfast he sat cross-legged on his bed and did not come out for a long time. His family looked in, and he had already passed away sitting up.

Wu Shengchang, whose courtesy name was Menghong, was a man of Wuxian. He had taken refuge with Master Dixian and founded the Pure Heart Lotus Society in Suzhou. Admiring the legacy of the Eastern Grove, he gathered a hundred and twenty-three members of the society to devote themselves exclusively to the pure karma. Shengchang was chosen as president and led the assembly in practice, and the pure companions held him in willing esteem. On the first and fifteenth of each month and on the birthdays of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas they held Dharma assemblies, bowing to the Buddha and chanting the sutras without cease. The Dharma connections were abundant and the way of practice spread far. So it was for more than thirty years. In his sixties he contracted cancer of the esophagus, and medicine was of no avail. More than two hundred members and lay friends who joined in held an intensive seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat for him, day and night. Though Shengchang was stricken with grave illness, he could still finger his beads and recite the Buddha’s name with the assembly. At the last, amid the sound of the great assembly’s recitation, he passed away with a smile. His two nieces were at his side, and both saw two beams of white light going off to the West. The next day the three-period mindfulness service was held, and his smile was still on his face; all who saw it were filled with admiration.

Huang Nianxuan was born in the wuyin year of the Guangxu reign, and his home was in Caojia Lane inside the Chang Gate of Suzhou. He was kind and generous by nature and never quarrelled with anyone. He had served as deputy manager of the Shunkang Money House, and conducted business fairly. At sixty, reading the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, he resolved to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name. He also invited Master Yin to his home and took refuge with utmost sincerity. From then on he advanced with vigor and threw himself into the practice with warmth. He joined in every session of the Pure Heart Lotus Society at Zhuanjia Lane. For long periods he kept the Eight Precepts of the fast, taking no food after noon. Each month he spent more than thirty pieces of silver buying creatures to release. When he met anyone in hardship who asked for help, he always gave all he could. In his later years he shut his door and did not go out, reciting the Buddha’s name with one heart and seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Half a month before his rebirth he foreknew his hour.
