By the twenty-third day of the ninth month her condition suddenly grew grave, and she asked the Dharma Master Xingci to give her instruction at her sickbed. When the Master came, Shengzhao at once joined her palms in homage and said to him: ‘My illness has gone on for months; why is my karmic obstruction so deep and heavy?’ The Master said: ‘All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. You should contemplate this body as empty. The body is born of karmic obstruction from beginningless time, and karmic obstruction arises from deluded thought. When right mindfulness is born, deluded thought is extinguished and karmic obstruction is removed. The body is not even real — from where should illness come? So you should rouse right mindfulness and be mindful of the Buddha, recite the Buddha’s name. In being mindful of the Buddha, visualization is best; or you may simply contemplate the single character “Buddha.” As for reciting the name, the six-character form is good, the four-character form is good, and even a single character is good.’ He spoke to her further of the Way, saying: ‘Formerly there was a monk at Jinshan Monastery who practiced Chan samadhi, and afterwards took up the abbacy of another monastery, so that his mind was divided and his practice slackened. He suddenly fell ill, and was turned about by circumstances and could not be master of himself. A companion of his old days came to visit him in his sickness and asked him why he did not bring out the skill of former days. Roused by this man, the monk roused his right mindfulness, his samadhi appeared before him, and he passed away peacefully. Thus you may know that right mindfulness at the point of death is of the first importance. If one does not meet a good knowing one, one may still fear rebirth through the six paths — truly that is too terrible.’ Shengzhao nodded. The next day at dawn she suddenly cried out again and again: ‘Bodhisattva Guanyin has come! Bodhisattva Guanyin has come!’ Then she joined her palms and recited the Buddha’s name in a strong voice. More than an hour later she asked those nursing her to raise her up to a sitting position, facing west, and she passed away peacefully. It was the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, 1942.

Xu Huang lived at No. 6, Lane 67, Shaanxi Road, Shanghai. Though she could not read, she reverently honored the Three Jewels, her faith and vow were true and keen, and she recited the Buddha’s name without cease. She also urged her family to believe in the Buddha. In 1951, at eighty-three, she passed away at the hour of the rat on the ninth day of the twelfth lunar month. Before her passing she felt slightly unwell. She slept peacefully in her bed without the least pain, a smile on her face, her palms joined in recitation. Her family invited a recitation-aid group to recite for her. Before her death she formed the Amitābha mudra with her hands and placed it on her breast. After some time she told her family to change her clothes and set her head straight. Asked, ‘Have you seen the Buddha?’ she nodded again and again. Her spirit was clear and her eyes did not dim. Amid the sound of the great assembly’s recitation she passed away peacefully.

Wang Jiunai was a Hangzhou woman; her husband was the ninth child of his family, and so she was called. Her father Ren Qihua held office in the last years of the Qing, and afterwards kept a wine shop at Ta’ertou by the Qingbo Gate in Hangzhou. In her thirties Jiunai resolved to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name. She once went to Putuo and received the five precepts, and afterwards lived at the Yanshui Nunnery at Shentankou in the outskirts of Hangzhou. Jiunai recited the Buddha’s name with one mind and sincerely sought rebirth. In 1952, when Jiunai was already eighty, on the second day of the ninth month she felt unwell, and asked her fellow cultivators at the nunnery not to go out, and to boil water and make sugar tea as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha. She herself sat upright on her bed reciting the Buddha’s name. She joined the assembly in chanting the Amitābha Sutra, her voice full and strong, no different from ordinary times. When one stick of incense had burned she passed away with a smile. She sat cross-legged without moving, her countenance as if alive.

Huang Dechun was the mother of the upasika Wu Dewen. By nature wholly filial, she lived in the world with kindness and compassion. She pitied the suffering and relieved the poor, delighted in good and gave alms, and was praised by her neighbors. She took refuge with the Great Master Yinguang and received the five precepts. Near fifty she undertook the fast of requiting kindness, reciting the Rebirth Mantra three hundred thousand times. When that was complete she began to keep a long-term vegetarian diet. Though Dechun could not read, by diligent and bitter study she came to be able to recite the morning and evening lessons and the great Mahayana sutras — the Ksitigarbha, the Diamond, the Practices and Vows, and the Surangama. Dechun often went to the Lotus Society to sit the seven-day Buddha-recitation retreats. Whenever there was a Dharma assembly she never failed to rejoice in it. At home in ordinary times she recited the Buddha’s name with one mind. One summer day when she was eighty-four, she fell asleep in the afternoon and in a daze saw a great Buddha dwelling in empty space, so tall that the top of his head could not be seen. When late autumn came, illness of the liver and gallbladder broke out, and medical treatment brought some relief. Then she said to her daughter: ‘I am eighty-four; even if I lived to a hundred it would be nothing wonderful. Better to attain rebirth and see the Buddha — there is no need to take medicine.’ From then on she single-mindedly held the name. Her daughter, because her mother was old, wished to invite Dharma friends to recite in aid, and conveyed this to her mother. Her mother said: ‘No need to trouble anyone; I can recite myself.’ On the day of her death, at twelve o’clock at night, her breath suddenly came short and her eyes closed, but she still recited the Buddha’s name as before. Asked, ‘Is there pain?’ she answered: ‘I feel a little short of breath, but it is not hard to bear.’ Her daughter at once knelt and struck the chime, reciting the Buddha’s name aloud to aid her. Dechun, on the bed, said to her daughter: ‘Recite more slowly, and recite the four-character Buddha — it is too fast to follow.’ The family obeyed. When they had recited one or two hundred times, her mother said: ‘Light the incense quickly; many Buddhas and bodhisattvas are descending together!’ Some of the family wept, and her mother shook her hand again and again, saying: ‘Do not weep; reciting the Buddha’s name is what matters!’ The assembly recited for about ten minutes more, and she passed away peacefully with a smile. When she was encoffined, thirty-six hours later, her face was ruddy and her body soft. It was the fifth day of the tenth lunar month, 1957.

Luo Miaozhi was a Fuzhou woman who lived at the Shanjie Garden on Fengyang Road, Shanghai. When her husband took a concubine she left in anger and returned to her mother’s house. Mother and daughter together took refuge under the Dharma Master Xiaocan of the Zhenjing Lotus Society in Cihe Lane, Yunnan Road. She kept a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, and sat long through the night without lying down to sleep. On the fifth day of the twelfth lunar month, 1957, while she was reciting the Buddha’s name, she suddenly heard a voice tell her: ‘You are about to be reborn; you should make ready.’ Thereupon she stopped eating and lay in bed for several days. Her mother asked her: ‘You will not eat or drink — do you mean to wait for death by starvation?’ Miaozhi answered: ‘Not at all! I do not eat in order to cleanse my inward parts.’ Her mother bought water chestnuts and set them before the bed, urging her to eat. Miaozhi took one and ate it, saying as she ate: ‘Eat a water chestnut, gain a bodhi.’ Her mother asked the date of her rebirth, and Miaozhi said: ‘The twenty-eighth day — I shall be gone!’ Her mother said: ‘The twenty-eighth is close upon New Year’s Eve; the household will be busy, and we must also see to your last affairs — what is to be done?’ Miaozhi said: ‘Then let it be the twenty-second.’ On the morning of that day she asked her mother: ‘Is there hot water in the thermos?’ Her mother said: ‘There is none.’ Miaozhi took two bottles herself, went to the hot-water stove and bought boiling water, came home and bathed, sat cross-legged, and passed away reciting the Buddha’s name. She was forty.

Mao Dazang was of Xiyanmao in Tiantai, Zhejiang. Her mother kept a long-term fast and served the Buddha, and Dazang was steeped in it from childhood, so that right faith was awakened in her. At seventeen she married Chen Fuchu. She managed the household with diligence and thrift, was kind by nature, and relieved others in their need. She received the refuges from the Chan Master Mingguan. In middle age she adopted a vegetarian diet and practiced the Pure Land with the utmost earnestness. She urged and converted her neighbors and never wearied of it. She bore four sons and one daughter, all of whom came to believe firmly in Buddhism. Her youngest son, Lijun, passed away with such manifest auspicious signs that the Great Master Hongyi wrote his biography. In her late years her eldest son, Hailiang, brought her to live in Shanghai. Morning and evening she recited her lessons, and in old age she was more diligent than ever. In her spare time she sat in stillness, practicing contemplation. In January 1958 she fell ill. On the eleventh of February she passed away smiling, reciting the Buddha’s name. She was seventy. After cremation several dozen pale-yellow, round and smooth relics were obtained. Struck with a stone they remained firm and unbroken. She was buried at Chicheng Mountain in Tiantai.

Long Huirui was of northern Jiangsu. Her family was poor, and she was given as a child bride to a family named Zhu. At nine she entered a silk mill near the Little Mido Bridge outside the Xu Gate of Suzhou as a child worker. Her husband worked as a lineman for the Suzhou telephone exchange. In middle age, feeling the poverty and hardship of her lot and having no children at her knee, she turned to the Three Jewels for refuge, kept a vegetarian diet, and recited the Buddha’s name. She took refuge with the Great Master Yinguang and received the dharma name Huirui. She then joined the Pure Land Recitation-Aid Group founded by Lü Huiqiao of Qingyuan Lane, Mayike. She was diligent in Buddhist practice, and for decades it was as one day. Her nature was upright and she would have nothing to do with falsehood. Whenever she went up to the hall on Buddha-recitation days and met monks or lay followers whose deportment was careless, she would scold them. For this all held her in awe. To poor fellow cultivators she showed the most thorough care. In her late years her husband died of illness and her living grew harder, yet she could be content in poverty and delight in the Way, and never relaxed her practice. With the help of her colleague Zhu Chen Yuanjing her livelihood at last was free of care. From then on she recited the Buddha’s name with even greater diligence. Not long after she fell ill with diarrhea and could not rise from bed, and medicine did no good. Knowing that her Saha affinities were exhausted and the fruit of the Pure Land ripe, she asked Zhu Chen Yuanjing to come and entrusted her last affairs to her. With right mindfulness clear, her palms joined and the Buddha’s name on her lips, she passed away in the auspicious posture. It was five o’clock in the afternoon on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth lunar month, 1960. She was sixty-seven.

Zhu Xu was the elder sister of the physician Zhu Baoliang of No. 16 Madaqing Lane, Suzhou. She married Xu Zhichao of Wuxi, and husband and wife practiced the pure karma together. In 1961 she fell ill and knew she would not rise again, and charged her husband beforehand to arrange her last affairs. On the day of her rebirth it happened that Xu Jueyi came to the house to inquire after her illness, and saw her sitting on the bed facing west with no one at her side. She at once asked Jueyi to stay and recite the Buddha’s name. Jueyi struck the chime and recited the great name aloud, and she joined her voice with his. After about an hour, a smile on her face, she passed away in peace. Three days later her remains were sent to Lingyan for cremation, and there were several relic flowers.

Wang Aying was a native of Dinghai, Zhejiang, and lived at Baxian Bridge in Shanghai. From childhood she suffered from asthma, which never healed. In 1962, when Aying was sixty-three, she fell dangerously ill. At the year’s end her daughter Yajun knelt before the image of Bodhisattva Guanyin and prayed with utmost sincerity, asking that her mother’s life be extended by five years, and vowing to urge her mother to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name. That night Yajun dreamed of an old woman who led her and her mother into a temple. In the hall she saw a man in a yellow robe, wearing a ruler’s crown and tassels. The old woman bade the mother and daughter come forward and stand there. Beside them a man holding a sheet of yellow paper drew several circles on it with a writing brush. When he had finished he handed it to the crowned man to look at. The crowned man nodded, his face pleased, and gave the paper to another man, who passed it to Yajun, saying: ‘Take it!’ Then the old woman saw the mother and daughter out of the door. With that she woke. It was exactly the first day of the first lunar month. Having had the dream, Yajun went at once to her mother’s house and told Aying of it, saying: ‘Your illness is nothing to fear; five years have been added to your life. But you must keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name.’ Aying accepted her daughter’s urging and at once made the vow to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name, and her illness daily improved. On the night of the seventh day of the first month Aying dreamed that Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha comforted her in gentle words. From then on she sat cross-legged three times each day, silently reciting the Buddha’s name. She died on the first of February, 1967. At the end she had no illness and no suffering, and with a smile on her face she said to Yajun: ‘It is you who saved me. Amitābha Buddha has come now to receive me — I am going!’ With these words she passed away. A rare fragrance, rich and full, filled the room and only dispersed after some time. She was sixty-eight: she had indeed gained five years of added life. How strange!

Ding Youzhu was a native of Wujin, Jiangsu. The Ding were a great clan of the county, physicians for generations. Youzhu received the family teaching and set up a clinic in Furen Lane, Suzhou, under the sign ‘The Aizhu Medical Hut.’ He was skilled at treating external ailments and boils, and healed countless people. From the poor who sought treatment he asked little or nothing. Those whose illness was grave he had stay at the clinic for careful treatment. The cutting, the applying of medicine, the bandaging — all he did with his own hands. He once said: ‘This way, though the work is busy, I can observe the patient’s afflicted part closely and use medicine accordingly, lightening his pain and bringing him to recovery sooner.’ To those who could not afford treatment he often gave food, drink, and medicine, and comforted them with kind words to lessen their worry. To monks who came for treatment he gave consultation and medicine without taking payment. In his early years Youzhu resolved to study the Buddha, kept a vegetarian diet, and observed the precepts. The Great Compassion Mantra, the Universal Gateway chapter, the Diamond Sutra, and the Amitābha Sutra he set as his daily lesson. In middle age he took refuge with the Great Master Yinguang. He constantly urged people to recite the Buddha’s name and turn to the Pure Land, saying: ‘You should read more of the Elder Yin’s Collected Writings; every sentence is true, and it points the practitioner the way. If one does not follow it, would one not let a whole life slip by?’ In 1974 he fell ill with gout, and treatment was of no avail. Yet even in sickness he did not cease holding the name. In the spring of 1975 he recovered without medicine. On the nineteenth day of the eighth month of that year — the thirteenth day of the seventh lunar month, the yimao year — at seven in the morning, with right mindfulness clear, he passed away smiling as he recited the Buddha’s name. His countenance did not change, just as in life. He was cremated according to the Buddha’s rule. He was eighty.

Yao Daoming was a native of Wuyou Town, Yancheng, Jiangsu. He took refuge with the Dharma Master Liaoran and received the dharma name Xinghai. Earlier, when Gao Henian gave over his private house at Liuzhuang as the Zhenjie Pure Land Institute, it housed more than a hundred aged and infirm women in pure cultivation. In 1927 Daoming, entrusted by Gao Henian, took charge of all the affairs within the institute. He led the assembly in the practice of the Way and shrank from no toil. He recited the Buddha’s name with diligence and the utmost sincerity. When at times provisions ran short, he held firm with the community through the hardship, and together they weathered years of want without ever falling back. So it went for several decades. With one mind he recited the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the West. In 1977 he was eighty-six. Three months before his rebirth he foreknew the time. At eight in the morning on the twenty-seventh day of the first lunar month, with no illness and no suffering, facing west, he formed the mudra and passed away sitting.

He Xingqin lived at Huabo Bank in Suzhou. He took refuge with the Great Master Yinguang. All his life he had no kin to care for him, and shut his door and recited the Buddha’s name. The Diamond Sutra, the Universal Gateway chapter, and the other great Mahayana sutras he set as his constant lessons. At seventy-four he fell ill, and the illness lasted half a year. Reflecting on the heaviness of his karma, he held the name with ever greater diligence. Three days before his rebirth he saw Bodhisattva Guanyin appear. So he said to a Dharma friend: ‘I shall be reborn at three in the afternoon tomorrow; you may come and see me off.’ The next day, when he had bathed and changed his clothes, he sat upright in the middle of the room and asked two Dharma friends to sit to left and right, and together they recited the Amitābha Sutra. When they came to the point of single-mindedness undisturbed, he suddenly fell silent. The friends asked him to go on, and Xingqin opened his eyes a little and said: ‘To the West!’ Then he sat at ease without moving and attained rebirth as he wished.

Wu Qianxiang was a native of Shu. She was versed in the classics and histories and able in letters. Past twenty her husband died, and she kept her chastity and raised her orphaned child, turning her heart to the Pure Land. She accepted appointments at schools in Sichuan, Hubei, Zhejiang, and Shandong, lecturing on literature and history. Whenever she spoke of human life she would, with a grave and earnest manner, guide her students toward the Buddha-dharma. The school authorities were taken aback that she propagated religion, but they valued her learning and respected her character and could not dismiss her. Having taught for so long, her transforming influence was wide. Past fifty she and her female disciples, a certain Xia and others, founded a Lotus Society in Jinan, Shandong. She ate one meal a day at noon, and at midnight lay down only briefly before rising. Reading scriptures and bowing in repentance, she never relaxed her lessons. Of few desires and diligent, she followed the Vinaya throughout. She once went south from Shandong to Jiuhua, walking on bound feet a distance of two thousand li; her vow was long accumulated, and she shrank from no hardship. She had two sons: the elder she had marry and establish a family, to continue the ancestral line; the younger she had leave the world, in quest of right awakening. When the Lotus Society was founded she had her youngest son take charge of the circulation of the scriptures. When people saw a monk sitting upright among the scripture stands, majestic and utterly still, it was Qianxiang’s son. The son then suddenly fell ill and could not rise, and Qianxiang and her disciples recited the Buddha’s name day and night. When the son was about to die he said through his tears: ‘My mother is old and has toiled for me, and yet your son goes first.’ Qianxiang said: ‘You have followed me for many years, and do you still have such worldly feeling? You will be born high in the lotus ranks; do not cling to the dust of the world. Recite with one mind and go; do not grieve!’ The son wiped away his tears and passed away at peace. Afterwards Qianxiang too passed away reciting the Buddha’s name.

Dong Heqing was an employee of the ginseng and birds’-nest department of the Lei Yunshang shop on Nanjing Road, Shanghai. His wife, of a certain family, was over seventy and kept a long-term fast and recited the Buddha’s name. They lived at No. 4 Malusi New Village, where she set up a Buddha hall on the third floor. She had a daughter afflicted with mental illness, which caused her much distress. At that time the Great Master Xuyun was in Shanghai, and she went to him and took refuge. Through the Elder’s instruction her affliction suddenly dissolved, and she devoted herself to reciting the Buddha’s name. In the months before her rebirth she often saw a single red lotus, and told her husband of it. After her rebirth a rare fragrance struck the nostrils, from the ground floor up to the Buddha hall on the third, and for three months the fragrance did not fade. The neighbors all smelled it and praised her without exception.

Li Pu’an took refuge with the Dharma Master Xingci. He awakened to the impermanence of the world and recited the Buddha’s name with great reverence. His morning and evening lessons he never interrupted. He loved to grow flowers as offerings to the Buddha, and also grew many kinds of medicinal herbs to give to people to cure their illnesses. Ordinarily he was silent and sparing of words, hardworking and plain, and never contended with anyone. When he reached eighty he attained rebirth in the West on the sixth day of the twelfth lunar month. Seven days before, he had told his Dharma friends: ‘I shall soon be reborn.’ Three days before his rebirth he went alone to the Western Garden Monastery to bow to the Buddha, and sat cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name for two hours, and then had a photograph taken as a keepsake. On his return he did not leave his room again, but recited the Buddha’s name with all his heart. On the third day the family went into the room to look at him, and he had already passed away sitting propped up.

Fang Zhimi, whose original name was Keqin, was the daughter of Fang Zhikai of Wuzhong. After finishing higher primary school she worked at home and never spoke of it as toil. At twenty-one she took refuge with the Elder Yin and recited the Buddha’s name with diligence. Whenever there was a sutra lecture or Dharma assembly she would go and take her seat, through wind and rain without fail. At twenty-two she married into the Donghai family of Yushan. On the seventeenth day of the first lunar month in the yihai year, when her time came, thirty-two hours passed and she did not deliver. The doctors operated and delivered a girl. Because she had lost too much blood she lay gravely ill, but she silently recited the holy name of the Great Being. Her mother recited in aid at her side. Suddenly she told her mother: ‘In the night I dreamed of Amitābha Buddha and the two bodhisattvas, who sent out light and led me around them; my time in this world is not long.’ Then she took calm leave of her husband and her parents-in-law, and arranged her last affairs one by one, without the least sign of suffering or attachment. She only said again and again: ‘I am going!’ Then she lay down on the bed and closed her eyes, and was gone. To the very end her speech and her mind were as clear as ever.

Wang Huici was a native of Jiangyin. By nature compassionate, she delighted in giving. For herself she was extremely frugal. Toward others she was generous and forbearing, and had little habit of anger. At thirty-two she took refuge with the Great Master Yinguang and at once began a long-term vegetarian diet. Morning and evening she recited the Avatamsaka and the Lotus, and read the great Mahayana sutras and the Great Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings. On the ten fast days she shut her door and kept to her room, the great name in her hands. She was deeply humble, never displayed her own merits, and was always giving rise to shame. From fifty she kept the precept of not eating after noon. At seventy-five she built a pure chamber in Wuque Bridge Lane, Suzhou, and kept to it for three years, sitting the seven-day retreats on fixed dates, never letting her side touch the mat. At eighty-one, on the fifth day of the eleventh month, she took a chill and lay down. On the evening of the eleventh she foretold the time of her rebirth and asked people to recite the Ksitigarbha Sutra and to aid her with the Buddha’s name. All her goods she gave away in full, and she herself wore only old clothes. She rinsed her mouth with fragrant water, lay on her right side facing west, her mind clear, without the least pain, and passed away with palms joined and the Buddha’s name on her lips. Twenty-four hours later she was arranged in the full double cross-legged posture, and her legs were very supple. When she was placed in the coffin she looked as if alive.

Lin Zhang Kuanda lived on Lindun Road in Suzhou. At thirty she resolved to keep a long-term vegetarian diet. She first took refuge with the monk Xuyun and received the dharma name Kuanda. At sixty-nine she received the five precepts from the Dharma Master Xuexiang. Every night at one in the morning she rose to bow and recite. As she could not read, she devoted herself wholly to reciting the Buddha’s name, whether bowing or sitting or walking in circumambulation as she recited. Whether at leisure or busy, the sound of the Buddha was always on her lips. From the first month of the year she turned eighty-three she felt an aching pain in both legs and could not walk. It went on until the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month, when she stopped eating and drank only water; the pain ceased, her spirit improved, and she moved about as usual. Someone asked: ‘If you do not eat, how is it that your spirit is better and your body stronger?’ She answered: ‘If I told you, you would not believe me: the Buddhas and bodhisattvas often grant me food and drink.’ So it went for half a month, until the fourteenth day of the fifth month, when at a quarter past one in the afternoon she attained rebirth. Three days before, she foretold that she was going, and someone asked: ‘Where are you going?’ She answered: ‘I am going to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I have been there already and seen the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Buddha said to me: “This place is not easy to reach; you may come here and cultivate again.”’ From then on she sat constantly on her bed reciting the Buddha’s name, without the least pain. On the thirteenth day of the fifth month she charged her family: ‘Keep the incense burning without a break; many Buddhas and bodhisattvas have already descended.’ At the time of her rebirth she asked for three mouthfuls of sugar water. Her face was covered with smiles, and she recited the Buddha’s name without cease. Presently the sound of recitation grew faint and low, and she passed away peacefully.

Hu Liaochang was the second wife of Chen Xizhou of Wuwei County, Anhui. She believed firmly in the Buddha-dharma. Her husband at first did not believe, and she set forth for him the truth of cause and effect, earnestly urging him to cultivate with her, to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name, and together with her to take refuge with the Elder Yin. Ordinarily she relieved the poor and aided the distressed; whatever good work it was, there was none she did not do according to her means. Later, because Liaochang had long been ill, her body was weak and she had no wish for food or drink. One day, in the midst of reciting the Buddha’s name, she saw in a daze two youths holding a long banner on which was written: ‘The West receives and guides.’ So she told her husband: ‘This omen is fortunate for me but unfortunate for you’ — since she would go to the West and there would be no one to look after the house. She then asked four monks to chant sutras and bow in repentance for nearly a month, praying that if her allotted span were not yet run she might quickly recover, and if it were run she might quickly be reborn in the West. From then on her body and mind were at ease and glad, without the least illness or pain. So it went for a month. Afterwards she again felt unwell. Knowing that her homecoming was near, she recited the Buddha’s name with one mind, seeking swift rebirth. The whole family recited the great name for her, and monks were asked to recite in relays day and night, so that the sound of the Buddha did not break; she herself only followed it in silence. On the day of her rebirth she asked before noon that the bathing things be made ready. When she had bathed she changed her clothes and bowed to the Buddha; when she had offered incense, she returned and had her bed moved to face west and lay on her side, reciting the Buddha’s name alone, and said nothing at all about farewells. At the hour of the boar she saw the Buddha come and wished to rise and bow. They raised her up and had her sit, and with palms joined and head bowed she said: ‘There are still three recitations of the Buddha’s name; when they are done I shall go.’ The whole household, more than thirty monks and laypeople, recited aloud together, and Liaochang too recited the Buddha’s name aloud and passed away. Her face wore a smile and the room had a rare fragrance. When she was encoffined the next day, the crown of her head was warm and her feet soft, and the fragrance still remained.

Old Madam Qi was a Suzhou woman. In her fifties she was abandoned by her husband. She had no sons or daughters at her knee. Her whole life was poor and lonely and bitter, and her younger brother took her in and kept her, and there she ended her days at home. The old lady thought human life too bitter, and resolved to recite the Buddha’s name. Morning and evening she recited the Great Compassion Mantra and the Amitābha Sutra. Sometimes she joined Dharma assemblies, and as she had no money for incense she would offer rice dumplings to the assembly. Hearing a neighbor say that there was a laywoman, Wu Dewen, warm-hearted and devoted to the Way, she greatly wished to meet her. When word was sent, Wu came to call. The old lady said at once on meeting her: ‘That you can come is very good; then I need not worry that no one will see me off at the end.’ Wu gave her instruction, saying: ‘Only recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; when the conditions ripen, the Buddha will come of himself to receive you.’ She also gave her a picture of the Buddha for her to use in visualization. Wu, thinking of her poverty, brought food to her every day, and so it went for more than ten days. Another five or six days passed, and Wu asked another Lotus friend to go and look in on her. The old lady asked at once on meeting her: ‘Has Dewen come? I am about to go!’ The Lotus friend told Wu, and Wu went as promised. She had scarcely come in at the door when the old lady said: ‘I have already seen Amitābha Buddha and seen the Buddha’s light shining everywhere. Quickly help me sit up — lying down is not respectful.’ Wu said: ‘I am not strong enough to help you up; the Buddha is compassionate and will not blame you for disrespect. What matters is to recite the Buddha’s name with one mind.’ Then with her Dharma friends she raised the incense praise and recited the Amitābha Sutra, and the old lady recited the sutra with the assembly. When they came to ‘In the Western world there is the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,’ she closed her eyes and passed away.

Li Tangshi, whose given name was Siman, had lived for generations at Pingchao Township, Nantong, Jiangsu. Reared in the teachings of her family, she was by nature kind and gentle. In the hours between her household duties she would hold and recite the Buddha’s name. Though she had no fixed daily regimen, she was diligent and unremitting. Whenever a family member traveled afar or felt unwell, she would recite all the more earnestly. She was granted responses from time to time, but kept them secret and never spoke of them. In the spring of the wuyin year she fled the turmoil to Shanghai, where four years passed. Unused to the life of the city, her health declined daily; she soon fell into a deficiency of vital qi and returned to her hometown to recuperate, and gradually recovered. Yet as summer turned to autumn her illness worsened again, and Chinese and Western treatments alike proved of no avail. On the eleventh day of the tenth lunar month, at the hour of hai, she passed away quietly at the age of sixty-four. When she was critically ill her mind was clear and unobstructed: single-mindedly she recited the Buddha’s name and bade her family to chant in support of her. At the moment of death her left hand formed the Cundi mudra, and she was serene and free of pain. After the first of the tenth month she would ask those present, ‘Is it the eleventh today?’, as if she already knew when her hour would come. After she had passed, within two hours her son first saw a vapor rising from the crown of his mother’s head, spiraling gently upward, and then the whole family saw it as well.

Lady Guo, the mother of the layman Jiang Weinong, was by nature broad-minded, kind, thrifty, and respectful. She served her parents-in-law with filial devotion and helped her husband and raised her children, possessing much of the virtuous-mother bearing of ancient times. In daily life she wore no fine clothes and ate no delicacies; she liked to do everything by her own hand and never relied on others. In her later years she met with upheavals of the age and her family fortune was swept away, yet she remained at peace. She would often say, ‘All beings experience suffering; all dharmas are empty. What flourishes must fade, and what is born must die — this is the natural order. Whoever does not understand this and gives rise to vain sorrow or joy only adds to his suffering.’ From her youth Lady Guo revered Avalokiteshvara and regularly recited the Heart Sutra of Prajna. In her later years she began to keep a long-term vegetarian diet, and her chanting and worship grew ever more devout. Each day she recited the Heart Sutra seven times and the sacred name of Amitābha five thousand times. Whenever she was interrupted while reciting she would start again from the beginning, never willing to skim past it carelessly; her practice was meticulous for the most part. In the summer of 1921 her appetite suddenly failed, and she often spoke to the family of the impermanence of the defiled world. On the evening of the second day of the sixth month, seated cross-legged upon her bed, she closed her eyes, joined her palms, and said to the layman Weinong, ‘When I die, let it be just like this. Do you see that it is all right?’ In early June she drank only half a bowl of rice gruel each day and asked her son, the layman Weinong, to speak on the Amitābha Sutra; Weinong and his family took turns sitting and chanting the Buddha’s name beside her, and Lady Guo was greatly pleased. When she was sixty she had suffered from partial deafness, but now her hearing suddenly became acute, so that even a whisper in another room she could hear distinctly. On the morning of the fifteenth she said to the lay devotees chanting nearby, ‘The weather is hot; please rest a while, the hour is still early. I will not go until noon.’ At ten minutes past twelve she asked to be raised and seated, arranged her clothes and shoes herself, faced the West, joined her palms, and gazed up into the sky with a fixed smile; and so she passed away in peace. Her eyes were closed yet her smile could still be seen. She was eighty-two years old. After her passing her body was supple and her crown warm, and when she was encoffined the next day her complexion was rosy and full, like a person of some fifty years.

Madam Zhang was a native of Qingdao with one son and one daughter, and her family was poor. Her husband made his living pulling a cart at the harbor. Madam Zhang lived near the Zhanshan Hermitage in the city of Qingdao; within the hermitage there was a Buddhist Study Society, and on each Sunday Master Tanxu would come there to lecture on the sutras. Through this connection she took refuge in the Three Jewels and came to hear the Dharma. In the winter of the twenty-sixth year, one morning at dawn, she suddenly said to her husband, ‘Look after the children well. Today I shall be reborn in the Buddha-land.’ Her husband took it for a joke, made no answer, and went off to pull the cart at the dock. Madam Zhang then admonished her two sons, ‘Today I shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You two must obey your father and not be mischievous.’ The boys were still young and did not understand; they went on playing as before. Madam Zhang tidied the household, then washed her face, combed her hair, changed into clean clothes, and sat cross-legged on the bed facing West; and reciting the Buddha’s name she passed on to rebirth. When her two sons returned to the room and saw that their mother had died, they ran weeping to the neighbors’ house to give word, and the neighbors hurried over and saw that Madam Zhang had been gone for some time. Her husband returned from the dock and wept bitterly; and because the family was too poor to prepare the coffin, the lay devotees of the Buddhist Study Society pooled their funds to settle her funeral affairs. Master Daguang recorded the matter thus.

Lu Liaoshun was a native of Wuxian County who lived in Yuejin Lane, Suzhou. She was born in 1911 outside Tuanzi Jing in Lijia Township. Her family had farmed for generations, planting in the busy season and reeling silk in the slack. At seventeen she married Lu Nianxiang, who worked in the silk-weaving trade. The lady was by nature kind and gentle, thrifty in managing her household, filial to her mother-in-law, and attentive to her husband. In November 1933, while working in the fields, she was blinded in one eye by the lime dust of a pigpen, and before long both eyes went dark; no treatment could cure them. Nianxiang reflected that his mother’s ailment had been cured through sincere recitation of Avalokiteshvara, and that only by reliance on the Buddha’s power could he hope to restore his wife’s sight. So he took his wife to pay respects to the Elder Yinguang and told him the whole matter. The elder said, ‘The Universal Gate chapter states: “Spotless pure light, the sun of wisdom breaks all darkness, stills the disasters of wind and fire, its universal brightness illumines the world.” So long as you sincerely invoke the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara, you will obtain a response.’ The lady followed the elder’s instruction, resolved to eat only vegetables, and earnestly chanted the bodhisattva’s name. After seven months of this, on the third day of the sixth lunar month — the festival of Weituo (Skanda) Bodhisattva — she happened to be staying at Ruyi Convent on Zhusi Lane. When she had finished the morning service and walked out of the great hall she suddenly felt a flash of light before her eyes; looking up she could make out the rows of roof-tiles, and the peach trees by the house, heavy with fruit, she now saw clearly as well. Overjoyed beyond measure, she knew that both her eyes had completely recovered. From then on she could thread a needle and manage every household task, just as before her illness; and afterwards she also learned the two daily services. On the first day of the ninth month of 1940 she knew beforehand the hour of her coming and said that three days later, at the hour of xu, she would pass on to rebirth. And when the time came she did, lying in a peaceful and auspicious manner, at the age of thirty-three.

Lu Liaokong was a native of Lijia, Wuxian County, Jiangsu. Her mother’s family was named Que, and she was born in the thirteenth year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing dynasty. Her family had been poor farmers and lived in Yuejin Lane, Suzhou. When she was some thirty-five or thirty-six she was suddenly stricken with gout; her hands and feet contracted and could not move, and hospital treatment proved entirely without effect. Her son Lu Nianxiang, a devoted Buddhist, was able to show her filial love, and seeing his mother’s incurable illness he was greatly distressed. When the lady was forty-nine her son Nianxiang supported her to the Baoguo Monastery on Chuanxin Street, where she took refuge with the Elder Yinguang. Moved by the master’s compassionate acceptance, she was enrolled as a disciple and given the name Liaokong; Nianxiang too took refuge at the same time and was given the name Liaozhong. The elder instructed the mother and son to sincerely invoke the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara, and that in time they would surely obtain a response. After returning home the mother and son reverently followed the teacher’s instruction and ceaselessly chanted the bodhisattva’s name; and seeking his mother’s early recovery, Nianxiang cut his own arm to heal her. After nine months her illness was indeed cured, and her hands and feet could bend and stretch once more, no different from before. At fifty-six, in the renwu year of 1942, on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth lunar month, she passed away without illness. Two days before her passing she said to her son Nianxiang, ‘In two more days I shall go to the West; you must help me recite the Buddha’s name with all your heart and see me off to rebirth.’ Nianxiang did as she bade and chanted the sacred name for her, and his mother likewise chanted with utmost sincerity, the sound of the Buddha’s name unbroken; and indeed on the twenty-ninth she sat and passed away in peace.

The mother of the venerable layman Fei Fanjiu of Nantong was named Li Gui. She was a native of Nantong and lived in Pingchao Township of that county. At seventeen she married Fei Jianqing, the father of the layman Fanjiu. She managed the household with thrift and good order; and after her husband died she took refuge in Buddhism and recited the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara daily, never once ceasing even when illness and pain came upon her. Whatever the household trifles, she did herself and never employed servants. Her house had ample ground, and she turned it into a vegetable plot, planting and watering and weeding it herself and finding joy in this; around the plot she planted fruit trees everywhere. She would say, ‘Even an inch of ground should not be left waste.’ Wherever she saw a living creature on the land she forbade people to tread on it; and fruit and melons she would not let be picked until they were ripe, and once picked she first offered them to the Buddha and her ancestors before sharing them with the family. In 1938 she fled the turmoil to Shanghai, where her lodging was cramped and mean; and in the winter of 1941 she returned to her old home in Nantong. After her return she fell ill in the tenth month, and after five months of sickness passed away. Throughout her illness her mind remained extraordinarily clear. Three days before her passing she dreamed of wandering to a place where she saw majestic halls and countless jeweled trees, and she saw a lotus flower as large as a peck measure, fresh and red and lovely. When she woke she told her family, ‘Ever since I have seen this flower I no longer hold you all in my heart.’ Eight hours after her death the crown of her head was still warm. Mother Fei was born in the ninth year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty and died in the third month of 1943, at the age of seventy-four.

Chui Yuxian was from East Street, Fufeng County, Shaanxi. She took refuge with Master Liangqing at Famen Monastery and embraced the Pure Land teaching. With faith and vow she recited the Buddha’s name, and within less than three years she passed on to rebirth. Her son Ran Hengtong, a pure-hearted devotee, urged his mother to embrace the Buddha; but as she was old the mother feared she could make no attainment and could not decide. When she went to Famen Monastery to pay respects to Master Liangqing, the master knew her concern and encouraged her: ‘In the practice of Buddha-recitation there is neither old nor young; only see that you are utterly sincere, and you are sure to succeed.’ He then recounted several stories from the ancients of attaining rebirth through ten recitations. The lady believed without doubt, made her vow, and practiced diligently, never ceasing to recite. On an evening in the autumn of 1953, while she sat in a dark cave dwelling, she suddenly saw the Three Holy Ones of the West seated high above. Forgetting that she was in the dark cave, she said in great joy, ‘I have chanted the Buddha’s name so long, and only today do I see you, venerable ones.’ Before she had finished speaking the images vanished and the cave was dark again as before. The next day she asked the master about it, and the master cautioned her not to give rise to a mind of joy. When she went home she recited with even greater effort: in doing her household chores, one pull of the bellows and one recitation, one stroke of the broom and one recitation, one cut of the knife and one recitation, one turn of the spinning wheel and one recitation — and even walking along carrying a child, she never ceased silently invoking the sacred name. In the spring of 1954, on the evening of the third day of the third month, while she was performing the evening service in the cave, she suddenly saw a radiance shining through the cave, dazzling and bright. At first she thought the grandchildren were playing with fire and went to stop them; but when she stepped outside she saw the Three Holy Ones hovering in the sky, and she at once knelt and bowed. She heard Avalokiteshvara say, ‘On the morning of the eleventh I shall come to receive you.’ Knowing her hour of rebirth had come, she hastily settled her affairs, told her family to prepare a bed and seat, and had her son Hengtong take out the clothes for the dead. On the evening of the tenth of the third month, Master Liangqing came with the masters Huiming and Shaoguang and the layman Li Bingbo to assist the recitation; and on the morning of the eleventh she ended her life without illness, at eighty-three. Three hours later her crown was still warm; she sat upright and straight for a whole day and night as if still alive. The incense burned in the cave was ordinary, yet everyone smelled the fragrance of sandalwood and orchids pervading the whole room, and all held it to be extraordinary.

Mei Zhongfu was the mother of the layman Shi Chunfu. She was illiterate. She took refuge with the Venerable Master Xuyun and was given the Dharma name Kuanyi. In 1945, at seventy-one, her son Chunfu brought her to his residence in Tianjin to care for her. Chunfu was a pure-hearted devotee and had long since received the refuge and precepts from Master Cizhou. After his mother arrived in Tianjin, Chunfu urged her to eat only vegetables and recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land; the mother answered vaguely, still hesitant in mind. One night she dreamed of an old woman in white, tall and graceful, of very solemn bearing, holding a vase in her left hand and a long object in her right, coming slowly and calmly. The next morning she asked her son about it; the son showed her the sacred image of the White-robed Mahasattva, and his mother said, ‘It is she!’ From then on she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, never relenting in her constant practice. Later Chunfu established a Buddhist scriptures distribution center in Hong Kong, and in 1957 his mother was eighty-three. At year’s end Chunfu came back from Hong Kong to visit. She was suffering from cataracts and had been blind for a long time. She said to her son, ‘These past year or two I sit facing the wall. Time and again I see a broad open road, very distant; at the end of the road there is a great monastery, supremely majestic. On the road men and women, old and young, all in ancient dress, are walking calmly toward the monastery. What I see is extraordinarily clear; I often gaze on it for hours, until my eyes are quite tired before I stop.’ She also said, ‘I often dream of a great monastery, resplendent and magnificent beyond words, with Amitābha Buddha seated in the midst of the hall.’ In the months before she gave up her body she had such dreams again and again. A few days before her passing she said to her daughter-in-law, ‘I have myself seen the sublime and marvelous land of Ultimate Bliss. I tell you now so that you will record it carefully and show it to Chunfu when he returns to Tianjin.’ She also instructed, ‘Write quickly to Chunfu and tell him to get home before the seventeenth of the eleventh month, to see me off to rebirth.’ Chunfu received the news and hastened back to Tianjin, but his mother had already passed six hours before; and when he saw what his wife had recorded, and that it matched the descriptions in the Pure Land scriptures, he was all the more amazed. His mother passed away at two in the morning of a winter month in 1958. At the moment of her death her daughter-in-law was keeping watch in the room; through a haze she heard the sound of flutes and drums and music outside the bedroom, and heard someone say, ‘It is this very house.’ Suddenly a gust of wind blew the door open and she awoke with a start: the mother had already ceased to breathe. Three days later, when she was encoffined, her whole body was soft as in life.

Chen Deyi was from Suzhou; her husband’s family name was Ni. Both her father’s family and her husband’s family were chiefly silk merchants. After marriage the couple were not in harmony, yet they had one son and one daughter. In middle age she came to feel deeply the emptiness of life and that wealth and honor could never long be kept, and so by degrees she grew in faith toward the Dharma. In 1931 she went to Lingyan and took refuge with the Elder Yinguang, who gave her the name Deyi. In her daily practice she knew only to recite the Buddha’s name wholeheartedly and studied no other methods; she revered the Three Jewels and delighted in giving to others. In 1962, at seventy-two, feeling unwell, she set her mind single-mindedly on seeking rebirth in the West. At the end, amid the gathered Dharma friends reciting the sacred name in support, she was still able to join them in chanting; with clear right mindfulness she passed away peacefully.

Chen Zhiqi was from Suzhou, known to all as Old Madam Chen, and lived at No. 1 in front of the Wenshan Temple in Suzhou. She had taken refuge with Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Zhiqi; later she also took refuge with the Venerable Master Xuyun and received the name Kuanrong. The old lady had root conditions from a former life; from childhood she had known to follow her mother in reciting the Buddha’s name. In middle age her husband died, and having no children she lived very poor. By nature gentle, she could endure any hardship, loved to help others, and never stinted even in her own straitened circumstances. Every day she recited the Surangama Mantra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the Universal Gate chapter, the Diamond Sutra, and the Amitābha and other Mahayana scriptures, never once interrupting. The old lady knew well that birth and death are great matters; she practiced repentance with vigor and recited the Buddha’s name with a single mind, vowing to attain rebirth. On the twenty-sixth of March, 1974, around ten in the morning, a fellow devotee came bringing vegetables and pushed open the door. The old lady said, ‘You have come just in time; please help me wipe my body and change into clean clothes.’ At this her friend understood at once and urged her to recite the Buddha’s name. The old lady said, ‘There is no need for many words; I already know my hour has come.’ Then she burned incense before the Buddha and sat down, and sang out, ‘Cast the refuse to the East; I go now to the West.’ Having said this she passed away smiling, at the age of eighty-two.

Zhu Huiying was from Dongshan, Suzhou, and kept her chastity without marrying. From the womb she had been a vegetarian: when her mother made her eat meat she firmly refused, and her mother could not force her. She took refuge with Master Desen and practiced the Pure Land path. She was extremely poor, and her younger sister and brother-in-law gave her constant support. In 1976 she fell ill with stomach bleeding. A few days before death she saw two small children beating her legs, and wherever they struck there were bruises; knowing this was the effect of past karma, she recited the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and the apparitions disappeared. As she was about to die she saw the Buddha come, and said she must see the lotus flower before going; in a short time the lotus appeared in the empty sky, and only then did she pass away. By her last instruction her ashes were mixed with flour into balls and cast into the sea.

Xu Liaofa was a native of Wuxi, Jiangsu, residing at No. 11 Yuqing Lane on Yunnan South Road, Shanghai. She had embraced Buddhism in her youth, and in middle age her husband died; having no children, she was quite alone. The lady had great zeal for spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings. She led a society of fellow practitioners and with devout mind recited the Buddha’s name, and had made pilgrimage to famous mountains and monasteries in many places. Whenever the monastic community, or laypersons who were struggling, needed aid, she would come at once; and in tending the sick and chanting for the dying she did her utmost, sparing no toil. Her strength was very weak, and later she suddenly contracted breast cancer, yet of her own accord and heedless of danger she still tended the illnesses of others without any sign of weariness. Poor in worldly means, she lived by selling off her clothes and never asked anyone for help; and if anyone gave her goods or money she would sincerely dedicate the merit before the Buddha. Before her passing her home had nothing left on its four walls but a wooden cabinet she used for offerings. By then the breast cancer had reached its late stage, and since she also suffered from other illnesses she could not undergo surgery; knowing that medicine could no longer save her, she earnestly prayed before the image of Avalokiteshvara, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Though the diseased part had ulcerated and pus and blood flowed, she felt no pain. On the first day of the seventh lunar month of 1977, at eleven in the morning, she passed on to rebirth. She had known her hour beforehand and said that on the first of the seventh month she would go. When that day came, past eight in the morning, after she had eaten some watermelon she said to those attending her, ‘Make haste and burn incense for me — the Mahasattva’s coming has arrived.’ She asked to be raised, joined her palms, and made a bow toward the south window, invoking the sacred name of the Mahasattva. After a moment she lay down again, and those attending her all chanted the sacred name intently. The lady said, ‘Please lower your voices and recite more slowly, or I shall not be able to keep up.’ The neighbors on either side all came to look; her lips moved slightly, and her countenance was as usual. They said among themselves, ‘Old Madam Xu is still reciting.’ Little did they know that the lady had already, amid the sound of recitation, passed on to rebirth in peace. She was seventy-one.

Li Huiguang was from Suzhou, Jiangsu, living at No. 4 Hexiadang in Suzhou; her husband’s family name was Song. She bore one son, who died just at twenty. Grieving deeply over the impermanence of the defiled world and the manifold sufferings of life, she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and embraced the Buddha, taking refuge with Master Yuanying of the Yuanming Lecture Hall in Shanghai, who gave her the Dharma name Huiguang. Later she also took refuge with the Tiantai master Venerable Jingquan, and with the Suzhou bhiksuni Runtian. In her life the lady delighted in charity and was especially reverent toward the monastic community. Each day, besides the morning and evening services, she recited the Lotus Sutra, and for several decades never once missed a day. In her later years her circumstances were poor and her health failing, but she never stopped reciting the Buddha’s name. She was used to hardship and endurance, and when she saved a little from her household expenses she would give it to those she saw in poverty. A few days before the Spring Festival of 1959 she felt slightly unwell. On the morning of New Year’s Day, Nun Runtian came to visit; the lady said, ‘Please place some fruit as an offering before the Buddha’s image.’ And she added, ‘When I pass on, it is best that no one be by my side, so as not to disturb me; I shall recite the Buddha’s name myself.’ On the second day of the new year, at eleven o’clock and five minutes, she passed on to rebirth. A moment before she said to those attending her, ‘Please light a stick of incense for me before the Buddha.’ And having spoken, she lay still and silent; when they looked, she was gone. After she passed, the Dharma friends gathered and recited the Buddha’s name, and for five days and nights the sound of recitation did not stop. When she was carried to the cremation her complexion was rosy and her face wore a smile. By her last instruction her ashes were made into balls and cast into the pond of releasing life at the Western Garden, thereby forming a bond with the water-dwellers. She was eighty-two.

Yang Chenian was from Xizuo Village, Fufeng County, Shaanxi; her husband’s family name was Zhao. At twenty-four she lost her husband and resolved to keep her chastity and filial virtue in the Zhao household. She served her in-laws well and did her utmost in filial devotion, raising her husband’s brother’s children as her own. She lived in harmony with her sisters-in-law, restrained herself, bore labor without complaint, and dealt with relatives, friends, and neighbors with gentleness and courtesy, never contending; everyone called her virtuous and kind. By nature she loved quietness and delighted in performing good deeds. She took refuge with Master Liangqing, who taught her the Pure Land practice; and so she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, hoping to be reborn in the Pure Land. She practiced diligently, never relaxing by day or night, for more than thirty years. In November 1980 she took to her bed; although she could no longer kneel and bow or chant, she still sat in stillness cultivating contemplation. In the first ten days of the twelfth month her long illness gradually healed, and she resumed bowing and chanting as usual. But she said to her family, ‘Do not think my illness is mending — without fail I shall go West in the first month.’ Since her limbs were light and easy, the family did not pay much attention. Her nephew’s wife, Li Fengxia, who had root conditions from a former life and loved her aunt dearly, invited monks to hold a seven-day retreat in prayer that the aunt’s calamities be dispelled and her life extended. On New Year’s Eve the altar was purified and the session began, the four assemblies gathering. The lady alone tidied her clothes and her stores, giving them away to relatives, friends, and the monks, and asked them to assist in chanting for her at death; moved, they all consented. On the night of the fifth of the first month of the next year, around eleven o’clock, the lady suddenly asked the group to rest, and said that at six the next morning she would surely go West; the more earnestly they chanted. The next day, exactly when the clock pointed to six, she sat upright and straight, and amid the sound of the Buddha’s name passed away in calm. She was seventy-six. Three hours later the top of her head was still warm, her limbs were supple, and her bearing was serene, as in life. After her passing some of the family dreamed of a man affixing a certificate of merit to the door, and some dreamed of a man offering five-colored flowers before her portrait.

Tang Quennlang, whose Dharma name was Jingxiu, lived in Zhangjia Residence, north of Chengqiao on Chongming Island, Shanghai, and made her living spinning yarn. After marriage she bore no children of her own and adopted a son and a daughter. When the son grew up he was of a vicious temper, showed her no filial devotion, and tormented her in every way. Tang had taken refuge in the Three Jewels and devoutly practiced, never once skipping the morning and evening services. During the Cultural Revolution religious policy was destroyed, and this son repeatedly snatched away his mother’s prayer books and beads, handing them to the rebel faction as evidence of guilt, so that she suffered great persecution. Having taken vows to refrain from killing and to eat only vegetables, she was yet forced by this son to eat meat. Unable to bear the abuse, she once left home and entered a home for the aged; but since it was inconvenient to keep a vegetarian diet there, she returned home. In her extreme suffering she once contemplated suicide. Someone counseled her, ‘A disciple of the Buddha should not take his own life; one who kills himself must be full of hatred and countless other afflictions and loses the right mindfulness of Buddha-recitation. Not only will he fail to be reborn in the Pure Land, but he will fall into evil destinies. You must endure with boundless patience, keep reciting the Buddha’s name, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.’ Tang heeded these words and accepted what came with resignation; in her harsh circumstances her faith grew all the firmer, her longing for the Pure Land and renunciation of the world became all the more earnest, and her vegetarianism and recitation became all the more vigorous. On the fourteenth day of the third lunar month of 1981 she was still in good health at lunch, but by evening her daughter discovered that Tang had already sat and passed away in a small room. What was especially remarkable: the seat had no backrest, yet Tang sat upright and straight, her countenance as if alive. She was seventy-eight.

Wu Zhengguo was the third daughter of Mr. Wu Baohe of Yanling. At twenty-one she married into the Du household. Being too poor for a home of her own, she lodged in the Wu household of the same village; and she was content there, never once repining in the least because she had been born into wealth. Though she lived in poverty, she disciplined herself in hardship, diligent and thrifty, saving up her earnings little by little; and after more than ten years she finally built herself a house. When she moved, her landlord, unable to part with her, wept as he saw her off, and she wept too. Ever afterwards, at every festival she would prepare gifts to show her regard, never forgetting the kindness of having been lodged there. Throughout her life the lady was upright, kind-hearted, of humble and gentle disposition, hardworking and thrifty, and glad to help and give. She was filial to her mother-in-law, strict in raising her son, and gracious with her neighbors, so that she was praised throughout the village. From childhood she had revered the Three Jewels, and from age forty she kept a long-term vegetarian diet. At sixty-eight she followed her son Taifeng to Jiangpu and settled at Dufeng, where she formally took refuge in the Three Jewels and received the Dharma name Zhengguo. From then on she was resolved and never stepped beyond the door; apart from her daily work she had only Amitābha in mind. Past ninety she was still as clear-minded as anyone, and at ninety-four she even grew three new teeth, a thing indeed strange. On the tenth of January 1985, catching a slight cold, at seven in the evening she felt mildly unwell; in a while she recovered and lay on her left side. At half-past eleven in the night, in the stillness when all sounds were hushed, amid the recitation in support of her, she passed away in peace. The next day, when they changed her clothes, her limbs were supple, her lips and cheeks rosy, and her face as in life: her eyes closed, her mouth shut, as if in sleep. On the third day she was placed in the jar, and on the seventh day, when the round was completed, the funeral pyre was lit. From the cremation were obtained five-colored relic flowers: over twenty green ones, some ten yellow, a few pieces of a green hue, some ten red, and one white one as large as a jujube. All who saw them marveled, and those who knew declared this was proof of her rebirth. The lady was born on the fifteenth of the second month of 1890 and lived ninety-four years. Master Yuanche composed a verse in praise:
A hundred years, a finger-snap, and all is gone; the sudden news of death was ever well foreknown.
Blest that in this very life she attained release — her jewel-relic flowers now bless the unknowing many.

The mother of the layman Cai Chu’ang was from Zhenjiang, Jiangsu. She was virtuous and refined and lived a hard, simple life. The layman Chu’ang lost his father at thirteen; his mother kept her widowhood and raised her orphan, teaching her son to become a man. The layman served his mother with the utmost filial devotion: whenever she was displeased he would kneel long before her until her heart was happy again before rising. Mother Cai originally knew nothing of Buddhism. At sixty-five, through Chu’ang’s earnest persuasion and his explaining the general meaning of the Dharma, she began to believe and to recite the Buddha’s name. At seventy-two she suddenly fell ill, took to her bed for nearly ten days and nights, and ate very little. Chu’ang invited many Dharma friends for his mother, who took turns chanting for ten days and nights. On the ninth day Mother Cai suddenly opened her eyes and said, ‘Tomorrow at noon I shall pass on to rebirth in the West.’ And indeed at noon the next day, chanting the Buddha’s name in peace, she passed away. More than ten hours after her death the top of her head was still warm.

Old Madam Wu of Shanghai lived in the lane beside the Buddhist Study Society on Changzhi Road. By nature kind, she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name. Three years before her death she learned to recite the Lotus Sutra, one scroll a day, and at other times she would recite the Buddha’s name. Later she suffered from a back ailment and could not leave her bed, yet she never ceased her sutra-chanting and recitation. Her husband and daughter did not believe in Buddhism and mocked her as deluded. At the time of her death her husband and daughter were at her side when they suddenly saw Avalokiteshvara appear — now the whole body, now half the body. Filled with joy and wonder, they all knelt and bowed. The old lady saw them and said, ‘So today you too believe!’ Having said this she closed her eyes and passed away.

Han Yeshi was the wife of the layman Han Huazhong, president of the Shaoxing Buddhist Study Society of Zhejiang. She was originally from Xiaoshan. In her thirties she began to keep a vegetarian diet and serve the Buddha. At forty she journeyed to Putuo of the South Sea and took refuge with Master Jingwu of Fayu Monastery, receiving also the Five Precepts and the Eight Precepts of fasting. She made pilgrimage to Putuo five times in all, and also made pilgrimage to the Guoqing Temple at Tiantai. She joined the Shaoxing Buddhist Study Society and went often to recite the Buddha’s name. Seven days before her death she dreamed of a bodhisattva whose fingers emitted light, and within the light appeared the image of Amitābha Buddha; and seven days later, joining her palms and sitting cross-legged, she passed away reciting the Buddha’s name. She was fifty-seven.

The layman Xiao Houzhai of Hangzhou had a daughter, whose name is forgotten. When the girl was born, her mother dreamed of an old woman holding a baby and giving it to her, and telling her it was a girl. As she grew she was extraordinarily clever, loved to handle brush and ink, and delighted in sketching and painting. She had great faith in Buddhism and was very diligent in revering the Buddha and reciting the sutras. At twenty-one she suddenly fell ill, and long treatment could not cure her. In that same year, on the nineteenth day of the second lunar month — the festival of Avalokiteshvara — she passed on to rebirth. After her death a strange fragrance filled the room and did not waft away for days.

The daughter of the layman Chen Yiren, whose name is forgotten, kept a long-term vegetarian diet from childhood and knew the path of Buddha-recitation. At nineteen she knew of herself that her hour of rebirth had come, and her mother invited many Pure Land friends to chant the Buddha’s name and see her off to rebirth. The girl then said, ‘I have already seen Amitābha Buddha, seated upright with palms joined, ready to pass into stillness.’ Among those chanting there was a bhiksuni who repeatedly stroked the girl’s head with her hand and had her mother place silver in the girl’s mouth, this being the custom of the time. Her mother was chanting and waved her hand to decline, but the nun went on chattering endlessly. At that the girl suddenly cried out sternly, ‘My going to the West is ruined! It is all this nun’s doing. I had seen the Buddha come to welcome me, and I grasped the sleeve of the Buddha’s robe with my right hand and was rising into the sky toward the West. Though I had gone with the Buddha, I could hear your recitations and all your actions with perfect clarity. This nun touched my head with her hand and told my mother to put silver in my mouth; the moment I heard it I was displeased, and before I knew it the thought stirred, and Amitābha Buddha vanished.’ Her father, the layman Chen Yiren, hearing this, said, ‘This is a great pity indeed, but it is no obstacle. You have the merit of years of practice. Make haste and diligently keep the sacred name, and you will surely attain rebirth as you wish.’ The girl heard her father’s words, repented wholeheartedly, and continued chanting the Buddha’s name for seven days. When the seven-day session was complete she once again saw Amitābha Buddha appear before her; then she sat upright, joined her palms, and amid the sound of recitation passed away with a smile.
